0.title: The Magna Carta of Christian Liberty: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
0.overview:
Paul wrote to the Galatians in a state of controlled fury. He was angry not for himself but for them — and for the gospel. Every other letter he wrote to a church opens with thanksgiving or blessing to God; Galatians has neither. He moves immediately, in the very first verse, to defend his apostolic authority, and by verse 6 he is in open astonishment: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel.” The urgency that presses through every paragraph of this letter was born of Paul’s conviction that the gospel itself was at stake — not a peripheral issue but the very core of what he had preached and what they had received.

The crisis had been created by a group scholars call the Judaizers — Jewish Christians who insisted that faith in Christ was necessary but not sufficient. Gentile believers also needed to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic law in order to be fully accepted by God and fully included in God’s people. This seems, on the surface, like a minor addition: faith in Christ plus a few religious practices. But Paul saw it with total clarity for what it was: a fundamental contradiction of the gospel. If anything in addition to Christ is required for justification — even something God-given and ancient like circumcision — then Christ is no longer sufficient, grace is no longer free, and the cross is no longer enough. “If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21).

Where were these churches, and when did Paul write? Galatia was both an ethnic region in the north of Asia Minor, settled by Celtic tribes, and a Roman province that also took in the southern cities of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Some think Paul wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, whom he may have visited on his later journeys (Acts 16:6; 18:23), and date the letter in the mid-50s. The more likely reading is that he wrote to the southern churches he founded on his first journey (Acts 13–14): Paul normally used the Roman provincial names, and Acts tells us plainly about those churches and nothing about any in the north. On that reading the letter was written around AD 48, just before the Jerusalem Council, which would explain why Paul never mentions the Council’s decision (cf. 2:1). It may well be his earliest letter. Its message does not depend on the answer.

Galatians is structured in three movements. Chapters 1–2 are autobiographical: Paul defends the divine origin of his gospel (he received it not from men but from Jesus Christ directly) and recounts his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, where the gospel’s logic was at stake in a table-fellowship dispute. Chapters 3–4 are theological: Paul argues from Scripture (Abraham, the covenant, the law’s purpose, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah) that the gospel of grace by faith preceded the Mosaic law by 430 years and is not superseded by it. Chapters 5–6 are practical: the freedom of the gospel is not license for the flesh but the only true basis for life in the Spirit and love for the neighbor.

Martin Luther’s Commentary on Galatians (1535) is among the most celebrated commentaries in the history of the church. He called this letter his “Katie von Bora” — his beloved, the one he was married to. For Luther, Galatians was the text that articulated what the Reformation was about: the righteousness of God is not a demanding standard to be met but a free gift to be received. Justification is by faith alone, in Christ alone, by grace alone. Anything added to that formula is a subtraction from it.

Read Galatians as the most passionate defense of free grace in the entire canon. Every person who has ever felt that their standing before God depends on their performance needs to hear it. Every church that has drifted toward moralism — toward making the Christian life about spiritual self-improvement rather than trust in the finished work of Christ — needs to be dragged back to Galatians and made to sit with it until the gospel is clear again. Paul wrote it because the gospel is always under threat, and the threat almost always comes from the same direction: the desire to add something to Christ, to make grace a little less free, to make human effort a little more decisive. Galatians says: no. The cross is enough. Christ is enough. Grace is enough. “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

1.title: No Other Gospel: The Divine Origin of Paul’s Message
1.overview:
Galatians opens with a defence of Paul’s apostleship and, almost at once, a curse: anyone, even an angel from heaven, who preaches a different gospel is under God’s judgment, and Paul says it twice (vv. 8–9). The severity has a simple reason. If the gospel could be changed by human authority, by apostles, tradition or church consensus, it would be a human message, and a human message cannot save.

Paul then makes his case from his own life. He did not get his gospel from the Jerusalem apostles but received it by revelation from Jesus Christ, and his conversion and his slight contact with Jerusalem in the years that followed show it. It is the same gospel the other apostles preach, but its authority rests on Christ, not on their endorsement.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by stressing that his apostleship came directly from Jesus Christ and God the Father, not from any human source, the very point his opponents disputed. His greeting already gives the gospel in a phrase: Christ gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, as the Father willed, and the glory is God’s.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace begins with God

Verses 3–5 are among the earliest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament, and they show that salvation starts wholly with God. The Son gives himself freely; he gives himself for our sins; he rescues us out of an evil age rather than improving us within it; and he does it by the Father’s will. That rules out two mistakes. One makes the cross a late repair to a plan that went wrong, but Christ was delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

The other sets a stern Father against a merciful Son, as though mercy had to be pulled out of heaven by the death of Jesus. Verse 4 forbids it: the Father willed the giving and the Son gave himself, one in love toward sinners. Grace is God’s own first move, and it ends in glory to God (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had received a complete gospel and were being told it was only a foundation that needed a second storey. Paul’s opening answers that before the argument starts: his apostleship came straight from Christ (v. 1), others stand with him (v. 2), and the gospel of vv. 3–5 leaves no gap for a human contribution.

Now: The same instinct survives wherever the gospel is treated as the way in and something else as the real substance of the Christian life: a sacramental record, a moral achievement, an intense spiritual experience. Christ gave himself, the Father willed it, and nothing remains to be added.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead— and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians is Paul’s most urgent letter, written to defend the heart of the gospel: sinners are justified before God, that is, declared righteous by him as judge, by faith in Christ alone, not by keeping the law of Moses. After Paul planted churches in Galatia, teachers came insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law to be truly saved. Chapter 1 sets the stage. The greeting already says that Paul’s apostleship came straight from Christ, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us (vv. 1–5). Instead of a thanksgiving comes astonishment that they are turning to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all, and a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches another (vv. 6–10). Then Paul shows that he received his gospel by revelation from Jesus Christ, not from any human being: his former life as a zealous persecutor, his call by grace, and his independence from the Jerusalem apostles all prove it (vv. 11–24). The chapter that opens with a curse on every rival gospel closes with the churches of Judea glorifying God for what grace had done to their worst enemy.

The setting. Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey), the inland high country. Many think Paul wrote to the southern Galatian churches he planted on his first missionary journey: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13–14), perhaps around AD 48–49, before the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, which would make Galatians perhaps his earliest letter. Others think he wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, later, around AD 55. The message is the same either way. These were Paul’s own congregations. In Lystra he had been stoned, dragged out of the city and left for dead (Acts 14:19). He had bled for these people.

No warm-up. The credentials arrive in the first breath, jammed into the opening line, and they are not modest. An apostolos is one who is sent, an envoy carrying the authority of the person who sent him. A king’s messenger does not improve the message or soften it to suit the room he is standing in; he delivers it, and he answers to the throne, not to the audience. That is the office Paul is claiming in his opening words, and everything in the next five chapters depends on whether the claim is true.

Not from men nor through man. Two small prepositions doing very large work. Not from men: no human authority is the source of what he preaches. Nor through man: no human being was even the channel of his appointment. Paul closes both doors at once, and he closes them before he has told us why they need closing. Somebody in Galatia had evidently been describing him as a second-hand apostle, a man who got his gospel from Jerusalem and quietly dropped the awkward parts along the way. Paul simply refuses the description in his opening sentence.

Through Jesus Christ. Christ commissioned him directly on the Damascus road (Acts 9:15; 26:16–18). And look where Christ stands in the sentence. Paul has just denied that any man was the source of his apostleship, and then he names Jesus Christ as its source, side by side with the Father. If Jesus were merely a man, the sentence would make no sense. Paul does not pause to argue for the deity of Christ. He assumes it in his grammar.

Who raised him from the dead. It reads like a devotional flourish. It is load-bearing. The Twelve were commissioned by a Jesus they had walked beside for some three years, eaten with, watched. Paul was commissioned on a road outside Damascus by a Jesus he had never met, and the only thing that makes that a commissioning rather than a hallucination is that the man is alive. Take the resurrection out of the sentence and Paul is a zealot with a story. Leave it in and he is precisely what he says he is (Acts 9:3–6; 1 Corinthians 9:1). The resurrection is God’s seal on Christ’s work, and the risen Christ is still the one who sends.

To the churches of Galatia. He is angry, and he is not alone. Whatever is about to be said in this letter, a company of Christian men are saying it with him. This is not one man’s grievance dressed up as doctrine. Then the address, and it is bare. No “to the saints.” No “beloved.” No word of praise. Just the destination, written the way you would write it on the outside of an envelope. The situation is too serious for compliments.

Why does it matter where Paul got his gospel? Because a message is only as reliable as its source. If Paul’s gospel came from the Jerusalem church, then the Jerusalem church could correct it, and the teachers in Galatia could claim to be bringing the fuller, official version. If it came from the risen Christ, nobody may correct it, not Jerusalem, not a council, not a modern scholar, not your own feelings on a bad day. When you open Galatians you are not reading one early Christian’s opinion among many. You are reading the message the Lord himself gave to his apostle, and it carries his authority over you.
verseByVerse.note: Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor. Many think the letter went to the churches Paul founded on his first journey — Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe; others think of ethnic Galatians farther north.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to you and peace. Paul is still in the address, and he has already preached the gospel. A Greek letter opened with chairein, greetings; a Jew said shalom, peace. Paul seems to take the first word, bend it into its cousin charis, grace, God’s free and undeserved favour, and set the Hebrew blessing beside it. Two worlds greeted each other daily with these words and meant almost nothing by them. Paul fills them again. And the order never reverses in his letters. Grace first, then peace. Peace, the wholeness of being right with God, is not the price of admission; it is what grace leaves behind it. In a letter about to fight for grace, the first word of blessing is grace.

From God and the Lord Jesus. One source, two persons. Grace is something only God can give, and Paul names Jesus as its giver alongside the Father without any sense that he has said something daring. For him it is simply true.

Who gave himself for our sins. The gospel in a phrase, and the pronoun is deliberate. Not who was given. Not who was taken. In the garden there were more than twelve legions of angels within reach and a Roman detachment that drew back and fell to the ground at his word, and he handed himself across (Matthew 26:53; John 18:6). Nobody prised the Son of God out of the Father’s hand. He walked forward. As he said himself, no one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18).

For our sins. Not for our disadvantages, our wounds, our unrealised potential. For the thing that is actually wrong. And the little word “for” carries the whole weight of the cross: to atone for them, in our place, on our behalf, the innocent standing where the guilty should have stood (1 Corinthians 15:3). Not our works but his self-giving deals with sin. And this is exactly what the teachers in Galatia were quietly undermining. If Christ gave himself for our sins, then nothing remains to be added; if something must be added, then he did not finish what he gave himself to do. Paul puts the answer in his greeting before he has stated the problem.

To deliver us. The verb is exaireō, to snatch out, to rescue, the word Peter used when the Lord rescued him from Herod’s prison (Acts 12:11). It is the picture of a rescue party pulling a man out of a burning building, not a renovation crew improving the building. Much Jewish teaching divided all of history into two: this present age, and the age to come when God would put everything right. Paul says the age to come has already broken in, in the risen Christ, and believers have already been hauled out of the old one while still walking around inside it. The present evil age is this world under sin, Satan and death (Ephesians 2:2). And the law, as a way of standing before God, belonged to the old age; going back to it is going back into the building Christ pulled you out of.

What the present evil age looks like. The phrase sounds like a line from a hymn. It is the age in which a scan comes back with bad news. In which a marriage that began with vows ends with lawyers. In which children are trafficked and old men die alone in wards, and the news is the same news every year with different names. It is also the age in which your own heart quietly prefers itself to God on a Tuesday morning. That is what Christ gave himself to pull people out of: not only its sorrows, but its guilt and its grip.

The Father’s will. Paul will not let anyone think the cross was a rescue plan improvised late, or that a reluctant Father had to be talked round by a loving Son. The Son’s self-giving was the Father’s will. The cross was the Father’s plan from before the foundation of the world (Acts 2:23; 1 Peter 1:20). The Father is not one degree less loving than the Son; he never was.

To whom be the glory. And so the greeting cannot finish itself. It breaks off into worship. Paul has not written a line of his argument, and already he cannot get through his own opening without stopping to adore. This doxology is also the argument in miniature. Salvation by grace gives all the glory to God. Salvation by works, even partly, would share the glory with us, and a gospel that lets man take a bow has stopped being this gospel.

If Christ has rescued me from the present evil age, why is my life still so hard? Because the rescue has happened in two stages, and you are living between them. You have already been delivered from the age’s guilt, its condemnation and its claim on you: sin is no longer your master, and death is no longer your end. But you have not yet been delivered from its presence. You still get ill, still grieve, still fight temptation, still live in a world that does not love Christ. The age to come has begun in you, by the Spirit, and will arrive in full when Christ returns. Your hardships do not mean the rescue failed. They mean the rescuer has not finished, and he will.

Does “for our sins” really mean in our place? Yes. Paul will say it outright in 3:13: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. He bore the penalty our sins deserved, so that we would not bear it. This is called penal substitution (penal because it concerns the penalty, substitution because he bore it in our place), and it is not one theory among many but the heart of what Scripture says the cross accomplished (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Some sincere Christians are uneasy with it, fearing it pictures an angry Father punishing an unwilling Son; but this very verse rules that out, since the Son gave himself according to the will of our God and Father, one in love and purpose. Christ’s death also defeated the powers and showed us God’s love, but it does those things precisely because it first paid for sin.

On a Tuesday. When your conscience accuses you, notice which way you instinctively look: back at your own week, to see whether it was good enough, or up at the one who gave himself for your sins. The Galatians were being taught to look at themselves. Paul’s greeting points them, and you, at the cross before a word of argument, and you come to God after a bad week exactly as you came the first time.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Instead of thanksgiving, Paul expresses astonishment that the Galatians are so quickly turning from the God who called them by grace to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all. Anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one they received, even Paul or an angel, is under God’s curse. And he is not seeking human approval; if he were, he would not be Christ’s servant.
verseByVerse.theology:
The gospel stands over the church that preaches it

The double curse of vv. 8–9 means the gospel is not the church’s property, to be developed by councils or refined by consensus. A message that human authority gave could be amended by human authority. So Paul puts himself and even an angel under the same test he asks the Galatians to apply: not the standing of the teacher but faithfulness to what was first delivered. Luther saw in these verses the controversy of his own century.

Paul’s own practice shows that the curse is not aimed at every disagreement among Christians: he allows real freedom on food, days and disputable matters (Romans 14). What cannot be renegotiated is the ground of acceptance with God. And no one may edit this gospel because it was bought, not drafted: the curse had already fallen on the Son, who redeemed us by becoming a curse for us (3:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The troublers in Galatia were very probably sincere, and saw themselves as the ones taking the Old Testament seriously. Circumcision was God’s own ordinance and the law was God’s gift. Their error was that they had turned the relation of law and grace upside down, which is why verse 10 matters: sincerity was never the test.

Now: A different gospel rarely announces itself. It presents itself as the fuller, more serious version. The question this passage teaches is whether a teaching changes the ground on which a sinner is accepted by God, or only touches a secondary matter Christians have long disagreed about. And for someone with a mother or brother in such a church, the curse falls on the one preaching, not on the people being misled.

verseByVerse.quote: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The loudest silence. Every other letter Paul wrote to a church begins with thanksgiving or blessing. The Corinthians were tolerating a man sleeping with his father’s wife and getting drunk at the Lord’s Table, and they still got a thanksgiving. The Galatians get this. It is the loudest silence in the New Testament letters, and the first readers would have heard it instantly, the way you hear it when someone who always greets you by name simply starts talking.

In the flow. Here Paul names the problem the whole letter exists to answer. Verses 1–5 have given the true gospel in a phrase, Christ gave himself for our sins; now Paul names its rival. Everything after this is his reply. The rest of chapters 1 and 2 shows that his gospel came from Christ, not from men; chapters 3 and 4 prove from Scripture that a person is right with God by faith and not by the law; chapters 5 and 6 show how people set free by grace actually live. The letter begins with the Galatians walking away, and it ends by calling them to stand firm in the freedom Christ has won (5:1).

I am astonished. The Greek thaumazō can mean wonder at something glorious or bewilderment at something absurd; here it is plainly the second. It was also a standing formula in ancient letters of rebuke (I am astonished that you have not written), so the readers heard both the shock and the reprimand folded into one word.

So quickly. Not years. Paul had been there. He had preached, they had believed, the Spirit had come, and by the time this letter was written they were most of the way to something else, whether soon after their conversion or soon after the false teachers arrived. The gospel’s hold on a human heart is more fragile than we like to assume, and a church can be evangelical on paper and drifting in practice inside a year.

Deserting. The verb metatithēmi is the word for changing sides: a soldier crossing to the enemy lines, a politician turning his coat, a man transferring his loyalty from one commander to another. It is not the language of a slightly mistaken opinion. It is the language of defection. And it is in the present tense: they are in the act of deserting. The door is still open behind them.

Him who called you. This phrase is the heart of the charge. They are not deserting a doctrine. They are deserting a person: God himself, who called them. You cannot leave the gospel of grace behind and keep the God of grace; he does not come apart from his message. Every step away from grace is a step away from the one whose grace it is, however religious the walk looks from outside.

The grace of Christ. And grace here is not a substance or a mood; it has a face. Paul has already said in his greeting what the grace of Christ is: he gave himself for our sins (1:4). To be called in the grace of Christ is to be summoned into the shelter of a finished gift, a cross already borne and a debt already paid. That is why Christ plus anything distorts the gospel rather than supplementing it. Every addition says that his self-giving left something undone, and asks the Galatians to complete what the Son of God, dying, declared was finished (John 19:30).

Does this mean that true believers can desert Christ and be lost? No. Paul writes to the Galatians as to people he believes are Christ’s: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view (5:10). Their danger was real, and the warning is the means God uses to bring them back; but those who are truly his do not finally fall away (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). The warnings of Scripture are not a contradiction of perseverance. They are one of the ways God makes his people persevere: the same God who promises to keep them uses the alarm to wake them. The point of no return is the danger a church faces when it keeps the words and changes the gospel, not a sentence already passed on these believers.

Who were the troublers? They are usually called Judaizers, and since the word appears in almost every book about this letter it is worth saying plainly what it means. They were Jewish Christians who professed faith in Jesus, honoured the Scriptures, and taught that Gentiles who came to Christ must also take on the marks of the Jewish law, circumcision above all, along with the food rules and the sacred calendar, before they could be counted as full members of the people of God and truly saved (Acts 15:1, 5). Faith in Christ, and then also this. Not Christ instead of Moses. Christ plus Moses. They would have described themselves as the conservative party, the ones taking the Old Testament seriously.

A different gospel. Paul’s verdict on Christ-plus-anything is surgical. Two Greek words sit behind the phrase, and English blurs them. Heteros can mean another of a different kind, and allos another of the same kind, though Paul does not always keep them rigidly apart. Either way, what they are moving to is not a second version of the good news. It is not good news at all, and it is not a rival gospel, because there is only ever one.

Trouble and distort. “Trouble” is tarassō, to stir up, unsettle, throw into confusion: the word used of the stirred-up water of the pool in John 5:7 and of the disciples’ troubled hearts in John 14:1. “Distort” is metastrephō, to turn a thing inside out, to reverse it. That is the point a reader must not miss. Adding law-keeping to grace does not top grace up. It inverts it. The moment my acceptance depends even one per cent on my performance, the whole structure has flipped: God is no longer the one who justifies the ungodly but the one who audits the diligent, and I am back keeping score.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the false teachers denied Christ entirely. They added to him. That is precisely what makes it another gospel: Christ plus something. The most dangerous error is rarely the one that throws Christ out. It is the one that keeps him and gives him a partner.

What does Christ-plus look like today? Rarely circumcision. More often it is a list of things a Christian must also do or be before he is properly accepted: a particular experience, a particular church, a sacrament treated as the ground of salvation, a standard of personal devotion, a set of cultural rules about dress, drink, music or schooling. Many of these things may be good in their place. The question is whether they have quietly moved from being the fruit of acceptance to being the condition of it. You can usually tell by asking what you think of a believer who lacks them. If the answer is second-class Christian, the plus has arrived.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers had come insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A curse, written twice. Accursed is anathema. In the Old Testament an anathema was something placed under the ban, devoted to God for destruction and not to be salvaged: Jericho and everything in it, Achan and the silver under his tent (Leviticus 27:28–29; Joshua 7). To be anathema is to be handed over to the judgment of God. There is no stronger word available to him. He does not reach for it about the immorality in Corinth; when the word appears in that letter, it falls on anyone who has no love for the Lord (1 Corinthians 16:22). He reaches for it here, because a false gospel does not merely damage lives; it destroys souls.

Even if we or an angel. The two examples are chosen to be impossible. Even if we: Paul puts himself first in the line of fire. If the man who planted these churches came back through Galatia next spring with a revised message, the Galatians are to consign him to the judgment of God rather than believe him. Or an angel from heaven: not a demon in disguise, but heaven’s own courier, glory and all. The gospel does not take its authority from whoever carries it. It stands over its messengers, and Paul is one of them.

I say again. Verse 8 could be dismissed as temper, a man saying something enormous in the heat of the moment. So he says it again in cold blood. He may simply mean the sentence he has just written, but more likely he had told them this face to face on an earlier visit, before the trouble started. He is not losing control. He is repeating a settled verdict, and the second time he drops the hypothetical altogether: not “even if,” but if anyone is preaching. Someone is.

Contrary to the one you received. The test is not novelty or eloquence or results. It is the gospel they received: the apostolic gospel, now preserved for us in Scripture. Everything that claims to be Christian preaching is measured against that, and nothing measures it.

Why the gospel cannot be revised. The gospel is not a philosophy that later minds might improve. It is news: the report of something God has done in history. Paul gives its shape elsewhere: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, he was buried, he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). An angel can no more amend that than he can roll the stone back across an empty tomb. What happened at Golgotha and in the garden on the third morning stays happened. That is why Paul can curse a rival message without quoting its wording: any gospel that adds to Christ’s finished work is announcing something that never took place, a Christ whose death was not enough. That is also why insisting on one gospel is not arrogance. Reporting what happened is not boasting, and this report humbles the one who carries it, because it says he could not save himself either.

Where Christians differ: how serious is false teaching? Many today treat doctrinal differences as unimportant, as long as people are sincere. Verdict: Paul shows that changing the gospel itself, especially adding works to faith as the ground of justification, is a matter of eternal life and death. Not every disagreement is a matter of the gospel; Christians may differ charitably on secondary matters (Romans 14). But on the way of salvation, there is no room for compromise. Justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone is the article on which the church stands or falls.

Does every doctrinal disagreement fall under this curse? No, and Paul’s own practice proves it. He allowed real latitude on food, on holy days, on matters where believers see differently (Romans 14). What he anathematises is a gospel contrary to the one received, and the whole letter tells us exactly which question he means: on what ground is a sinner accepted by God? Church government, the details of the last days, the mode and subjects of baptism: Christians have argued these for centuries without either side being outside the faith. Change the ground of acceptance from Christ’s finished work to anything a person contributes, and the argument is no longer inside Christianity.

Does this include those who claim new revelation from an angel? Yes, and it is the plainest test the Bible gives. Joseph Smith said the angel Moroni led him to the Book of Mormon; Islam teaches that Gabriel gave the Qur’an to Muhammad. Paul anticipated exactly this: even if an angel from heaven should preach a different gospel, the messenger is cursed and the message rejected. No later revelation, however supernatural its claimed source, may contradict the gospel the apostles preached, whether it is claimed by an angel or by a church authority. Paul warns elsewhere that even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).

And what of churches like Rome? The test is the one Paul gives. The Council of Trent taught that a person is justified by a righteousness God pours into him, received in baptism and increased by good works, and it condemned those who teach that we are justified by faith alone. That teaching falls on the wrong side of Paul’s line. Yet the Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches also confess the Trinity, Christ’s deity, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, and many of their members trust Christ alone in spite of what their church teaches. The curse falls on the false gospel and those who preach it, not on everyone who sits under it, and our part is to make the true gospel plain to them.

Is Paul saying my mother is accursed? This is the question that actually keeps people awake. You have a mother in a church that teaches something like this, or a brother who has gone somewhere that adds requirements to Christ. Read the sentence again and see who is in it. Let him be accursed: the one preaching. The anathema falls on the teacher who corrupts the gospel, not on the troubled congregation being taught. And we know what Paul calls the Galatians themselves, because he tells us three chapters later: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth (4:19). Those are not the words of a man consigning them to destruction. They are the words of a mother in labour. The severity is aimed at the wolves precisely because he loves the sheep. Pray for your mother, love her, and gently show her Christ alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may curse people personally. Paul pronounces God’s judgment on those who corrupt the gospel; he does not authorise us to call down private vengeance. Our response to false teachers is to warn, refute and pray for their repentance, remembering that Paul himself was once a persecutor of the gospel and received mercy.

Should I leave a church that preaches a different gospel? If a church has made something other than Christ’s finished work the ground of a sinner’s acceptance, and its leaders will not be corrected, then yes: you should find a church that preaches the gospel, because you and your children need to be fed and not starved. Do it without bitterness, after honest conversation, and not over a secondary matter. A church with weak preaching, poor music or a pastor you disagree with on the millennium is not under this verse. A church that has changed the gospel is.

For worship. Why is Paul willing to place himself and an angel of God under a curse to keep this message intact? Because of what it cost to obtain. There was already an anathema in this story before Paul ever used the word, and it did not fall on a false teacher. It fell on the Son. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (3:13). He stood where the ban falls, under the wrath that Jericho met and Achan met, and he did it to buy this gospel for sinners at the price of himself. That is why nobody may edit it. It is not Paul’s to amend. It was paid for, and it is perfect.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — handed over to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? The question is probably an echo of what his critics were saying about him. The charge seems to have been that Paul was a crowd-pleaser: a travelling preacher who had noticed that circumcision was a hard sell in a Gentile town and had quietly dropped it to fill his meetings. His answer is the passage they have just read. A man trying to please people does not pronounce a curse on angels in his third paragraph. The verb behind “seeking the approval” is peithō, to win someone over, to talk them round. Am I, he says, canvassing for human votes or for God’s?

In the flow. Verse 10 looks both ways: back to the curse, which no crowd-pleaser would pronounce, and forward to the defence that runs to the end of chapter 2, where the story of his life proves his gospel came straight from Christ. Whose approval matters is not a side issue in Galatians: it is exactly the pressure that would move Peter from one table to another at Antioch (2:12).

The scars are the argument. He has a second answer, which he gives later in the letter and which settles the matter completely: if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? (5:11). If pleasing people had been the aim, keeping circumcision was the obvious move. It would have delighted the synagogue, defused the opposition, and kept him out of prison. The man-pleasing option was the one he refused. The stones of Lystra had left marks on him, and scars like these he calls the marks of Jesus (6:17).

Or am I trying to please man? “Please” is areskō, to make oneself agreeable, to aim at someone’s satisfaction. And the little word “still” in the next phrase is a confession. There was a time when he did live to please people: in his former life he arranged everything around the approval of his teachers and his nation’s leaders (1:14). Not any more.

I would not be a servant of Christ. The word is doulos, slave: owned, not employed. And that is the logic. A slave has one master. To need the approval of the room is to have taken a second owner, and no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). A slave of Christ lives for his master’s approval, and his master’s approval is the only one he needs. And this master first took the form of a servant himself and went down to a slave’s death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8). A man owned by him has no need to buy approval anywhere else.

How the crisis actually worked. Bad theology usually travels on the back of a longing to be approved of. It was not really an argument about theology that a Gentile believer in Galatia lost; it was the ache of being told, by impressive religious men from the mother church, that he was a second-class Christian, and the enormous relief on offer if he would just submit to the knife and be counted properly. Everyone has a face whose disapproval is hardest to bear, and the Judaizers had found the Galatians’.

The arithmetic of grace. That is why Paul’s freedom here is not toughness of personality. It is the arithmetic of grace, and the comfort is on the reverse side of the warning. A man whose acceptance is still being decided must manage everybody’s opinion of him, because any one of them might be the verdict. A man already accepted in Christ has had the verdict handed down in advance, in his favour, at the cost of the cross, and every other opinion in the world has been demoted to an opinion (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Proverbs saw it long ago: fearing people sets a trap for the feet, and trusting the LORD is the only safe place to stand (Proverbs 29:25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about people. He became all things to all people, that by all means he might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). He adapted his manner, his customs and his approach. But he never changed the message to please them. Nor does it mean tact is a sin or that being liked is wrong. Paul tells Christians to please their neighbours for their good, to build them up (Romans 15:2). The line is crossed when someone’s approval becomes the thing you cannot live without, and the truth bends to keep it.

How do I get free from the fear of what people think? Not mainly by trying harder to stop caring, which usually just makes you anxious about your anxiety. Start by naming the specific person and the specific thing you have softened or left unsaid to keep their approval. Then bring it to the cross and remind yourself what God has already said about you in Christ: accepted, forgiven, his child, and not on probation. The more that verdict fills your sight, the smaller every other one becomes. Then take one small step of obedience you have been avoiding, and notice that you survive their frown.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul now argues from his own life, in order of time. The gospel he preached is not a human message: he was not handed it or taught it, but received it by revelation of Jesus Christ (vv. 11–12). The evidence follows: his violent and successful past in Judaism (vv. 13–14); God’s setting apart, calling and revealing of his Son, with the commission to the Gentiles in the same breath (vv. 15–16); and years spent far from Jerusalem, with only fifteen days with Peter and a meeting with James (vv. 17–19). He swears to the truth of it (v. 20), and ends with the churches of Judea, who did not know his face, glorifying God for the persecutor turned preacher (vv. 21–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
Chosen, called and shown the Son

Verses 15–16 are among Paul’s most compact statements of God’s free grace. Three acts of God stand in order, and Paul starts none of them: God set him apart before birth, called him by grace, and was pleased to reveal his Son in him. The call is effectual, God’s summons that brings about what it calls for, not an invitation waiting for a reply; the last thing Saul intended on that road was to become a Christian. And the revelation is in him, inward as well as outward: he had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Grace that reaches a man riding the other way with warrants in his bag is not a reward for seeking (Romans 8:29–30; Ephesians 1:4–5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s critics could point to his absence from Jesus’ earthly ministry and his late arrival among the apostles. His answer is the record of vv. 17–22: Arabia rather than Jerusalem, three years, a fortnight, two men, then years in Cilicia, unknown by face to the churches of Judea.

Now: A shameful history made into evidence for the gospel (vv. 13–14), a calling that began before the one called was looking (v. 15), and hidden years that turn out to be part of God’s work (vv. 17, 21–22): each of these reaches an ordinary believer directly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I would have you know. A formula: gnōrizō, I make it known to you, the phrase a writer uses to flag the thing he most wants remembered. And he calls them brothers. He has just spoken of angels under a curse, and the next word out of his mouth is a family word. He is fighting for them, not with them.

Not man’s gospel. The claim comes in three parts, and each closes a door. Not man’s gospel: kata anthrōpon, literally not according to man, not measured by a human standard, not shaped to a human taste, not invented by a human mind. Then not received from any man, and not taught.

The vocabulary of the rabbis. Those last two verbs are the exact vocabulary of the world Paul came from. Receiving and being taught were how a rabbi was made: tradition passed down hand to hand, master to pupil, from the school of Hillel to Gamaliel to Saul of Tarsus (Acts 22:3), every link named and verifiable. It was the most respectable pedigree a Jewish teacher could have, and Paul had it. He is saying that the machinery which made him a Pharisee had nothing whatever to do with this.

A revelation of Jesus Christ. “Revelation” is apokalypsis, unveiling, the pulling back of a curtain. The phrase can mean a revelation from Jesus or a revelation about Jesus, and Paul most likely intends both at once, because on the Damascus road they were the same event: the risen Christ pulled back the curtain, and what was behind it was himself. Christ revealed it to Paul there and in the years afterwards.

In the flow. The rest of chapter 1 and most of chapter 2 argue the claim made here, that the gospel came from Christ himself: his former life, which no man could have converted; his years away from Jerusalem; his fifteen days with Peter; the meeting where the pillars added nothing; and the clash at Antioch, where he corrected Peter himself by this gospel. And the claim carries the weight of the whole book. If justification by faith (2:16) were Paul’s own idea, it could be bargained over. Because it is Christ’s revelation, it cannot.

Received, or not received? A careful reader will feel a problem here, and should. Writing to Corinth, Paul seems to say the opposite in almost the same words: I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received, that Christ died, was buried, was raised and appeared (1 Corinthians 15:3–5). Received from whom? Plainly from the church before him. So which is it? Both, and they are not in conflict. What Paul received from others were the facts on the ground: the dates, the burial, the names of the witnesses, the sort of thing anyone in Jerusalem could have told him and which he very likely heard from Peter over those fifteen days. What no one gave him was the meaning of those facts and his commission to carry them. He knew perfectly well before Damascus that a man called Jesus had been crucified; he was persecuting people over it. What he did not have, and could not be taught, was that this crucified man is the Son of God, that his death is the end of the law as a way of acceptance, and that Paul himself was to take that news to the nations.

Should I expect God to reveal his truth to me directly, as he did to Paul? No, not in that way. Paul was an apostle, and the revelation he received was foundational: it was given once, through the apostles and prophets, and it is now written down for the whole church (Ephesians 2:20; Jude 3). The canon is closed. What the Spirit does for you is not to give new revelation but to open your eyes to the revelation already given, so that you see Christ in the Scriptures and believe (1 Corinthians 2:12; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is not a lesser thing. The same Christ who unveiled himself to Paul on the road unveils himself to you in the pages Paul wrote.

On a Tuesday. A gospel that comes from human consensus can be amended by human consensus. One that comes from the revelation of Jesus Christ cannot be amended by anyone, because nobody in the discussion outranks him. So when the culture, a bestseller, or your own doubts suggest that the old message needs revising for modern people, you are free to say no.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My former life in Judaism. Paul now produces his own past as evidence. They had heard: it was the first thing anyone in the Christian world knew about him. Judaism here means the Jewish religion and way of life as he had practised it, in its strictest form.

Persecuted the church of God. He gives three details, and each is worse than the last. The phrase behind “violently” is kath’ hyperbolēn, from which we get hyperbole: beyond all measure, past the point where anyone was keeping count. And tried to destroy it: the verb portheō is what an army does to a city it intends to leave uninhabitable, ravage, sack. Not to intimidate the church. To finish it. And whose church it was matters. The church of God. He was not fighting a sect. He was fighting God.

Why are you persecuting me? The risen Lord had already told Paul what it meant to attack the church of God. On the Damascus road the voice did not ask why he was persecuting the disciples. It asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). Christ is so joined to his people that a blow aimed at the least of them lands on him. Every door Saul kicked in and every name he wrote on a warrant struck at the Head through his body. And the one he was wounding was the one who stopped him, not to repay him, but to call him.

The pictures Luke supplies. Saul going house to house, dragging off men and women and committing them to prison; the detail about women is not decoration, it tells you the thing had stopped having limits (Acts 8:3). Saul casting his vote against believers when they were put to death. Saul going from synagogue to synagogue trying to make them blaspheme, and following them to foreign cities because Jerusalem was not enough, in raging fury against them, as he put it himself to Agrippa (Acts 22:4; 26:10–11). There were families in Judea who still lived with what he had done.

Advancing in Judaism. The third detail is the one that makes the argument. The verb prokoptō means to make progress, to get ahead: the word for a career going well. He was not a failing religious man looking for something gentler. He was winning. Trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), ahead of his contemporaries, on a fast track, and by every standard he recognised he was succeeding. That is the uncomfortable point for every respectable person. Religious success can keep a heart further from God than open rebellion, because a man who is winning sees no need to be rescued, and Paul later counted all his gains as loss for Christ (Philippians 3:4–8).

Extremely zealous. “Zealous” is zēlōtēs, a zealot, and the word had history: Phinehas with his spear, Elijah at Carmel, the Maccabees in the hills. The traditions were the oral law of the Pharisees, the fence built around the law of Moses (Mark 7:3). And that is exactly why he brings all this up. The suggestion in Galatia was that Paul’s gospel was a softened Judaism, the religion trimmed down for people who could not manage the whole thing. His answer: look at who I was. Nobody drifts from the top of a system he is winning at, into a message that got him flogged, because he wanted an easier life. No human could have converted such a man. Something had to happen to him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean zeal is bad. Paul was zealous before and after; the problem was what the zeal served. It means zeal for the wrong cause is deadly, and sincerity is no guarantee of truth. Saul was entirely sincere on the road to Damascus. He was also entirely wrong, and he had blood on his hands to prove it.

Does my past disqualify me from serving God? No. Some reader carries a history he has never said out loud: something done at twenty-two, something a family still lives with, something that surfaces at three in the morning and argues that whatever else grace is for, it is not for that. Paul had helped to kill Christians, and God made him an apostle. Your past may have consequences that are real and must be faced honestly; some offences rightly bar a man from certain offices, and wrongs must be put right where they can be. But your past cannot put you beyond forgiveness, and it cannot stop God using you. Often he uses exactly the history you are ashamed of to show others what his mercy can do.

On a Tuesday. Think of the most hostile unbeliever you know, the one who mocks your faith or has hurt people you love, and pray for his salvation today. Saul was the last man in the world the church expected to see converted, and the church had been taught by its Lord to pray for those who persecuted it (Matthew 5:44); Stephen died praying that this sin would not be held against his killers (Acts 7:60), and Saul was standing there.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he. The sentence has been building since verse 13, and now it turns. Everything before this was Paul acting. Everything from here is God acting, and there are four verbs, and not one of them belongs to Paul: God set apart, God called, God was pleased, God revealed.

Set apart before I was born. Literally, from my mother’s womb. Before. Before the zeal, before the persecution, before the promising young man in Gamaliel’s classroom, before there was a person there at all to be either good or bad. The language deliberately echoes the prophets: before I formed you in the womb I knew, and before you were born I consecrated you (Jeremiah 1:5), and the Servant of Isaiah 49:1 who was called from the womb. Election is God choosing freely, before a person exists, whom he will save and what he will give them to do. Here it is Paul’s appointment as an apostle, and the same freedom stands behind every believer’s salvation (Ephesians 1:4).

The separated man. There may be a quiet play on words here that the first readers would have caught. “Set apart” is aphorizō, to separate or appoint, and the word Pharisee most likely comes from a root meaning the separated ones. Paul had spent his adult life separating himself: from Gentiles, from the unclean, from the careless, by rigorous effort, and it had made him the most dangerous man the church knew. God’s reply is that he had been set apart before he separated himself from anything at all, and set apart, of all things, to go to the Gentiles.

Called by his grace. Not who called me because of my zeal, or in spite of my record, or on account of anything visible at the time. By his grace: the call had no cause outside God, and Paul deserved the opposite. And this is a call that does what it says. God’s call in Paul’s letters is not an invitation left on the table awaiting a reply; it is the effectual summons that raises the dead man who is being summoned (Romans 8:30). The last thing Saul intended, riding to Damascus with warrants in his bag, was to become a Christian.

Pleased to reveal his Son. Eudokeō: it was God’s good pleasure, his delight. Not a duty discharged. The Father took pleasure in showing this man his Son. Read that with Acts 9 in view: at the moment Paul is described as still breathing threats and murder against the disciples, God is described as glad. And the phrase is more intimate than most translations can carry: literally, to reveal his Son in me. Not merely a bright light on a road, an external event Paul witnessed and later reported. Something opened on the inside. God shone in his heart to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). He had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Now the Son himself was unveiled within him, and everything he already knew rearranged itself around a living person.

To preach him among the Gentiles. The commission arrives in the same breath as the conversion (Acts 9:15; 26:17–18). There is no gap, no probationary period, no question of what this is for. He was not saved and then, later, given something to do. He was set apart for it before he was born. And note what he was to preach: him. Not a system, not a programme, but the Son.

I did not consult. Literally, I did not confer with flesh and blood. He did not go to human authorities for interpretation or approval. The revelation needed no second opinion.

Is this about every believer, or only Paul? In the first place it is Paul’s own call to be an apostle, in words that echo Jeremiah. But the same pattern holds for every believer: God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4) and calls them by grace (Romans 8:29–30). Not every Christian is called to be an apostle; every Christian was chosen before he was born and called by grace.

Where Christians differ: did God choose those he foresaw would believe? Some Christians hold that God’s choice rests on his foreknowledge of who would freely trust Christ. Others hold that God’s choice rests on his own free grace alone, and that faith is the result of election, not its cause. Verdict: election is unconditional. Paul’s own case is the strongest answer: what God foresaw in Saul was a persecutor, and grace called him anyway. Elsewhere Paul says God chose us that we should be holy, not because we were (Ephesians 1:4–5), and that the choice was made not because of works but because of him who calls (Romans 9:11). Brothers who hold the other view love the same Christ; but the verse in front of us puts the whole initiative with God.

Did I choose God, or did God choose me? You can settle it here without a word of philosophy. Ask a simpler question than the usual one: on the day it happened, was I looking for him? Paul was not merely uninterested; he was riding in the opposite direction with legal authority to arrest the people who loved the name. If grace reached him there, then grace is not a reward handed to the seekers, and you need not audit the sincerity of your own first steps to find out whether you are safe. You did choose Christ, really and gladly; but you chose him because he first chose you (John 15:16). The question is not who moved first. The answer to that is already in the verse.

If God chose people before birth, why should I evangelise? Because God’s choosing works through the preaching of his Son, and this very verse says so: he revealed his Son in Paul in order that Paul might preach him among the Gentiles. Election is not a reason to keep quiet. It is the reason preaching works. You do not know who the elect are, so you tell everyone; and you tell them with confidence, because God has people he intends to reach, and the hardest heart in your street is no harder than Saul’s was.

On a Tuesday. On the days you doubt that God could want you, go back to the verbs. Not one of them depends on you. He set you apart before you were born; he called you by his grace; he was pleased to reveal his Son to you. If your standing rested on your seeking, it would be as unsteady as your seeking. It rests on his pleasure, and his pleasure is not moody.

For worship. Before the world had a Saul in it to hate the church, the Son of God had already been appointed to be revealed to him. The Father set him apart, and called him, and was pleased, delighted, to unveil his Son to a man on his way to do harm in the name of religion. Heaven was not scandalised by Saul of Tarsus. Heaven had made arrangements for him before his mother knew she was carrying him. This is what the grace of God is like, and it has never once been embarrassed by the material it was given to work with.

parallels.desc: the LORD called me from the womb

verseByVerse.quote: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nor did I go up to Jerusalem. If his gospel had come from the Twelve, this is where he would have gone, immediately. Newly converted, freshly commissioned, with no Christian instruction behind him and a lifetime of persecution to explain, every instinct says go to headquarters. He did not go for authorisation. He went the other way. And “before me” is chronological, not hierarchical: they were apostles earlier, not higher.

Into Arabia. Arabia here is not an empty desert of sand dunes, whatever the paintings suggest. It means the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus: a real state with towns, trade routes and a capital at Petra, ruled by King Aretas (2 Corinthians 11:32). Why Arabia? Perhaps for prayer and rethinking the Scriptures in the light of Christ. Perhaps to preach, and Paul lets slip elsewhere what may have followed: the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize him, and he escaped through a window in the wall, lowered in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:32–33). Kings do not post guards for men who have been quietly meditating. Some also connect it with Mount Sinai, which Paul places in Arabia (4:25), as Elijah went there to meet God (1 Kings 19:8). Then he returned to Damascus and preached boldly in its synagogues that Jesus is the Christ, until a plot forced him to flee (Acts 9:19–25).

Three silent years. Paul gives the span himself: three years (1:18) between the road to Damascus and the first conversation with Peter, in which a man of extraordinary gifts, freshly given a commission to the nations, is almost off the map. Scripture does not say what happened in those years, and it is better to admit that than to fill it in. What is certain is that the Paul who wrote Romans did not have Romans in his head on the Damascus road. Somewhere between the light and the letters, the whole of the Old Testament was rebuilt around Christ in that mind, and Paul names no teacher but Jesus Christ himself (1:12). The nearest picture Scripture gives is the Emmaus road, where the risen Lord, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interpreted to two disciples the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The Pharisee who had read the Scriptures all his life now found them full of the one he had been hunting: the seed promised to Abraham, the suffering Servant, the son of David.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Acts is wrong in not mentioning Arabia. Acts 9:23 says that after many days had passed the Jews plotted to kill him, leaving room for it. Luke tells the story he needs to tell, and Paul supplies the detail his argument needs.

The hidden years are part of the work. There are believers whose lives feel like a waiting room. The gifts are there and nothing is being asked of them. The training was done and the door never opened. Illness took the decade that was supposed to count. Scripture’s pattern runs the other way so consistently that it is almost the rule. Moses had forty years in Midian minding another man’s sheep after Egypt and before the burning bush. David was anointed king as a boy and spent the following years hunted through caves. Joseph went from the dream to the throne by way of a pit, a false accusation and a forgotten promise in a prison. And the Son of God himself spent about thirty years in a workshop in a town of no consequence, and about three in public. The hidden years are not the delay before the work. They are part of it, and generally the part that makes the rest possible. The apostle who could write I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content (Philippians 4:11) did not learn it by accident.

What should I do in a season when I feel unused? Do the next faithful thing in front of you, and do it as to the Lord. Read Scripture and pray, not to earn the next assignment but because the God who is preparing you is worth knowing for his own sake. Serve in the small ways that are open: the visit, the meal, the child in Sunday school, the colleague who needs a kind word. Ask mature believers whether there is something you are not seeing. And refuse the lie that God has mislaid you. A season without visible fruit is not a season without God’s work; he is often doing in you what he will later do through you.
verseByVerse.note: Arabia here is the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after three years. Three years. Fifteen days. Two men. Paul is counting, and every number in the sentence is doing work. He does eventually go to Jerusalem; his case would collapse if he pretended otherwise, and he is not pretending. He is dating it. Three years after his conversion, probably about AD 35–36, not three weeks.

To visit Cephas. The verb translated “to visit” is historeō, from which we get history, a rare word found nowhere else in the New Testament. It means to go and see a person in order to get to know them, to make the acquaintance of someone worth meeting, to enquire. It does not mean to be examined, trained, or commissioned. He went to meet Peter, not to be certified by him, and perhaps to learn about Jesus’ earthly ministry from an eyewitness, not to receive his gospel. Paul calls him Cephas here and in most of the letter, though 2:7–8 has Peter: it is simply Peter’s name in Aramaic, the everyday language he and Paul spoke. Both words mean rock, the name Jesus himself gave him (John 1:42).

Fifteen days. The length is the argument. Fifteen days is long enough for two men to talk themselves hoarse. It is nothing like long enough to train an apostle; a rabbinic apprenticeship took years, not a fortnight.

One would like to have been in that house. Peter had denied the Lord three times beside a charcoal fire and been restored beside another one (John 18:18; 21:9). Paul had hunted down the people Peter was pastoring. Neither man had a past he could be proud of, and both had been handled by the same mercy. Whatever else those fifteen days contained, they very likely contained the eyewitness accounts: Peter describing what it was like in the boat, in the courtyard, on the shore, and a man who had never seen any of it listening to every word.

James the Lord’s brother. This is Jesus’ own brother, raised in the same house in Nazareth, and during the ministry he did not believe: for not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). Then his brother was killed, and then, we are told in a single line, he appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). Whatever passed between them, that meeting turned an unbelieving brother into the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; 21:18) and the author of a letter that calls himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ (James 1:1). It takes something considerable to make a man worship the boy he grew up beside.

Was James Jesus’ full brother? The plain reading is that he was a son of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus, and so his half-brother, since Jesus had no human father. The early church developed other views, that he was Joseph’s son by an earlier marriage or a cousin, to protect the belief that Mary remained a virgin, but the New Testament never suggests either. Many Christians through the centuries, including some of the Reformers, held one of those views, and faithful believers still differ; nothing in the gospel turns on it. And Paul’s except James probably shows that he counted James among the apostles in a wider sense; the risen Christ had appeared to him, and he became the leading elder at Jerusalem.

Does Paul contradict Acts? One honest difficulty should be faced here rather than stepped over. Luke’s account of the same visit says Barnabas brought him to the apostles, plural, and that he went in and out among them at Jerusalem (Acts 9:27–28). Paul says he saw none of them except James. Is one of them wrong? Most likely not, and the best explanation lies in ordinary speech rather than special pleading. Luke is summarising a visit in two verses and uses “the apostles” the way anyone uses a collective term, Peter and James being, between them, the most prominent figures of that circle and its recognised leadership. We do the same thing constantly: a man who met the Prime Minister and the Chancellor says he met the government. Paul, whose whole argument depends on the precise number, gives the precise number. The other apostles were probably elsewhere. The accounts are answering different questions, and both answers can be true. Believers hold both accounts true, and this is the likeliest way they fit, even if we cannot reconstruct every detail of the visit.

Did Paul and Peter preach the same gospel? Yes, and Paul says so: whether it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed (1 Corinthians 15:11). The point of these verses is not that Paul had a different gospel from Peter but that he had the same gospel from the same source. Two men, one a fisherman and one a Pharisee, received it independently from the same risen Lord, and when they compared notes they found they were preaching the same Christ. That is not a weakness in the evidence. It is one of its strengths.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. James the Lord’s brother led the church in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before God, I do not lie! Paul stops the narrative, turns to the reader, and swears an oath. He is halfway through a plain account of dates, places and names, and he breaks off to call God as his witness that he is not making it up. Nobody does that unless something is at stake.

He was being called a liar. Paul was not merely arguing with people of different opinions. A rival account of his life was circulating in the Galatian churches: apparently that he had been taught and authorised by Jerusalem and had then departed from their teaching. Somebody had told these congregations a different story about where their founder got his message, and the story was sticking. So Paul swears before God that his account is true.

Did Jesus not forbid oaths? There is a fair question here for any reader who knows the Gospels. Did the Lord not say do not take an oath at all, and let what you say be simply yes or no (Matthew 5:34–37)? Does James not repeat it (James 5:12)? And here is an apostle swearing in writing. Look at what Jesus was actually forbidding. The system in view was one where oaths had become a sliding scale of honesty: swear by the temple and you may wriggle out; swear by the gold of the temple and you are held to it (Matthew 23:16–22). The whole apparatus existed so that a man could indicate how much of what he was saying he intended to stand behind, which meant that his ordinary word was worth nothing. Christ abolishes the scale. A disciple’s plain yes is to carry the full weight of an oath, always.

A solemn witness, not a sliding scale. That is not what Paul is doing. He is not grading his own truthfulness; he is under formal accusation, testifying to the truth of a matter on which souls depend. Scripture is not embarrassed by that kind of solemn witness. The same Paul does it more than once (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23), and God himself, having no one greater to swear by, swore by himself to guarantee a promise (Hebrews 6:13–17).

The faithful witness. Behind Paul’s oath stands his Lord’s. When the high priest said, I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God, the Lord who had forbidden careless oaths answered under oath, and his true answer was the sentence that sent him to the cross (Matthew 26:63–66). A lie would have saved his life. He would not tell one. Scripture calls him the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), and Paul, under accusation, is walking where his Master walked: telling the truth before God when it costs him, because the truth in question is Christ himself.

May a Christian take an oath in court? Yes. The Reformed confessions, the 1689 London Baptist Confession as well as Westminster, teach that a lawful oath is part of religious worship, in which a person solemnly calls God to witness what he asserts, and that it may rightly be taken when lawful authority requires it in a weighty matter (Westminster 22.1–3; 1689 23.1–3). Swear only to what you know is true, and only when the matter is serious. Some Christians, from tender conscience, prefer to affirm instead of swearing, and most courts allow it. Either way, the point is the same: you are speaking before God, and you speak that way every day.

The tell is what he protects. Paul does not defend his character: no wounded paragraph about years of service, no list of what these churches owe him. He swears to one thing only: the facts of where the gospel came from. That restraint is the tell. A man defending his reputation protects his reputation. Paul lets his name take whatever damage it takes and puts the oath where the danger actually is, because he is not the thing under threat. If the Galatians conclude that Paul is unimpressive, nobody is lost. If they conclude that the gospel is a human product, everything is.

On a Tuesday. Speak the truth as before God, always, because you always are before God, and the Spirit of truth lives in you. Notice the small untruths that ease a day along: the exaggeration in the story, the excuse that is slightly more flattering than the reason, the I’m fine.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Syria and Cilicia. The point is still the distance. Syria included Antioch; Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus, where he was born (Acts 22:3). Which is to say Paul went home. Luke fills in why: the Hellenists in Jerusalem were seeking to kill him, so the brothers brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus (Acts 9:29–30). And then Luke leaves him there, and the book of Acts simply carries on without him, until Barnabas, some years later, goes to Tarsus to look for him and brings him to Antioch (Acts 11:25–26).

The years nobody reported. Add up the years between and it may be as many as ten, years with no recorded sermon, no named convert, no letter, no church we know the name of. He was preaching (v. 23), and he may have founded the churches of Syria and Cilicia that the Jerusalem Council later wrote to (Acts 15:23, 41). But the New Testament does not consider the details worth reporting, which is a striking thing to be true of the man who wrote a quarter of it. The years in Cilicia produced no headline, but they produced the apostle to the Gentiles.

Unknown in person. Literally, unknown by face. The churches in Judea, the very congregations he had once hunted through, would not have recognised him if he had walked past them in the street. That is the argument. These are the churches closest to Jerusalem, most saturated with apostolic teaching, most likely to have shaped a young convert’s theology. If Paul’s gospel had been absorbed from that world, its members would at least have known what he looked like. They did not. He could not have been their student or their representative. He was, to them, a name in a story.

That are in Christ. Paul describes those churches with care: not the churches of Jerusalem’s region, or of the apostles, but the churches of Judea that are in Christ. Being in Christ is not a vague sense of closeness. It means being joined to him by faith, so that what is true of him is counted true of everyone joined to him: his death is their death to sin, his righteousness their standing before God, his Father their Father (Romans 6:4–5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That is the only place where what happened next could have happened. The families Saul had broken and the man who broke them now stood before God on exactly the same ground, and it was not their own.

Someone who hurt me has become a Christian. Must I now be close to him? You must forgive him, and you should rejoice that God has saved him; that is what the Judean churches did. But forgiveness is not the same as restored trust, and it does not require you to put yourself back in harm’s way. God did not send Saul to live among the families he had wronged. Where a wrong was serious, and especially where there has been abuse, it is right to keep wise distance, to let the church and, where needed, the authorities deal with what must be dealt with, and to let trust be rebuilt slowly, if at all. You can bless a man from a distance. God often does his healing work on both sides without asking you to stand in the same room.
verseByVerse.note: Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus.

verseByVerse.quote: They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They only were hearing it said. Paul had not seen these churches. But something had reached them, and Paul preserves it: the actual sentence they kept repeating about him. The tense is continuous, the report going round and round the villages of Judea, told again at every gathering the way a church tells the story it cannot get over. They knew Paul only by reputation, and the reputation had changed.

He who used to persecute us. Mark the word us. The report is passed between the very people he hunted: families who had lost someone, congregations that had scattered, men and women who had been dragged out of their homes by the man now being described. “The faith” here means the gospel, the content of what Christians believe, the thing itself. The man who set out to make sure this message did not survive is now the one carrying it across the empire. It is one line long, and it is the whole gospel: a before and an after, a total change the man did not manage himself, and evidence in what he now does rather than in what he says.

They glorified God. Then the last verse of the chapter lands somewhere nobody would have predicted. Not: and they were reassured about my credentials. Not: and they admired my transformation. The literal phrase is that they glorified God in me. They looked at what had become of Saul of Tarsus and they worshipped. He was, to them, a piece of evidence about God, and the evidence made them praise.

In me. They are the same two words Paul used of his conversion: God was pleased to reveal his Son in me (1:16). What the churches of Judea glorified God for was the Son revealed in that man. They did not see a reformed character; they saw Christ living in a former persecutor, and they knew that no one but God could have put him there. That is what a converted life is: not a self improved, but a life in which Christ has taken up residence and begun to show. Christ by his Spirit gives a person new desires and a new direction, so that the man who once wanted the church destroyed now wants it built up and spends himself for it (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Paul says it outright later in the letter: it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me (2:20).

The question already settled. He has spent twenty-four verses arguing that his gospel did not come from men. The Judean churches settled the question years earlier, on the strength of one report, without weighing his credentials. They looked at the impossibility of what had happened and knew whose work it was. No committee produces a man like that. And the contrast with the teachers in Galatia is sharp. The Jewish Christians of Judea did not oppose Paul’s gospel; they praised God for it. If the churches nearest Jerusalem glorified God for Paul’s ministry, how can the Galatians reject it on the say-so of men claiming to speak for Jerusalem?

What if my conversion was not dramatic? Then your story still ends the same way: with God glorified. Most Christians were not knocked off a horse; many cannot remember a time when they did not trust Christ. That is not a lesser grace.
