A child kept from the far country by God’s mercy is as much a wonder as a prodigal brought home from it. What made the Judean churches praise was not the drama but the change: the persecutor now preaching. If you love Christ today and live for him, however quietly, the same God has done the same work in you, and it is right for others to give thanks for it.

Should I tell my story? Yes, simply and honestly, with Christ at the centre and not yourself. Paul’s story is told in this chapter so that the gospel can be seen, not so that Paul can be admired. Tell what you were, what Christ did, and what he is to you now, and resist the temptation to make the before more lurid or the after more impressive than it was. People can argue with your theology. It is much harder to argue with what God has evidently done to you.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of someone’s conversion, especially someone you had written off, give God the glory before you give anything else, including suspicion.

For worship. A chapter that opened with a curse pronounced on angels closes with worship rising from villages that had suffered at the hands of the man being spoken of. The persecutor is preaching. The people he hunted are glorifying God. The church he meant to leave uninhabitable is on its knees giving thanks for him. This is what the risen Christ does with his enemies when he means to have them: he does not merely stop them; he turns them into the reason his people worship. And the chapter ends in glory, and it is not Paul’s.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—<sup>2</sup>and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:<sup>3</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>4</sup>who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,<sup>5</sup>to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—<sup>7</sup>not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.<sup>8</sup>But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed.<sup>9</sup>As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.<sup>10</sup>For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.<sup>11</sup>For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel.<sup>12</sup>For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.<sup>13</sup>For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it.<sup>14</sup>And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.<sup>15</sup>But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace,<sup>16</sup>was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;<sup>17</sup>nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.<sup>18</sup>Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days.<sup>19</sup>But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.<sup>20</sup>(In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)<sup>21</sup>Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.<sup>22</sup>And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.<sup>23</sup>They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.”<sup>24</sup>And they glorified God because of me.

2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Chapter 2 completes Paul’s argument from his own story and turns it into doctrine. Two episodes stand out: the meeting in Jerusalem (vv. 1–10), where the apostles added nothing to Paul’s gospel and did not require the Gentile Titus to be circumcised; and the clash at Antioch (vv. 11–14), where Paul opposed Peter to his face because Peter’s conduct contradicted the gospel he believed. Both make the same point: justification by faith alone is not negotiable, even when the one who wavers is the most respected leader in the church.

Then comes the centre of the whole letter (vv. 15–21). A person is justified, declared righteous by God as judge, not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. And the chapter ends with Paul’s most personal testimony: crucified with Christ, Christ living in him, and the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Fourteen years on, Paul goes up to Jerusalem by revelation, with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Greek Titus, and lays his gospel privately before the leaders, not to have it approved but to keep the one church from splitting into two. Titus is not required to be circumcised. False brothers who came to spy out the believers’ freedom get no ground at all, so that the truth of the gospel might be kept for the Galatians. The leaders add nothing to Paul’s message, recognise the grace given to him, and give him the right hand of fellowship, asking only that he remember the poor.
verseByVerse.theology:
One gospel, one people, one way in

The decision about Titus (v. 3) settles a question of the first order: Jew and Gentile are justified on the same terms, and no covenant sign is added to faith as a condition of acceptance with God. This is not first a point about cultural inclusion but about what justification is: one covenant of grace, one people, one Saviour, one way in.

Two further principles sit in the passage. Entrusted (v. 7) is a steward’s word: neither Paul nor Jerusalem may edit the message, because neither owns it. And the order of v. 9, grace seen and then fellowship given, is how the church recognises anyone: it does not create a minister or a brother, but sees what God has given and says so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Galatia was being told that Gentile believers needed circumcision added to their faith. Paul answers that he took exactly this question to Jerusalem with an uncircumcised Greek beside him (vv. 1–3), and the men whose authority the troublers claimed added nothing (v. 6) and shook his hand (v. 9). The troublers were not following the Jerusalem apostles; they were contradicting them.

Now: Anything may be done for the gospel; nothing may be added to it. That is why Paul could circumcise Timothy (Acts 16:3) and refuse it for Titus. Where a practice is offered as helpful, Christians may differ; where it is required for full acceptance, the gospel is at stake. And having refused to add one thing to the gospel, Paul gladly takes up care for the poor, because that is not an addition but what grace does once it has come (v. 10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 2 completes Paul’s defence of his gospel and states it in its clearest form. First, on a later visit to Jerusalem, Paul laid his gospel before the leading apostles. They added nothing to it, did not require the Gentile Titus to be circumcised, and gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (vv. 1–10). Second, at Antioch, Peter himself, under pressure from Jewish believers, stopped eating with Gentile Christians, and Paul opposed him publicly, because his conduct denied the gospel: if Gentiles are accepted by faith, they cannot be required to live like Jews (vv. 11–14). Third, Paul states the gospel: a person is justified, declared righteous by God, not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. Paul has died to the law and been crucified with Christ; Christ now lives in him, and he lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him. If righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing (vv. 15–21). The chapter moves from a private meeting, through a quarrel over a dinner table, to the summit of the whole letter: the Son of God, who loved me.

After fourteen years. Paul is still counting years, and the number is the argument. Fourteen years after his conversion, or after the first visit: fourteen years of preaching, planting, and being run out of towns, without the Jerusalem apostles laying a hand on his message. If his gospel had needed their sign-off, it had been operating without it for well over a decade, and it had been working. And with Barnabas: the man who had vouched for Paul when the Jerusalem church would not go near him (Acts 9:27).

Taking Titus along with me. Titus is a Greek, an uncircumcised Gentile convert, and Paul walks him into the middle of a meeting about whether Greeks must be circumcised. He is carrying not a companion but an exhibit, a deliberate test case.

I went up because of a revelation. Not because he was summoned, not because his nerve had failed. It was God who sent him, not the Jerusalem apostles. If this was the famine visit, the revelation may have come through the prophecy of Agabus (Acts 11:28).

Privately. He took it to the leaders first, in a closed room, rather than staging a confrontation in front of a crowd. He might have forced a public showdown and won it. He chose the room where a thing can be settled instead of the platform where a thing gets performed. The phrase “those who seemed influential” is hoi dokountes, the ones held in repute. Paul is not overawed, but he is not sneering at Peter and James either; he calls them pillars and shakes their hands. He is refusing one thing only: the idea that reputation is what makes a gospel true. The Judaizers (the teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses) had been trading on Jerusalem’s prestige. Paul will grant Jerusalem everything except the right to be the reason.

Running in vain. This is the line most likely to be misread, because it sounds as if Paul had doubts about his message and went to have them settled. He did not, and the whole of chapter 1 forbids that reading. The danger he is guarding against is not that his gospel might turn out to be false. It is that the church might turn out to be two churches, a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms. He is not checking his doctrine. He is protecting the unity that his doctrine requires.

The gospel among the Gentiles. What Paul set on the table in that room was not a method of mission but a person: Jesus Christ, crucified for Gentiles exactly as for Jews, and received by faith without the law. The question was whether Christ alone is enough for a Greek, and Titus standing in the room was that question with a face. So the danger of running in vain was a danger to Christ’s own body. Two churches with two sets of terms would mean a Christ cut in half, and Paul’s indignant question to the Corinthians has only one answer: Is Christ divided? (1 Corinthians 1:13). There is one Lord, and so there can be only one church.

Which visit was this? Honest scholars land in different places, so it is worth stating plainly. Acts records several visits. Many take this to be the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, where exactly this question was decided, and the subject matter fits it. Others take it to be the earlier famine-relief visit of Acts 11:27–30, which would mean Galatians was written before the Council ever met. That view has one strong argument in its favour: Paul describes a private meeting, whereas Acts 15 was a public assembly; and if a formal apostolic ruling on circumcision already existed, it is hard to explain why Paul, fighting on precisely that issue, never once quotes it. The famine visit fits well with the southern Galatian churches and an early date for the letter. But nothing in the letter’s argument depends on settling it.

Should I submit my beliefs to church leaders? Submit them to Scripture first, and hold them humbly before the church. Paul would not let Jerusalem’s reputation decide his gospel; Christ and his word decide it. But Paul also did not go off alone. He laid what he preached before mature leaders and was glad to find them agreed. That is a healthy pattern: test your understanding against the Bible, and then against the wise believers and the historic confessions of the church. If you find yourself believing something no faithful Christian has ever believed, be very slow to trust it. If your leaders ask you to believe what Scripture contradicts, Scripture wins.
verseByVerse.note: It is debated whether this visit is the famine visit of Acts 11 or the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery— to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Titus. Everything came down to one man standing in the room, and whether anybody would reach for a knife. The apostles looked at an uncircumcised Gentile believer and did not require him to become a Jew. If the Judaizers were right, Jerusalem had a duty to say so with Titus standing there. Jerusalem said nothing of the kind. This settles the Galatian question.

The circumcision Titus already had. Titus did not need the knife, and the reason is a person. Paul tells the Colossians that believers have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by the circumcision of Christ, and buried with him (Colossians 2:11–12). The circumcision of Christ most likely means his death: there the old self under sin was cut away, and everyone joined to him by faith shares in it. Circumcision marked a man as belonging to God’s covenant people. Everything the sign pointed to, belonging, cleansing, a place in Abraham’s family (3:29), Titus already had in Christ. To demand the sign now would be to say that Christ’s work had not quite reached him. The believer is counted as having died with him (Romans 6:6) and is given the circumcision that matters, a new heart made by the Spirit (Romans 2:29).

Why circumcise Timothy and not Titus? A reader who knows Acts will feel this immediately. Paul later took Timothy and circumcised him (Acts 16:3). How is that not the very thing he refused here? The difference is everything. Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer (Acts 16:1), so he would probably have been reckoned a Jew by birth who had simply never been marked as one; and nobody was demanding it as a condition of his salvation. Paul did it so that Timothy could get into synagogues and preach. Titus was a Gentile, and the demand was being made as a requirement of acceptance with God. So the rule Paul is working by is not that circumcision is forbidden. It is that anything may be done for the sake of the gospel, and nothing may be added to it. The moment a thing stops being free and starts being necessary, Paul will not move, and the same man who circumcised Timothy would not let anyone touch Titus.

False brothers. Then the sentence turns dark. “False brothers” is pseudadelphoi: they claimed to be Christians but were not. The vocabulary that follows is the vocabulary of espionage. They were secretly brought in (pareisaktos), the word used of smuggling something in under cover; they slipped in like men getting over a wall at night; they came to spy out, the word for reconnoitring an enemy position. These were not honest men with a different opinion who lost an argument. They came to gather intelligence on how free the Gentile churches actually were.

To spy out our freedom. Paul names their object without softening it. Freedom: from the law as a way of justification, and from its ceremonies. Slavery: to the law as a way of standing before God (4:9; 5:1). That is the whole letter in a single phrase. What was on offer looked like a promotion: full membership, proper standing, the marks of the covenant. What it actually was, was chains. Anything that makes acceptance with God depend on a performance puts a man back on a treadmill he cannot get off, because the performance is never finished and the verdict is never in.

We did not yield. Not for an hour. Compromise never looks like surrender from the inside: it presents itself as a small, reasonable, temporary allowance for the sake of peace. Paul knew what the first inch was worth.

Preserved for you. And then he says why, and it is the most pastoral sentence in the paragraph. Not so that Paul might win. Not for the principle of the thing. For you: for a congregation of Gentile converts hundreds of miles away who would never know the meeting had happened. The truth of the gospel is the gospel in its true meaning, free grace, kept from being bent into something else.

What exactly is Christian freedom? It is freedom from the law as a way of earning God’s acceptance, from its curse on our sins, and from the ceremonies that pointed forward to Christ, such as circumcision, the food laws and the sacrificial system. It is not freedom to sin: Paul will say so sharply in 5:13. It is freedom for something: to serve God as sons rather than slaves, gladly, from love. A slave works to avoid punishment; a son works because he belongs to the family. Christian freedom means you never again have to wonder whether today’s obedience was enough to keep you in. You are in, and you obey from there.

On a Tuesday. Notice the small, reasonable allowances. A rule that began as a helpful habit and has quietly become a test of whether someone is a real Christian. A preference about worship, schooling or Bible translation that you now hold over other believers. Ask of each one: is this free, or have I made it necessary?
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised — a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Added nothing to me. Two words in Greek, and they end the argument. The Judaizers’ case rested on the claim that Paul’s gospel was incomplete: that the men in Jerusalem had the full version and Paul had been handing out an abridgement. So Paul reports the outcome of the meeting in the bluntest possible terms. The pillars of the Jerusalem church heard his gospel in full, and they had nothing to add to it. No correction. No supplement. No condition attached. Whatever the Galatians were being told is missing, the men supposedly missing it did not think so.

God shows no partiality. Whatever status they had, as companions of the earthly Jesus or as his relatives, does not matter to the question. The phrase is close to an Old Testament formula: God does not lift up faces, does not take the important man’s side because he is important (Deuteronomy 10:17; 2 Chronicles 19:7; Acts 10:34). Paul turns it on the apostles themselves. Peter had walked with Jesus and Paul had not, and it makes no difference to the truth of the gospel, because God is not impressed by credentials. It is a dangerous principle to hold and a liberating one: the same God who is unimpressed by Peter’s record is unimpressed by anyone else’s, which means nobody in the room outranks the truth.

Entrusted. Then the reason they added nothing, and it is not that they were persuaded by Paul’s arguments. They looked at the evidence. Something had plainly been happening in the Gentile world, and it was not Paul’s doing. And the word is entrusted: the language of a steward handed something that belongs to someone else. It quietly settles the entire dispute. A man entrusted with a message has no authority to revise it; that is what entrusting means. Paul cannot edit this gospel to please Gentiles and Jerusalem cannot edit it to please Jews, for exactly the same reason. Neither of them owns it.

Just as Peter. The parallel is careful. One gospel, two mission fields: Peter mainly to Jews, Paul mainly to Gentiles. Not two gospels, and not a senior apostle with a junior assistant.

One Lord behind both commissions. The parallel has a face behind it. Peter was recommissioned by the risen Christ beside the Sea of Galilee, told three times to feed his sheep (John 21:15–17). Paul was commissioned by the same risen Christ on the Damascus road and sent to open the eyes of the Gentiles (Acts 26:16–18). One had walked with Jesus for about three years and the other had hunted his followers, and the commission came from the same mouth. That is why the gospel to the circumcised and the gospel to the uncircumcised are one gospel. It has one owner and one content, the crucified and risen Christ, who is the same Lord of Jew and Greek alike, rich towards all who call on him (Romans 10:12).

He who worked through Peter. Verse 8, in brackets, and the brackets hide the key to the paragraph: its subject. It is not Peter who worked, and not Paul. There is a third party in that sentence and he is the only one doing anything. The same God energised both ministries; the verb is the one from which we get energy. Peter and Paul are the instruments through which he worked. Which is why the comparison never becomes a competition. Two men were used, and one God was working, and the results in Jerusalem and the results in Galatia have precisely the same author.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there are two gospels, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. One gospel, different audiences. Peter would say it himself at the Council: we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will (Acts 15:11).

Does “God shows no partiality” mean church leaders deserve no respect? No. Paul honours these men; he calls them pillars and accepts their handshake gladly, and elsewhere he tells churches to esteem their leaders very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13). What he refuses is to let their status decide what is true. Respect your pastor, pray for him, follow his teaching gladly when it is faithful to Scripture. But never believe something because of who said it, and never dismiss something because of who said it. The question is always whether it is the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Perceived the grace. The order of this sentence is the point. They did not shake hands and then discover the grace. First they saw the grace; then they extended the hand. The handshake did not confer anything. It acknowledged something God had already done.

The church perceives; it does not manufacture. That is the pattern for how the church recognises anything. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church’s task is to perceive what God has given and then say so publicly. Where grace is evidently at work, the only faithful response is to acknowledge it, and where it is not, no ceremony will supply it.

Pillars. The picture is architectural: the men on whom the weight rests, the leaders of the Jerusalem church (Revelation 3:12). James here is not the apostle John’s brother, who had already been executed by Herod (Acts 12:2), but James the Lord’s brother. Then Peter, and John the son of Zebedee.

The right hand of fellowship. It is an ancient gesture, and it has meant much the same thing in every century: a pledge of good faith, a man saying that between us this is settled. The word behind fellowship is koinōnia, partnership: a joint stake in the same enterprise, not merely a truce.

A company of forgiven enemies. Consider what actually happened in that room. The apostle who had been hunting Christians and the apostle who had denied Christ in a courtyard put their hands together over a gospel neither of them had earned, and agreed to spend their lives on it in different countries. Each owed everything to the same person: Peter had been restored by the risen Lord after his denials, Paul stopped by him on the way to Damascus, and neither had been dismissed. Paul uses this same word for what every believer is called into: the fellowship of God’s Son (1 Corinthians 1:9). The handshake was a partnership in a mission because it was first a shared life in Christ. Nobody in it had a record worth defending. That is what made it possible.

To the Gentiles. A division of labour, not a division of message, and it was never watertight, since Peter opened the Gentile door in the first place (Acts 10) and Paul went to the synagogue first in almost every town he entered.

Remember the poor. One request. After a meeting about circumcision, the law, and the terms of salvation, the single thing Jerusalem asks is that the poor believers in Jerusalem not be forgotten. Not the law, but love. Years of his life went into the collection for the struggling believers in Judea, and he wrote whole chapters raising it (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

Not an addition. It is a striking place for the paragraph to land. Paul has just refused to add one item to the gospel, and immediately accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because it is not an addition. Nothing has been placed between a sinner and God. What has been named is what grace does once it has arrived. A church that has understood justification by faith alone and has no interest in the hungry has not understood it (James 2:15–17; 1 John 3:17).

Who are the poor I am to remember, and how? First, needy believers, the household of faith, as Paul will say in 6:10; then everyone in need as we have opportunity. Start near: the widow in your congregation, the family where a job has been lost, the asylum seeker who has turned up on Sunday, the student who cannot afford the trip. Give regularly and deliberately, not only when moved. Give through your church so that help is wise and sustained. Give time and friendship as well as money, because the poor are usually lonely as well as short. And remember the persecuted and impoverished church abroad. Do it gladly; Paul was eager, not pressured.

On a Tuesday. When you see grace at work in another Christian, especially one from a different background, church or tradition, perceive it and say so: give him the right hand, in words if not in a handshake.
verseByVerse.note: Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church. The poor were the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Antioch Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he drew back for fear of the circumcision party, and the other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed. Paul saw that they were not walking in step with the truth of the gospel, and he challenged Peter in front of them all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The gospel governs the feet, not only the confession

Peter’s failure was not in his doctrine. He had defended the acceptance of Gentiles and won the argument (Acts 11). What verse 14 exposes is a gap between a belief truly held and a life not walking in line with it, which is what Paul means by hypocrisy here, not the pretence of a faith one does not have. The gospel must govern table habits and the pull of social pressure, not only statements of faith.

Scripture also records, without embarrassment, an apostle publicly corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel. Whatever authority the Jerusalem leaders had, it was never authority over the message, which is the argument of vv. 6–9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch came from fear, not conviction: verse 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the snare Paul named at 1:10, the wish to please people, and it carried the other Jewish believers and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now: Two things here reach a reader directly: the room in which he is a slightly different Christian, and the question of when a leader should be corrected in public. Paul’s case met every condition at once: the conduct was public, the gospel itself was at stake, others were being carried away, and the rebuke was spoken to Peter’s face, not behind his back. And the friendship survived it (2 Peter 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I opposed him to his face. The scene changes to Antioch in Syria, the first great Gentile church (Acts 11:19–26), and the man who has just been called a pillar is about to be called wrong. Not a letter, not a word afterwards, not a delegation. Face to face, and in front of everybody (v. 14): openly, not behind his back.

In the flow. Verses 1–10 showed the Jerusalem leaders agreeing with Paul; verses 11–14 show that agreement tested, and failing in the most unlikely man. Paul did not get his gospel from Peter, because he could correct Peter by it. At Antioch the Galatian question was being asked without words: must Gentile believers become Jews to be fully accepted? Paul’s answer to it becomes his plainest statement of the gospel (vv. 15–21).

Because he stood condemned. The word is a courtroom word, and the tense matters: not that Paul condemned him, but that he stood already condemned, by his own behaviour, by the contradiction between what he believed and what he was doing, and by the gospel. Paul did not pass the sentence. He read it out.

Eating with the Gentiles. Eating together was not a casual matter in that world. A shared table meant shared life, mutual acceptance, family, and in the church it may well have included the Lord’s Supper. For a Jew to sit down to a Gentile meal was to declare that the wall had come down, and Peter had been doing it, meal after meal, which means the church at Antioch had watched their most famous visitor live out the gospel in the most visible way available.

He drew back. Two verbs, and both are gradual; the tense pictures him withdrawing bit by bit. He drew back, a word used of drawing in a ship’s sails or of troops pulling back from a position. He separated himself, aphorizō, the very word from which the name Pharisee may come, the separated ones. Nobody announced a policy. He simply began sitting elsewhere, and everyone knew what it meant.

Fearing the circumcision party. Paul does not let anyone pretend otherwise. It was not conviction. Peter had not changed his mind about anything; he changed his seat because of who was watching. It is the fear of man (Proverbs 29:25), the same weakness that once led Peter to deny Jesus.

How was this possible? This is the man who had the vision on the rooftop and heard the voice saying, what God has made clean, do not call common; who walked into Cornelius’s house and watched the Spirit fall on Gentiles; who defended the whole thing to the Jerusalem church and won the argument (Acts 10–11). He was not under-informed. He was the leading expert in the room on precisely this point. Which is the lesson, and it is a hard one. Knowing a truth and having settled it publicly does not immunise a man against abandoning it when the wrong people walk in. The mechanism had not changed in nearly twenty years: not doubt, not argument, but the sudden weight of a watching face. Fear of man is not a beginner’s sin that maturity leaves behind.

A table the Lord had opened. And Peter was not only stepping back from his own vision. He was stepping back from his Lord. Mark, whose Gospel the early church connected with Peter’s preaching, records Jesus teaching that what goes into a person from outside cannot defile him, and adds: thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). The voice on the rooftop in Joppa said the same again. So when Peter moved his plate away from Gentile believers, he was putting back a wall that Christ himself had taken down. The question at that table was never really about menus. It was whether Christ’s word and Christ’s cleansing were enough to make a Gentile fit company.

Certain men from James. The phrase has been used to blame James, and probably should not be. Luke records the Jerusalem church later writing to Antioch about men who had gone out from them and troubled them, although we gave them no instructions (Acts 15:24). They may have claimed James’s authority without his approval. Men who arrive claiming a great name are not always carrying it. What is certain is the effect: their arrival was enough, and there is no hint that Peter was even asked.

Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that Peter was the head of the apostles and the first pope, with a primacy passed to his successors, including infallibility in defining doctrine. Roman Catholic teaching limits that infallibility to formal definitions, not conduct; but the point here is wider. Verdict: Peter was a great apostle and leader. But here Paul publicly rebukes him for a serious error affecting the gospel. Peter was neither infallible in practice nor above correction by another apostle. The gospel judges Peter, not Peter the gospel, and that is true of every church leader since. The authority of the church rests on the apostolic teaching recorded in Scripture, not on the succession of one office (Ephesians 2:20).

Is it wrong to adapt to the people I am with? Not in itself. Paul said he became as a Jew to Jews and as one outside the law to those outside the law, so that he might win them (1 Corinthians 9:20–22). Adapting your customs, your food, your manner, for the sake of love and the gospel is Christlike. What Peter did was different in two ways. His motive was fear, not love. And his action told fellow believers that they were not fully acceptable unless they changed. The question to ask is: am I adapting to serve these people, or to protect myself? And does my adapting tell any brother or sister in Christ that they are second-class?

For worship. There is one man in all of Scripture who never once changed his table because of who was watching. He ate with tax collectors in front of the Pharisees and with Pharisees in front of the tax collectors, and he was called a glutton and a drunkard for it. He was not afraid of any face, because he lived before the face of his Father. And when Peter failed again, as he had failed before, that same Lord did not cast him off; he sent him a brother to tell him the truth. The Lord who restored Peter by a charcoal fire restored him again at Antioch, and he is patient still with every one of us who has changed seats.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church. Eating together was the test: strict Jews would not share a table with Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Acted hypocritically. The damage spreads in a single verse, and the name at the end of it is the one that hurts. The word is synypokrinomai, to play the actor together, from the theatre, the word for playing a part, speaking lines that are not your own. Paul is not accusing these men of secret unbelief. He is saying they were acting: behaving in a way their convictions did not support because the audience had changed.

Even Barnabas. The man whose name means son of encouragement (Acts 4:36). The man who had stood up for Paul when the Jerusalem church was afraid of him, who had gone to Tarsus to fetch him out of obscurity, who had travelled the first missionary journey at his side through all its dangers and defended Gentile believers (Acts 11:22–26; 13–14). If one man in Antioch could be counted on, it was Barnabas, and he was carried away too. That detail is not there to shame Barnabas. It is there to show how strong the current was. It did not take an argument; nobody has recorded a single word of persuasion in this passage. It took a few significant people sitting at a different table, and the whole church moved.

Not in step. The verb is orthopodeō, a rare word that apparently means to walk straight, made from orthos, straight (as in orthodox), and pous, foot: they were not walking straight, not keeping to the line. And this is the sentence that gives the whole episode its weight. Paul does not say their doctrine was wrong. Their doctrine was fine; every man at those tables would have signed the same confession. Their feet were wrong. The gospel is not merely something to be believed accurately; it is something to be walked in, and it can be denied by a seating plan as effectively as by a sermon. And the truth their feet contradicted has a name. In Christ Jesus there is neither Jew nor Greek, because all who belong to him are one in him (3:28). His death had made the Gentile believer clean, and his Spirit had made him a son. To leave that man eating alone was to say, without a word, that Christ had not been quite enough to bring him in.

I said to Cephas before them all. Public sin with public effect required public correction (1 Timothy 5:20). Peter had been living freely, eating what Gentiles ate, not keeping the Jewish food laws, so he plainly did not believe they still bound him. Yet by withdrawing he was telling Gentile believers that if they wanted his company at the table, they would have to take on the very rules he himself had stopped keeping: to have full fellowship with us, you must become Jews. That denied the gospel. And nobody had said it out loud: pressure does not have to be spoken to be applied, and Gentile Christians in Antioch had just been shown, with no words at all, what it would cost them to be treated as brothers.

Should a Christian confront leaders publicly? Usually not, and Scripture is careful about it. The Lord’s instruction for sin between brothers is to go privately first, and only widen the circle if there is no repentance (Matthew 18:15–17). Paul himself tells Timothy not to admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. But the same passage adds the other half: as for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all (1 Timothy 5:19–20). Four things line up here, and they rarely all line up. The conduct was public, so a private word could not undo it. The matter was the gospel itself, not a preference or a personality. Others were already being swept away, Barnabas among them. And Paul said it to his face, in the room, at cost to himself, not about him, afterwards, to somebody else. That last one is the test most often failed. A great deal of what calls itself courage in the church is a message sent to a third party, or a post written about a man who will never be in the room. Paul’s way is harder and kinder: he said it where Peter could answer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul relished confronting Peter. He did it because the gospel was at stake. And it did not end the friendship. Years later, an old man writing his last letter mentioned our beloved brother Paul, and the wisdom given him, and the things in his letters that are hard to understand (2 Peter 3:15–16). Peter took it. There is no bitterness anywhere in the record. Two men who both knew what it was to be forgiven could survive being told the truth.

What are the separate tables today? Rarely food laws. More often it is the church where the professionals sit together and the cleaners sit together, the congregation that welcomes newcomers who look like the existing members, the fellowship that is warm to the respectable and cool to the man who has come out of prison or the woman with a messy history. Wherever believers make others feel that full acceptance requires them to become like us, culturally, socially, in class or race, the Antioch problem is back. The gospel says that whoever is in Christ belongs at the table, and the table is the Lord’s, not ours.

What if I am the one who has been rebuked? Do what Peter evidently did: listen, and do not defend yourself first. Ask whether the rebuke is true, even if it was delivered badly. If it is, own it plainly before God and before those affected, without excuses, and change course. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6). A believer who can receive correction is a believer who is resting on Christ’s righteousness rather than his own, because he has nothing to protect.
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul now states the gospel plainly. Even Jews by birth are justified only through faith in Christ. That does not make Christ a promoter of sin; going back to the law as the way to God is what makes a person a transgressor. Through the law Paul died to the law so that he might live to God, crucified with Christ and now living by faith in the Son of God who loved him. To make righteousness come by the law would mean Christ died for nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The article by which the church stands or falls

Protestant theology came to call justification by faith the article by which the church stands or falls, a summary of Luther’s own conviction, and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is a declaration of our standing before God, not an infusion of goodness, though a changed life always follows. It is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and these stand or fall together.

One point of translation may meet a reader: the phrase rendered faith in Jesus Christ (v. 16) can also be read as the faithfulness of Jesus Christ. This commentary, with most Reformed readers, takes it as faith directed toward him; either way, faith is not a work that earns the verdict but the empty hand that receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). If the law cannot justify those to whom it was given, it will justify no one. And verse 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into a wall that had been pulled down.

Now: The person who comes to faith from a respectable life and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on the same ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability counts for as little in the verdict as the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centre of the letter. Here is the letter’s own centre of gravity. Paul says it, then says it again, then says it a third time inside one verse, because everything else stands on it. Paul is probably still addressing Peter, or expanding on what he said to him, and the words become a statement of the gospel for every reader.

In the flow. Everything before this verse has been leading here, and everything after it explains it: Abraham (3:6), the curse Christ bore (3:13), the law as guardian (3:24), sons not slaves (4:7), and the life of the Spirit (chapters 5 and 6). Every later argument in Galatians is this verse unfolded.

Jews by birth. Gentiles were regarded as sinners because they were outside the law, and Paul may be quoting the Jewish attitude. Take the most advantaged religious people on earth: the covenant, the Scriptures, the temple, the sacrifices, a lifetime of training. And they too believed in Christ Jesus. The insiders had to come the same way as the outsiders. If the law could have justified anybody, it would have justified them, and instead they abandoned the attempt and trusted a crucified man. That is good news for both kinds of people. The irreligious man is not too far gone to come by faith, and the religious man is not too good to need to.

Not justified. The word to get clear is justified (dikaioō), and it is not a word most people use on a Tuesday. It is a courtroom word. To justify is not to make someone good; it is to declare someone to be in the right: acquitted, accepted. A judge who justifies a defendant does not improve him or treat him or educate him. He pronounces a verdict, and the man walks out of the court with a status he did not have when he walked in.

A verdict, not a treatment. That distinction matters, because many people instinctively think of salvation in medical terms: God as a physician gradually curing us, with heaven at the end if the treatment works. Justification is not the doctor’s slow progress; it is the judge’s verdict, given whole, in a moment, and given at the beginning rather than the end. God does also heal the sinner he acquits, and that work goes on for a lifetime. But he does not acquit him because the healing is going well.

What “justified” means, and what it does not. It is more than not guilty: it is accepted as righteous, the opposite of being condemned (Romans 8:33–34; Deuteronomy 25:1). It does not mean being made inwardly good, though God does that too, in the separate work of sanctification. It does not mean God pretends we are good when we are not. He declares us righteous because the righteousness of Christ is counted to us, credited to our account (Romans 4:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Our sins were counted to him at the cross; his obedience is counted to us. The verdict rests on what he has done, not on what we are or do.

By works of the law. The ground of that verdict is the whole quarrel. Works of the law means, first, deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses, and particularly the visible markers that separated Jew from Gentile: circumcision, the food rules, the holy days. Those were the exact issues on the table in Antioch. But Paul’s conclusion is wider than the markers, and the last clause shows it.

No one will be justified. From Psalm 143:2: enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you. No one. Not the Gentile without the law, and not the Pharisee who kept it better than his peers. No human being will be declared righteous by keeping the law, because no one keeps it perfectly (3:10; Romans 3:20). Psalm 143 is a prayer of David, a man after God’s own heart, and even he begs not to be brought into court, because before a God of perfect holiness the best life ever lived by a sinner is no defence. The reason is not that the law is a bad thing. Paul will insist that it is holy and was given by God for good purposes. The reason is that the law is a mirror, and a mirror has never washed a face. It was given to show what righteousness looks like and, in showing it, to show a man what he is not.

But through faith in Jesus Christ. Faith receives Christ and his righteousness, and it justifies not because it is strong but because he is. A weak faith in a strong Saviour is as fully justified as a strong faith, because the righteousness it receives is his, not its own.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? Some scholars of the New Perspective on Paul, such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright, argue that works of the law mean mainly the boundary markers that separated Jews from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath. So justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people, not how a sinner is made right with God. Verdict: works of the law certainly include those boundary markers, as the Antioch incident shows; the New Perspective is right about the occasion. But Paul’s argument goes deeper: no one is justified by the law because no one keeps the whole law (3:10–12; 5:3). Justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, received by faith alone (Romans 4:4–8). It certainly has consequences for who belongs together at the table. But it is first about how a guilty person can stand before a holy God (the Westminster Confession 11.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.1).

Where Christians differ: declared righteous or made righteous? The Roman Catholic Church teaches (Council of Trent, 1547) that justification is a process in which God pours grace into the soul and makes the person inwardly righteous; it grows through the sacraments and good works, can be lost by mortal sin, and is restored by penance. On that view a person is accepted by God as far as he has been made righteous. The Reformers taught that justification is God’s once-for-all legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness alone, and that sanctification, the lifelong work of making us holy, always follows it but is distinct from it. Verdict: the Reformation view is right. Paul’s word is a law-court word: God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), which cannot mean he finds them already godly. Justification is complete the moment a person believes (Romans 5:1; 8:1), and so it cannot grow or be lost. Works matter greatly, but as the fruit of justification, not its ground (Ephesians 2:8–10; Westminster 11.1–2; 1689 11.1–2). If our acceptance depended on how far we had been made righteous, no one could ever be sure of it, and the cross would be only a beginning; but Christ died for no purpose if righteousness comes by anything we do (v. 21).

Where Christians differ: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? The Greek phrase pistis Christou, used twice in this verse, can be read as faith in Christ (our trust in him) or as the faith or faithfulness of Christ (his own faithful obedience to the Father, even to the cross). Some recent scholars prefer the second, and say Paul means we are justified by Christ’s faithfulness. Verdict: faith in Christ is the better reading. In this very verse Paul adds, “we also have believed in Christ Jesus,” which shows plainly that our believing is in view. Both truths are biblical: we are saved by Christ’s faithful obedience (Romans 5:19), and we receive it by trusting him. But here Paul’s point is that the way to receive righteousness is believing, not doing. Either way the doing is his; the receiving is ours.

Do Paul and James contradict each other? James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (James 2:24). No, they do not contradict. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is declared righteous before God, and answers: by faith, apart from works. James asks how a claim to faith is shown to be real, and answers that faith without works is dead (James 2:17). Paul opposes works as the ground of acceptance; James opposes a faith that is only words. Paul agrees that true faith works: faith working through love (5:6). We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is a work that earns justification. Faith is the empty hand that receives Christ. It is not what we are justified for, but how we receive the one for whose sake we are justified. Even the receiving is not a contribution.

If I am justified, why do I still feel guilty? Because feelings lag behind facts, and because you still sin, and a tender conscience notices. Real conviction of a specific sin is the Spirit’s kindness, calling you to confess it and be cleansed (1 John 1:9). But a general cloud of condemnation that hangs over you after you have confessed is not from God, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). When that cloud comes, do not argue with it from your record. Argue from his. Say to your conscience: the verdict was given at the cross, on the ground of what Christ did, and it does not move with my moods.

On a Tuesday. The verdict on you is not waiting on Friday’s performance. It was handed down at the cross and received by faith, and it does not move (Romans 3:20–24; Philippians 3:8–9). Begin each day by remembering it, and then obey from it, not towards it. Even your best obedience this week will fall short, and it is accepted for the sake of the Son whose obedience never did.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Found to be sinners. Paul stops to answer an objection, and it is the objection this doctrine has always attracted. The argument runs like this. If a man is accepted by God on the basis of faith rather than obedience, then his obedience does not finally matter, and look at what actually follows. Jewish believers who came to Christ stopped keeping the food laws and started eating with Gentiles. By the law’s reckoning they became sinners in the process, sinners like the Gentiles.

Is Christ then a servant of sin? So Christ has taken observant men and made them law-breakers. Is he then a servant of sin: not merely tolerating it but actively promoting it, running errands for it? Does Christ encourage sin by freeing people from the law? It was the common objection to justification by faith (Romans 6:1).

Certainly not! Paul’s reply is the strongest negative he has. The Greek is mē genoito, the phrase he reaches for when a suggestion is not to be weighed but thrown out of the room: may it never be, God forbid, perish the thought. Christ does not promote sin. Justification by faith leads to holiness, not licence (5:13–25).

An insult to a friend. And there is a reason that is more than logic. To call Christ a servant of sin is to say something about the character of the one who died to destroy it: the man who took the whole weight of it into his own body and went into the dark under it. The objection is not merely mistaken; it is an insult to a person, and Paul reacts the way anyone reacts when someone slanders a friend who is not there to answer.

A strange compliment. Paul faced the same objection in Romans, put more sharply: are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? (Romans 6:1). It is a compliment of a strange sort. If a preacher has never once been accused of making grace too free, it is worth asking whether he has actually preached it, because Paul, who was preaching it exactly right, was accused constantly.

Grace changes the person, not only the paperwork. Paul’s answer is not a retreat into rule-keeping. It is a statement about what happened to the person. Grace does not leave a sinner where it found him and merely change his paperwork. It puts him to death and raises him, and a man who has died to something does not go back to it as though nothing occurred. That is why Paul’s answer ends at a cross, I have been crucified with Christ (2:20), rather than at a code of conduct.

Then why do Christians still sin, and does that make grace a failure? Christians still sin because sanctification, God’s work of making a justified person holy, is lifelong; the old desires are defeated but not yet removed, and the war goes on until we see Christ (5:17; 1 John 3:2). That is not grace failing. It is grace still at work. The difference between a Christian and an unbeliever is not that one sins and the other does not, but that the Christian has a new master, hates his sin, fights it, confesses it, and is slowly changed. If you are using grace as an excuse to keep a sin you love, do not comfort yourself with this verse; it says certainly not. If you are grieving your sin and running to Christ with it, grace has not failed you. It has hold of you.

On a Tuesday. Free grace never means freedom to sin. Live holy because you are free. When you notice yourself thinking, it does not matter, I am forgiven anyway, stop and look at who forgave you and what it cost him. Then ask him for strength to obey in the very thing you were about to excuse; his Spirit lives in you for exactly this (5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I rebuild what I tore down. Paul answers the objection about himself, with a picture. Imagine a man who has spent years constructing a building, stone by stone, and has finally looked at it, judged it unsound, and pulled it down. Now imagine him going back and putting every stone up again. He has not merely wasted his time. He has publicly declared that the demolition was the crime.

What Paul tore down. It was the whole structure of acceptance by performance: the life he describes in chapter 1, advancing beyond his peers, zealous for the traditions, building a righteousness of his own. He took it apart when he met Christ. And this is the answer to the man who says grace makes sinners: the transgression is not in leaving the law behind as a way of righteousness but in going back to it. If he rebuilds that system, he condemns himself either way. Either he was wrong to pull it down, or he is wrong to put it up. What he cannot claim is that reconstruction is obedience. And there is a direct application to Antioch, which is probably why he uses the first person so pointedly. Peter had been living in the freedom of the gospel and had begun laying stones back in place, one meal at a time.

Through the law I died to the law. One of the strangest sentences in the letter. Through the law: not in spite of it, not by escaping it; the law itself was the instrument of his death to the law. In Christ, who bore the law’s curse, Paul died to the law’s claims (Romans 7:4).

How can the law make me die to the law? This is one of Paul’s most compressed sentences, so it helps to take it in steps. First, the law demands perfect obedience and pronounces death on every transgressor (3:10). Second, Paul was a transgressor, so the law’s sentence on him was death. Third, Christ took that sentence for him: he was born under the law (4:4) and died under its curse in his people’s place (3:13). Fourth, Paul was united to Christ by faith, so when Christ died, Paul died with him (v. 20). So the law did carry out its sentence on Paul: in Christ, he died. And a dead man is free from the law’s claim; the law has nothing more to say to someone whose sentence has been fully carried out (Romans 7:1–4, where Paul uses the picture of a marriage ended by death). That is why it was through the law: the law itself demanded the death by which he was set free from it. There is a second strand too: the law, by exposing his sin, drove him to stop trusting it and to flee to Christ (3:24; Romans 7:9–10).

How the law kills. Watch that second strand at work. The law came to a man doing rather well and kept pressing until it had him. Paul tells us which commandment found him out: you shall not covet, a law about the desire and not only the deed (Romans 7:7–11). Jesus read the whole law the same way: not just murder, but anger; not just adultery, but the look (Matthew 5:21–28). And the law kept saying it until the promising young Pharisee understood that he was not ahead of his peers at all, that the system he had trusted could only convict him, and that on those terms he was a dead man. So the law did precisely what God gave it to do. It killed him, and it killed him so that he could stop trying to live by it.

The last kindness of a schoolmaster. There is no gentler road to grace than this one, and it is where many people actually are. Nobody comes to Christ while his own account still looks solvent. The ache underneath religious striving, the sense that it is never enough, that the standard keeps moving, that a good week is only ever a reprieve, is not a malfunction. It is the law doing its work, and its work is not cruelty. It is the last kindness of a guardian who intends to hand the pupil over to someone else (3:24).

What it does not mean. Dying to the law does not mean becoming lawless. Paul died to the law as a way of being right with God, and as a master that condemns him; he did not die to God’s will. He is now under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21), and the Spirit leads him to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement in love (5:14; Romans 8:4).

So that I might live to God. The purpose of dying to the law is not lawlessness but life for God. That is what the whole demolition was for: not to leave a man in the rubble, but to get him out from under a life spent proving himself, and into a life lived toward God. The law could not make him live for God; Christ does.

Do Christians still need to keep the Ten Commandments? Not as a way of being accepted by God, and not under the law’s curse. But the moral will of God that the commandments express has not changed, because it flows from God’s own character. Jesus deepened the commandments rather than abolishing them (Matthew 5:17–48), and the apostles repeat their substance to Christians (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:1–3). So the believer reads the moral law as the shape of a life of love, the path his Father has marked out for children who are already his. Christians differ on how the fourth commandment applies today, and on how much of the old covenant law carries over; but no Christian is free to steal, lie, covet or commit adultery. The ceremonial laws that pointed to Christ, such as circumcision and the food laws, are fulfilled in him and no longer bind.

On a Tuesday. Notice the stones you keep laying back in place: the private rules by which you measure whether God is pleased with you this week. Put them down, and live towards God today, not to prove yourself to him, but gladly, as a man let out of prison lives towards the friend who paid his fine.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been crucified with Christ. This is the summit of the letter, and one of the best-loved verses in the New Testament, and it begins with a funeral. The tense is one English does not carry well: the perfect, a thing done in the past whose results stand permanently in the present. Crucified, and remain so. Not I am dying daily, and not I try to crucify myself. It happened. It is finished. When Christ died, Paul died, because Christ died as a representative, the way Adam acted for a race, so that what happened to him happened to everyone joined to him. His old self, under the law’s condemnation, died (Romans 6:6).

Crucified. It is a deliberate word to choose. Crucifixion was not a dignified death or a private one. Paul could have said he died with Christ; he says he was crucified, which is what you do to a criminal in public with nothing left of his standing. The old self, the impressive one, the one with the record and the achievements and the rising reputation in Judaism, did not retire honourably. It was executed.

Christ who lives in me. Taken alone, the sentence sounds as if Paul has been erased, as if becoming a Christian means being emptied out and replaced, personality and all. Two things forbid that reading. The first is the very next clause, where Paul says the life I now live: there is plainly still an I doing the living. The second is the letter itself. The man who wrote it is unmistakably himself on every page, angry, tender, sarcastic and affectionate by turns. Grace did not flatten Saul of Tarsus into a generic believer. It killed what he was living for and left him more himself than before. What died was the old Paul, the self-righteous Pharisee, the self that had to be somebody. What lives is a man indwelt. Christ now lives in Paul by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Colossians 1:27), the source and centre of his new life. What does that look like? The Spirit of Christ turns his will towards God and grows in him what Christ is like, love, joy, peace and patience (5:22–23), so that more and more he wants what Christ wants. This is real power, not a figure of speech: the Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in him (Romans 8:11).

In the flesh. In the body, in this world, in ordinary circumstances, with a stomach and a temper and a tentmaking business. Here “the flesh” means ordinary bodily, earthly life, not the sinful nature, which is how Paul uses the word in 5:16–24 and in Romans 8. Paul is saying that his new life in Christ is lived out in a real human body, in the everyday world, by faith. This is Monday he is describing.

By faith in the Son of God. Faith is not just the door into the Christian life; it is the way of living it, every day. People who love this verse sometimes expect it to feel like something and are troubled when it does not. Paul does not say he lives by a sensation of Christ’s presence, or by a continual awareness, or by spiritual experiences. He says he lives by faith: by trusting a person he cannot see, on days when nothing is felt at all. The indwelling is a fact about where Christ is, not a report on how the believer is doing.

Who loved me and gave himself for me. And then the last clause, and Paul’s grammar goes suddenly singular. He has spent the whole chapter on councils, delegations, apostles, mission fields, the terms of justification for the nations. And it ends here, with one man saying me twice. Paul does not say only that Christ loved the world, but that he loved me. Christ’s death was a personal act of love for each of his people. The cross is wide enough for the world and narrow enough to have a single name written on it. This is the same Paul who had been dragging women out of houses to prison (Acts 8:3). Luther urged his readers to read the words me and for me with great vehemence, and to take them as spoken of themselves.

What “crucified with Christ” does not mean. It is not a special experience that some advanced Christians reach, nor a feeling to be worked up, nor a command (crucify yourself!). It is a fact that is true of every believer by union with Christ: when he died, we died with him, and that death can never be undone (the perfect tense; Romans 6:3–6). What died was the old self: the person Paul was under the law, condemned and ruled by sin. It does not mean Paul no longer struggles with sin (5:17), or that he no longer has a will of his own. It means Christ has replaced self as the centre, the source of his life, and the object of his trust.

How do I live by faith on an ordinary day? By turning, again and again, from yourself to Christ. In the morning, before the list, remind yourself who you are in him: crucified with him, raised with him, loved by him. When temptation comes, say no on the strength of the fact that the old self who loved that sin was put to death. When you fail, go straight back to the one who loved you and gave himself for you, without waiting to feel better first. When you have to do something hard, ask him for the strength, and expect him to give it, because he lives in you. None of this needs a feeling. It needs only the habit of looking at him.

Can I say “for me” if I am not sure I am chosen? Yes. You do not need to look into God’s secret decree before you come to Christ; no one can. The gospel invites every sinner who hears it to trust Christ, and promises that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37). Christ did die for his people in particular, and his death secured their salvation; but you discover that you are one of them not by peering into heaven but by coming to him. This is what Reformed Christians call definite or particular atonement: the belief that the cross was aimed at saving a particular people and actually accomplished it (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). Many faithful Christians believe instead that Christ died for all in the same way; both gladly offer him to everyone, and neither asks you to settle the question before you come. If you trust Christ, you may say, without presumption, the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. Paul’s me is the word of every believer.

For worship. The Son of God loved: not the abstraction of humanity, but this particular man, with this particular record, while that record was still being written. And he did not send help; he gave himself, which is the only gift that costs the giver everything and leaves nothing in reserve. He had the Father’s glory and set it down. He went to a public execution for people who were his enemies at the time, and he did it gladly, and he would not be talked out of it (Ephesians 5:2; 1 John 3:16). There is nothing in heaven or earth to set beside a love like that, and eternity will not be long enough to get to the end of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not nullify the grace of God. The chapter ends with its sharpest sentence. “Nullify” is atheteō, to set aside, reject, cancel: the term for treating a legal instrument as void. And it is probably a charge being thrown back where it came from. Paul is the one being accused of treating God’s law as though it counted for nothing; he answers that it is the other side who are annulling something, and it is not the law. Going back to the law as a way of righteousness cancels grace.

In the flow. This verse closes the defence that began in 1:11, and it leads straight into the next chapter. Paul has told his story to show where his gospel came from; now he shows what is lost if it is abandoned: the cross itself. And the next words of the letter turn the point on the readers. O foolish Galatians, Paul cries: Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed before your eyes as crucified (3:1). Chapter 2 ends at the cross and chapter 3 begins there, because the cross is the one thing a gospel of law-keeping has no real need of.

If righteousness were through the law. The argument is a single move. Suppose there is any route to being right with God that runs through human obedience: any at all, even a small one, even as a supplement to grace. Then on that road God had a way of saving people that did not require the death of his Son. And in that case Calvary was not a rescue; it was the most appalling waste in the history of the universe. A Father watched his Son die in the dark for something that could have been managed another way.

For no purpose. The phrase is dōrean: without cause, for nothing, in vain. It is the same word Paul uses elsewhere for freely, as a gift (Romans 3:24), and the play is bitter. Either righteousness is given freely, or Christ died freely, for nothing. Every religion of human achievement, however sincerely held, ends up saying the second about the crucifixion, whether it means to or not.

Why Paul’s temper is not disproportionate. The Judaizers thought they were adding a little rigour to a message that had gone soft. Paul shows them what their addition actually implies about the cross, and the implication is blasphemous. You cannot say Christ plus my performance without saying, underneath it, that his performance was insufficient, and the cross does not survive being called a supplement.

Does this mean sincere, good people of other religions are lost? Paul’s logic answers it. If righteousness could come through the law of Moses, given by God himself, then Christ died for nothing; how much more if it could come through any other path. The cross was necessary because there is no other way to God, and so salvation is through conscious faith in Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). That is not arrogance on the Christian’s part; we are saved the same way, as beggars. Some Christians hope that God may save people through Christ without their ever knowing his name; Scripture gives no such promise to rest on, which is why the church sends missionaries, and every soul is safe in the hands of a Judge who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25). It is a reason for urgency and compassion. The people you love who trust in their own goodness need to hear about the one who died because their goodness could never be enough.

What if I keep feeling I must earn God’s favour? Most Christians do; the instinct to pay our way runs deep. Treat the feeling as a temptation, not a revelation. When it comes, answer it with this verse: if I could earn it, Christ died for nothing, and he did not die for nothing. Thank God out loud for what Christ has already done. Then go and obey, not to earn, but because you are loved; and when the obedience goes badly, do not let that reopen the question. The question was closed at the cross.

For worship. Had there been another way, the Son of God would have taken it; he asked in the garden whether there was, three times, and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground (Matthew 26:39–44; Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts). There was not. He went to the cross because nothing less would do, and he went knowing exactly what it cost, and he did not die for no purpose. He died for sinners, and it worked, and it is finished, and there is nothing to add to it (Hebrews 10:11–14).

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me.<sup>2</sup>I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.<sup>3</sup>But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek.<sup>4</sup>Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery—<sup>5</sup>to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.<sup>6</sup>And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me.<sup>7</sup>On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised<sup>8</sup>(for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),<sup>9</sup>and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.<sup>10</sup>Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.<sup>11</sup>But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.<sup>12</sup>For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.<sup>13</sup>And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy.<sup>14</sup>But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”<sup>15</sup>We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners;<sup>16</sup>yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.<sup>17</sup>But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!<sup>18</sup>For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor.<sup>19</sup>For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.<sup>20</sup>I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.<sup>21</sup>I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the heart of Paul’s argument in Galatians: God has always justified people by faith, not by the law. Paul argues first from the Galatians’ own experience. They received the Spirit by hearing the gospel with faith, not by keeping the law, and the faith that began their Christian life is the faith that carries it on. He argues from Abraham, who believed God and was counted righteous, so that all who believe are his children.

He argues from the law itself, which curses everyone who fails to keep it, and then comes to the centre of the chapter: Christ redeemed us from that curse by becoming a curse for us (v. 13). He took on himself the curse the law pronounces on all who fail to keep it, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. The law came centuries after the promise and cannot cancel it; it was added for a time, to expose sin and to guard God’s people until Christ came. Now all who believe are sons of God, clothed with Christ, one in him, and heirs of the promise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from defending his apostleship to the Galatians themselves, and instead of an argument he asks about their own experience: did they receive the Spirit by keeping the law, or by hearing the gospel and believing it (v. 2)? They knew the answer. Most of them were uncircumcised pagans who heard and believed, and God gave them his Spirit. To begin by the Spirit and then try to finish by human effort is folly (v. 3), and God is still at work among them on the same terms (v. 5).

The question runs straight on into Abraham (v. 6), who believed God and was counted righteous (Genesis 15:6). So it is those of faith who are Abraham’s sons (v. 7).
