Scripture announced the gospel to Abraham in advance, with the Gentiles already in view (v. 8), and every believer is blessed along with him, on the same footing (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Is Received by Faith

Paul’s appeal in vv. 2 and 5 is not to religious feeling but to a fact: how God gave them his Spirit. The Spirit unites us to Christ, and that union is received by faith alone; here Paul argues it from their own experience. If the Spirit came through hearing the gospel and not through works of the law, then law-keeping was never the channel, and no later addition can make it one.

Verse 3 shows that the Christian life does not have two stages, beginning by grace and advancing by performance. The same Spirit, received in the same way, is at work from first to last. And vv. 6–9 show that this is not new: Abraham was counted righteous by faith in Genesis 15, years before circumcision was given in Genesis 17. Justification by faith is how God has always dealt with sinners.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were not asking the Galatians to abandon Christ. They were offering completion: take the mark, keep the calendar, and become full sons of Abraham. Paul makes them look at their own conversion, when they had nothing in their hands and God gave them his Spirit, and then he takes Abraham, the Judaizers’ own best example, and shows that he too was justified by faith.

Now: Few believers decide to be justified by works; the drift of v. 3 is quieter. Over the years our empty hands fill with good things, a habit of prayer, a place on the serving rota, a reputation, and our confidence slowly moves from Christ to them. The cure is in vv. 6–9: there is one way in, by faith in God’s promise, and the newest believer stands in it beside Abraham himself.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 3 is Paul’s great argument that God has always justified people by faith, not by the law. He argues from the Galatians’ own experience: they received the Spirit by believing the gospel, not by keeping the law (vv. 1–5). He argues from Abraham, who believed God and was counted righteous, so that those of faith are his true children (vv. 6–9). He argues from the law, which curses everyone who fails to keep it, a curse Christ bore for us on the cross (vv. 10–14). He argues from history: the promise to Abraham and his offspring, Christ, came 430 years before the law and cannot be cancelled by it (vv. 15–18). The law was added because of transgressions, to imprison all under sin and act as a guardian until Christ came (vv. 19–25). Now all believers are God’s children through faith, clothed with Christ, one in him, and heirs of the promise (vv. 26–29).

O foolish Galatians! The letter has already left out the thanksgiving with which Paul’s letters to churches normally open. Now it drops the courtesy altogether. The word is anoētoi: not stupid, not uneducated, but without understanding, people with a perfectly good brain who have stopped using it on the one subject where everything is at stake. A man can hold a degree and read the market correctly every morning and still be anoētos about the gospel. Paul is not insulting their intelligence. He is saying they have stopped thinking about what they already know.

Who has bewitched you? The verb is baskainō, from the world of the evil eye: the malign look that was thought to wither a crop or sicken a child. Like the rest of the ancient world, Galatia was full of magic and superstition, and Paul’s readers knew the idea well. Paul does not believe in the evil eye, and he is not saying a spell was cast. He is reaching for the only category that fits what he is looking at: something has come over these people that ordinary argument does not explain. They have not been out-reasoned. They have been charmed. The false teaching worked like a spell, fascinating them away from the truth. And see where he puts the eye. Something has looked at them and done them harm, and yet what was set before their eyes was Jesus Christ crucified: two sights competing for the same congregation, and whichever one you keep looking at is the one that will shape you.

Publicly portrayed as crucified. The word is prographō: posted up, placarded, written large in a public place. In a Galatian town, if the governor issued a ruling or a runaway slave was being sought, a notice went up in the marketplace where everyone passing had to walk by it. That is Paul’s picture of his own preaching. He had not offered them a religious option or a spiritual perspective. He had put up a public notice in their town, and the notice said: the Son of God was executed, and it was for you. How could they look away from the cross to the law?

Before your eyes. None of the Galatians had been at Golgotha. Neither had Paul. So in what sense was it before their eyes? In this sense: preaching that does its work does not merely inform people about the cross, it sets the cross in front of them until they can see it, the plain announcement of what happened, made so clear that a listener in a Galatian market town could shut his eyes and see a man on a Roman beam dying in his place.

In the flow. Paul closed chapter 2 with his own confession, I have been crucified with Christ, and its sharp edge: if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose (2:20–21). Verse 1 picks up that word crucified and turns it on the readers. Paul has told his own story (1:11–2:21); now he argues from theirs (3:1–5), and then from Abraham and the law (3:6–4:7). The argument starts at the cross because the cross is what the false teaching quietly empties: if a little law-keeping must be added, Christ died for no reason.

How do I keep Christ crucified before my eyes? By putting yourself, deliberately and often, where the cross is set before you. Sit under preaching that is full of Christ and his cross, not only of advice. Come to the Lord’s Supper as the moment the Lord himself places his death in front of you (1 Corinthians 11:26). Read the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion slowly, more than once a year. Sing hymns that dwell on it. And when your conscience accuses you, train yourself to answer it by looking there first, not at your week. The cross does not fade because it changes. It fades because we stop looking.

For worship. God did not leave the Galatians to guess what he is like. He put it on a placard in their town, and the placard was his own Son, dying for enemies. There is nothing more to see of the heart of God than this. Every spell that dazzles us away from it is a cheap light beside a crucified Lord, and the God who painted that picture before our eyes is still the one who opens them to see it.
verseByVerse.note: “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye. “Publicly portrayed” uses the word for a public notice posted for all to read.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let me ask you only this. Paul has a whole letter of arguments ready, covenants, chronology, Abraham, Moses, an allegory about two women, and before he uses any of them he asks one question. If they answer it honestly, the entire programme of the Judaizers, the teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, collapses without another word being spoken.

Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The question is not about theology. It is about their own biography. He does not ask them what they believe now, because that is exactly what is in dispute and is being renegotiated weekly by men with impressive credentials. He asks them what happened to them then. That is not up for negotiation. It is a matter of record, and every one of them was there. And the Spirit is the decisive mark of belonging to God: anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). So if they have the Spirit, they already belong.

What had happened. They knew perfectly well. Paul had walked into their towns, a travel-worn stranger, and announced a crucified and risen Jew as Lord of the world. Some of them believed it, and God gave them himself. The Spirit came not as a doctrine they later worked out but as an event they lived through: sins forgiven, a new hunger for God, love for people they had despised, and in some cases manifest power. Most of them were uncircumcised pagans who had never kept a Sabbath or refused a piece of pork. They heard and believed, and God moved in.

The question answers itself. The Judaizers taught that the law completes what faith begins. Paul says: run the tape back. When God gave you the greatest gift he has ever given anyone, his own indwelling Spirit, what was in your hands? Nothing. You heard, and believed.

Hearing with faith. The phrase is akoē pisteōs, and it is deliberately loose in Greek. It can mean the hearing that consists of faith, or the message that is heard and produces faith (Romans 10:17). Paul may well intend both, because in his mind they are one motion: a message announced, and a heart that stops arguing and takes it. That is the whole of the human contribution, and even the taking is worked in us by the Spirit we are receiving.

A gift poured out by the risen Son. Why should hearing be enough? Because of who it was the Galatians heard about. The Spirit they received was not a reward for listening well; he was the gift Christ had won. Paul will say before the chapter is out that Christ became a curse for us so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith (3:13–14), and Peter told the crowd at Pentecost that the exalted Jesus had received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit and poured him out (Acts 2:33). So when the Galatians believed, they were not reaching up to God. The crucified and risen Lord was reaching down to them, sharing with the empty-handed what he had bought with his own blood.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit is received in a second experience after faith. They received him when they believed. There is no Christian without the Spirit, and no later stage at which a believer is given him for the first time.

How do I know I have received the Spirit? Not mainly by an unusual experience, though God may give one, but by what the Spirit does. He makes you trust Christ and call God Father (4:6; Romans 8:15–16). He makes Christ precious to you and the Bible alive to you. He gives you a new hatred of your sin and a new desire to please God. He grows love, joy, peace and the rest of his fruit, slowly and often unnoticed (5:22–23). He draws you to other believers. If you believe in Jesus and want to follow him, however weakly, the Spirit is already at work in you, because no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you so foolish? He asks it a second time, repeated in amazement, and this time he supplies the content of the folly. It is the sentence in this letter that ordinary Christians most need to hear: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?

Begun and perfected. Two words carry it. Begun is enarxamenoi and perfected is epiteleō, to complete, to bring to maturity: a matched pair that could be used in the ancient world of a sacrifice, where you begin the rite and you bring it to completion. So the Galatians are not proposing to abandon the Spirit. Nobody in Galatia was. The false teachers said: faith is the start, but circumcision and law-keeping complete you. Paul says the proposal is not maturity but madness: you began with the Spirit of God himself at work in you, and you now propose to finish with a knife and a calendar.

What “flesh” means here. Flesh here is not what most readers assume. It is not first lust or greed or temper. Circumcision is a cut in literal flesh; the whole programme of the Judaizers lands on the body. So the flesh Paul means is the entire realm of what a human being can do, mark, keep and show: religious achievement, visible, measurable, and yours. He is not warning them off sin here. He is warning them off religion as self-effort.

How it happens to us. That is why this verse finds the reader who is doing nothing obviously wrong. Almost no Christian consciously decides to be justified by works. What happens is quieter. You come to Christ with empty hands and are received with joy. Then, over a few years, the hands slowly fill: a devotional habit, a serving rota, a reputation for reliability. None of it is bad; all of it may be the Spirit’s own fruit. But somewhere the ground of your confidence migrates from the finished work of Christ to the evidence of your progress, and you never notice the day it moved.

Perfected by a single offering. The Galatians were being offered completion. But the New Testament has already said where Christian completeness lies. By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). He is our righteousness and sanctification and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30). The finishing the false teachers were selling had already been done on a cross, and the Spirit’s work in the believer is not to add to it but to make us, day by day, more like the one in whom we are already complete (Colossians 2:10). To reach for the flesh to finish what Christ has finished is not to go further. It is to step back from him.

Did you suffer so many things in vain? Then verse 4, and the tone changes. The verb paschō can mean suffer or simply experience. These people had paid for their faith. If, as many think, these churches included the towns of Acts 13–14, they had watched Paul stoned at Lystra and dragged out of the city for dead, and had taken their own share of it; Paul and Barnabas told them that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:2, 5, 19–22). Or Paul may mean the many blessings they had experienced. Either way, would they throw it away? He is asking whether all of that was for nothing.

If indeed it was in vain. And then he cannot finish the sentence. The great polemicist, mid-thunder, breaks off and will not pronounce them lost. He raises the possibility because they need to feel the danger, and then refuses to close his hand on it. That half-line is worth a paragraph of reassurance: this is a man who is furious with them and cannot bear the thought of losing them, and the two are not in tension (2 Corinthians 2:4; Galatians 4:19).

Where Christians differ: sanctification by effort? Some think justification is by faith, but sanctification is by our own effort and rule-keeping. Justification is the Judge’s verdict, given once and never revised; sanctification is the slow, real change by which the Spirit makes the justified person holy in practice. Verdict: sanctification, like justification, is a work of the Spirit received by faith. It involves real effort and obedience (Philippians 2:12–13), but effort that depends on the Spirit, not on the flesh. Christians grow not by adding laws but by walking in the Spirit (5:16, 25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians make no effort. It means the effort is Spirit-empowered faith, not self-reliant striving. Paul worked harder than anyone, and said in the same breath that it was not he, but the grace of God that was with him (1 Corinthians 15:10).

Then what do I actually do to grow? Use the means God has given, and use them as a needy child, not as a contractor. Read and hear his word, because the Spirit grows faith through it. Pray, because prayer is the confession that you cannot do it alone. Come to the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. Obey in the specific thing in front of you, asking for strength as you do it. Put sin to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13): name it, flee it, cut off what feeds it. The difference between Spirit and flesh is not whether you make an effort, but what you lean on while you make it, and who gets the credit when it works.

On a Tuesday. Take your worst week: the one where you prayed nothing, snapped at everyone, and went to church because it was easier than explaining why you had not. On that Sunday, was God as pleased with you in Christ as on your best Sunday of the year? The gospel answers yes: exactly as pleased, because on both Sundays you stood in Christ and not in your week. If something in you flinches at that answer, you have started finishing by the flesh what was begun by the Spirit, and the way back is the way you began: empty hands, and Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith— just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he who supplies the Spirit. The last of Paul’s questions, and it moves the argument from their past into their present. Not did God supply the Spirit, but does he: epichorēgōn, a present participle, going on supplying. And works miracles among you is present too (Acts 14:3, 8–10). Whatever the Judaizers were saying about the Galatians’ deficient standing, God had evidently not stopped moving among them. The evidence was in the room while the argument was going on.

Supplies. The word Paul chooses is worth a moment. Chorēgeō began in the world of the theatre: the chorēgos was the wealthy citizen who paid for a chorus for the civic festival, at his own expense and as an honour. By Paul’s day the verb simply meant to supply or provide, often generously, and the old picture still suits it. That is the verb for what God does with the Holy Spirit. He is not paying wages. He is underwriting the whole thing, generously, because he chose to.

Do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? The same question as verse 2, and the answer is just as obvious: by faith. And the question does not end there. It runs straight on into verse 6: or by hearing with faith, just as Abraham believed God? Abraham is not a new topic. He is the last clause of the question, and the question is still a question when his name arrives.

Just as Abraham believed God. The quotation is Genesis 15:6, and Paul chose his ground with care. The false teachers appealed to Abraham, who was circumcised (Genesis 17). Paul appeals to Abraham too: before he was circumcised, he was counted righteous by faith (Romans 4:9–11). So what happened in Galatia last year and what happened to Abraham two thousand years earlier are the same transaction: God spoke, a man believed him, and God credited it to him as righteousness. The Judaizers had managed to hold up the father of the Jewish nation as the argument against the very way he was justified.

Counted. The verb is a bookkeeping term: logizomai, to credit, to reckon, to post an entry to an account. Abraham had done nothing to earn the entry: a childless old man under a sky full of stars, told his descendants would be that many, he took God at his word. God wrote righteous in the ledger against his name. Not improving, not on probation: righteous, in full, that night, before circumcision, before Moriah, before any work could be set against the account. This is imputation: God credited righteousness to his account.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham’s faith was so admirable that God accepted it in place of the righteousness he lacked; that would make faith a rather cheap work, and put the ground of acceptance back inside the man. Faith is the empty hand that receives a righteousness belonging to another. The credit posted to Abraham’s account was real, and it was not generated by Abraham (Romans 4:3–5; Philippians 3:9).

Written for us also. Paul says elsewhere that the words it was counted to him were written for our sake also, who believe in him who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 4:23–25). Abraham believed God about a son not yet born; we believe the same God about the Son who has come, died and risen. And the entry God writes is no fiction. He can write righteous against a sinner’s name without falsifying the books because the debt was posted to Christ: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Where Christians differ: do miracles continue? They were the signs that accompanied the first preaching of the gospel in Galatia; Luke says that at Iconium the Lord bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands (Acts 14:3). Paul’s point is not that miracles are normal, but that God gave the Spirit and his powers to people who believed, not to people who kept the law. Continuationists, Christians who believe all the gifts of the apostolic age continue today, take the present tense here as evidence that such works go on in every church, and many of them are careful, faithful readers of Scripture. Verdict: the more likely reading is that these signs belonged to the apostolic founding of the churches, the signs of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and have ceased in that form; the Spirit himself, received by faith, remains, and God still answers prayer, heals and acts in his providence as he pleases. Brothers who see it differently are to be loved as brothers.

Do Paul and James disagree about Abraham? James quotes the same verse about Abraham and says he was justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac (James 2:21–23). Genesis 15 gives the verdict; Genesis 22, many years later, shows the faith was real. James speaks of faith shown to be real, Paul of faith counted before God. There is one Abraham, with one faith: the faith that received God’s verdict under the stars was the same faith that climbed Moriah.

Is my faith strong enough to be counted? It is not the strength of your faith that saves you, but the strength of the one you trust. Abraham’s faith was real but not flawless; between Genesis 15 and 22 he lied about his wife and tried to force the promise through Hagar. A drowning man who grabs a rope with a trembling hand is pulled out just as surely as one with a firm grip, because the rope does the saving. If you are trusting Christ, even with doubts and fears, God counts his righteousness to you in full. Ask him to strengthen your faith, as the father did who said, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24).

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those of faith. Paul is drawing a conclusion, and in a first-century synagogue it is a bombshell. To be a son of Abraham was a legal identity: inside the covenant, inside the promises, inside the people God had bound himself to. It was traced by blood and marked in the body, and a Gentile could enter only by becoming, in effect, a Jew. That was exactly the offer the Judaizers were making, and from the inside it looked generous: take the mark and be a full son of Abraham like us.

Faith, not blood. Paul cuts the ground out from under it in a single sentence. Abraham’s true children are not his physical descendants or those circumcised, but those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12, 16). Jesus said the same to men who boasted of their descent: if you were Abraham’s children, you would be doing the works Abraham did (John 8:39). Descent from Abraham was never the thing that made a man Abraham’s son in the sense that counted, or Ishmael and Esau would have been in.

The Scripture, foreseeing. Observe who is speaking. Scripture foresaw and Scripture preached: what Scripture says, God says, so entirely is the text his speech. God planned from the start to justify Gentiles by faith. Justify is the language of acquittal: not making someone good inside, but declaring him in the right, acquitted and accepted, as a judge pronounces a verdict (Deuteronomy 25:1). He meant to say that of Gentiles who simply believed him, and to say it on the ground of what his Son would do (Romans 3:24–26). So whoever opens his Bible is not reading about a God who once spoke. He is being spoken to.

Preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham. The verb is proeuangelizomai: to announce the gospel in advance. Paul is claiming that when God said to a childless man from Mesopotamia, in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 18:18), the gospel was already being announced: the actual gospel, the one Paul preaches, in its seed form. The gospel is not new; it is the fulfilment of God’s oldest promise.

The blessing has a name. In you all the nations shall be blessed: but how would a blessing reach every family on earth through one old man from Ur? Through his offspring. Peter, preaching in the temple, quoted the same promise and told his hearers what it meant: God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness (Acts 3:25–26). The blessing of Abraham is not a vague goodwill toward the nations. It is Jesus, crucified and raised, turning sinners back to God. When the Galatians believed, they were not slipping into Abraham’s family by a side door. They were receiving the very Person the promise had been carrying since Genesis.

Inside out. So the Judaizers had the story inside out. They treated Gentile inclusion as a late concession, to be granted only on Jewish terms. Paul says it was the point from the beginning: the family existed so that the blessing could reach everyone else.

Blessed along with Abraham. Not blessed after him, at a lower grade, in a side chamber. Along with him. “Man of faith” translates pistos, believing or faithful. An Anatolian farmer who believed a travelling preacher stands in the same blessing as the patriarch, and stands in it on the same footing: justification, the Spirit, and the inheritance.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists, who read the Bible as a series of distinct eras, distinguish sharply between Israel and the church as two peoples with separate promises; many of them are devoted students of Scripture and warm friends of the Jewish people. Verdict: Paul teaches that all who have faith, Jew or Gentile, are Abraham’s children and heirs of the promise (v. 29). There is one people of God across history, united by faith in the promised offspring, Christ. This is covenant theology’s insight: the one covenant of grace, administered in different ways, runs from Abraham to the church (the Westminster Confession 7.5–6). God has not cast off the Jewish people (Romans 11:1–2, 23), but they are saved within the one people, not alongside it.

Has the church then replaced Israel? Not in the sense the question usually means. Paul is not saying that the Jewish people have no future, but that Abraham’s true family has always been defined by faith, not blood. Gentiles who believe are added to that family; Jews who believe are its natural members; and unbelieving Jews can be grafted back in (Romans 11:23). The family was never replaced. It was enlarged to its intended size.

Do Jewish people today need to believe in Jesus? Yes, and to say so is not hostility but love. Paul, a Jew, wept over his own people and prayed that they would be saved (Romans 9:1–3; 10:1). Since Abraham’s true children are those of faith, and the promise was always to his offspring, Christ, there is no way to Abraham’s blessing that bypasses Abraham’s Seed. Christians should therefore love Jewish people, reject every form of antisemitism as a sin against the people from whom Christ came, and share the gospel with them gladly, humbly, and first (Romans 1:16).

For worship. Abraham has been a believer for four thousand years and is blessed by faith. You believed last March and are blessed by faith. There is one queue, and everybody in it got in the same way. And at the head of it stands not Abraham but the God who called him, who looked at a childless man under the stars and saw already the farmers of Galatia and the city-dwellers of every continent, and he will not stop keeping that promise until every nation has come in.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having made his case from Abraham, Paul now makes it from the law. Verse 10 says something unexpected: it is those who rely on the law, the serious and observant, who are under a curse, because the law demands that everyone do all that it requires (Deuteronomy 27:26), and no one does. Verse 11 adds Habakkuk 2:4: the righteous live by faith. Verse 12 sets the law’s own principle beside it, from Leviticus 18:5. The law’s offer of life was real, but no sinner can meet its terms.

Then v. 13, the summit of the chapter: Christ bought us out from the law’s curse by becoming a curse in our place, and the text Paul quotes, Deuteronomy 21:23, is the very verse that made a crucified Messiah unthinkable to Saul the Pharisee. Verse 14 gives the purpose twice: so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles, and so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith, which brings the chapter back to the question of v. 2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

Verse 13 says plainly that Christ bore in our place the penalty due to sinners, the law’s curse. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could come to those who had no claim to it. He did not only suffer with us; he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

This does not mean the Father stopped loving the Son; Jesus said the opposite (John 10:17). The sentence was real, and so was the Father’s delight in his obedient Son in that same hour.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement to faith. Verses 10–12 show that the law cannot be a supplement: as a way to God it accepts only perfect obedience, and no one has given it. Verse 13 names the one way out, and v. 14 explains how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up with the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 already afraid that God is disappointed with them. Read it exactly. The curse falls on relying on the law, the very thing we use to cover our failure, and v. 13 says what became of it: the sentence was carried out, and not on you.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who rely on works of the law. Paul has proved his case from Abraham; now he proves it from the law itself, and lets the law do the talking. He does not say that those who break the law are under a curse. He says that those who rely on it are: the serious ones, the observant ones. “Rely on” is literally are of the works of the law: those whose standing with God depends on law-keeping. The very people who thought the law was their shelter are standing under the one thing it guarantees for sinners. What does it mean to be under a curse? Not to be under a spell or a run of bad luck. In Scripture a curse is the opposite of God’s blessing: his sentence of judgement on the sinner, shutting him out from God’s favour and leaving him under God’s wrath (Deuteronomy 28:15; Matthew 25:41).

For it is written. And then the proof, quoted from the law’s own closing ceremony. In Deuteronomy 27, Israel is drawn up in two halves on two mountains, Ebal and Gerizim, with the covenant read aloud between them, and the last of twelve curses is the one Paul takes (Deuteronomy 27:26). At the end of every curse the whole nation answered Amen, ratifying the terms themselves. The law offers blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience.

Four words. Now weigh the words Paul leans on. Everyone: no exemptions, no distinguished-service discount. All things: the whole code, not a representative selection. Abide by: continuously, not in a good season. And do them: performance, not agreement; you can admire a command all your life without once obeying it. The law demands perfect, complete obedience. And the unstated premise of the whole argument is the one every reader knows: no one does all things.

A seamless garment. Put those together and the law turns out not to be a pass mark but a seamless garment. It cannot be scored out of a hundred. James says the same thing from the other end: whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it (James 2:10). That sounds harsh until you see why it is true. The law is not a list of separate regulations; it is the expression of one Person’s will. To break any of it is to have said no to him, and you do not need to say no on every subject to have said no.

A road and a cliff. So the choice Paul lays out is not between an easier and a harder road to God, but between a road and a cliff. Whoever takes his stand on law-keeping has entered a system with only two verdicts, flawless obedience and curse, and he has already failed, which is why the religion of the law-keeper is so often anxious under its composure.

An altar on the mountain of curse. When Moses gave the order for it, he told Israel to build an altar of uncut stones and offer burnt offerings and peace offerings on Mount Ebal, the very mountain where the tribes stood for the curse (Deuteronomy 27:4–7, 13). The sacrifice stood where the curse fell. Even on the day Israel said Amen to its own condemnation, God was pointing to the only way a cursed people could live: an offering made in their place. That altar was a shadow. The substance came when the one man who abode by all things, who could say I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29), went outside the city wall to take the law’s curse on himself.

Is God disappointed with me? This is where a certain kind of reader needs to be met honestly, because he is reading with his stomach tight. He is not one of the Judaizers, the teachers who made law-keeping a condition of acceptance. He has simply never been able to shake the sense that God is disappointed with him, and this verse looks like proof. If you are that reader, look at exactly what Paul says and what he does not. He does not say that people who sin are cursed with no way out; if he did, there would be no hope for anyone in this letter or out of it. He says that people who rely on law-keeping are cursed, because they have chosen a standard that will certainly convict them. The curse is not aimed at your failure so much as at the thing you were trying to use to cover your failure. And the curse did not stay where it was aimed: Christ redeemed us from it by becoming a curse for us (3:13).

Were the Israelites of the Old Testament all under this curse? Not those who trusted God. Old Testament believers were saved the same way Abraham was: by faith in God’s promise, looking forward to the Redeemer. The law itself provided sacrifices for sin, pointing to Christ, and the psalms are full of people who knew they could not stand on their own record and cast themselves on God’s mercy (Psalm 32:1–2; 130:3–4). What Paul condemns is relying on the law as the ground of acceptance, which the faithful in Israel never did. David, Isaiah and Daniel were not law-climbers; they were forgiven sinners who loved God’s law because they had first received his mercy.

On a Tuesday. Most of us stand on our record more often than we think: when you feel you deserve an answer to prayer because you have been faithful, or that God owes you a smoother life because of your service. Those are small reliances on works, and they lead to anxiety or resentment. Step back from the cliff edge. You do not have to stand on your own record: Christ abode by all things written for you and took the curse you earned, so his obedience is counted as yours (Romans 5:19), and your imperfect service is accepted for his sake, not weighed as wages.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evident. Two verses, two quotations from the Old Testament, and between them Paul settles the question of how anyone has ever been right with God. Evident is dēlon, plain, obvious, in view. He is not about to prove something contested; he is pointing at something already established. Before God: in his sight, by his standard.

For “The righteous shall live by faith.” The proof is Habakkuk 2:4 (also Romans 1:17; Hebrews 10:38). Habakkuk had been watching the Babylonians come, and he could not square the horizon with the character of God. The answer he was given was not an explanation but a way to survive: the righteous man will live, keep breathing, keep standing, keep his footing when everything visible is against him, by faith. Paul takes that sentence as the shape of the whole Christian life. Luther took it from Paul; by his own account it was the verse that opened the gospel to him, and through him it shook the medieval church.

The one who does them. The quotation is Leviticus 18:5. As a way to righteousness, the law works on a different principle from faith. The law’s principle is: do and live. Faith’s principle is: believe and live. Since no one does them perfectly, life by the law is impossible.

How can Paul set Moses against Habakkuk? It can look as if Paul is pitting one Old Testament verse against another. He is not. In Leviticus 18:5, God speaks to a people he has already redeemed from Egypt: keep my laws and you will enjoy life with me in the land. For them, obedience was the grateful way of life of the redeemed, and the sacrifices were provided for their failures. But the false teachers were using the law as a ladder to climb up to God: do these things and you will be accepted. Paul takes them at their word. If you make the law the ground of your acceptance, then Leviticus 18:5 states the terms: you must do them, all of them (v. 10), to live by them. No sinner can meet those terms. Habakkuk 2:4 states the other way, the only way open to sinners: the righteous live by trusting God. Christ is the one person who met the terms of Leviticus 18:5, and he did it for us (4:4–5; Romans 10:4–5).

A sound contract offered to a bankrupt. Leviticus 18:5 states the law’s principle truthfully. The law really does promise life to whoever keeps it. That offer was never a bluff, and there is nothing defective about the law: it is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). The defect is in the material it has to work with. As Paul puts it elsewhere, the law was weakened by the flesh (Romans 8:3), like a perfectly sound contract offered to a bankrupt. The terms are excellent. He cannot meet them.

Two kinds of sentence. So the two verses are not two rival roads to God, one strict and one generous. Do and live puts the weight on the doer; live by faith puts it on the one believed. They are two answers to one question, who is responsible for my standing before God, and the second answer cancels the first.

The coming one. Habakkuk’s sentence has a setting, and the letter to the Hebrews quotes it with its setting. The prophet was told to wait for the vision: if it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come (Habakkuk 2:3). Hebrews reads that waiting as waiting for Christ: yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith (Hebrews 10:37–38). Faith was never trust in trust. It was trust in what God would send, and what he sent was his Son. The righteous live by faith because the Righteous One has come, and every believer since Habakkuk has been leaning on that same arrival.

What does living by faith look like when life is hard? It looks like Habakkuk. He did not get an explanation of why the Babylonians were coming; he got a promise, and a God to trust. By the end of his book the fig tree has not blossomed, the fields have failed and the stalls are empty, and he says he will still rejoice in the LORD and take joy in the God of his salvation (Habakkuk 3:17–18). Living by faith does not mean pretending things are fine. It means telling God honestly that they are not, and then deciding to trust what he has said about himself over what your circumstances are saying. The righteous do not live by understanding. They live by faith.

For worship. Leviticus 18:5 was never revoked. Someone had to do the things and live by them, and someone did. One man on this earth could stand under the law’s own terms and claim its promise honestly. He earned the life. And then he went to a place where the law had nothing but a curse to give, and he took the curse instead, and left the life to us.

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith
by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. Everything in the chapter has been climbing to this sentence, and every word in it is load-bearing. Redeemed is exagorazō, a word built on the market-place: to buy out, to purchase and set free, as a slave could be bought out of slavery. It assumes a real transaction with a real price paid to secure a real release.

From the curse of the law. And what were we bought out from? Not from the law as God’s good will, but from the curse of the law, which is verse 10 come home. The curse is the penalty the law pronounces on lawbreakers: death and God’s wrath.

By becoming a curse for us. Then the mechanism, and it is deliberately shocking. Not by pitying us, not by identifying with us, not by showing us how much God cares. He became the thing itself. “For us” is hyper hēmōn, on our behalf, in our place. This is penal substitution: Christ bore in our place the penalty God’s law pronounces on our sin, so that it will never be laid on us (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). The penalty is what makes it penal; the exchange of places is what makes it substitution. He did not only suffer alongside us, or for our good in some general way.

Hanged on a tree. The proof text is one that no Jew could hear without flinching (Deuteronomy 21:23). That law is worth understanding precisely. In Deuteronomy 21 hanging is not the method of execution. A man convicted of a capital crime is put to death, and then his body is hung on a tree as a public sign of what he was, and it must be taken down by nightfall, because a hanged man is cursed by God and the land must not be defiled. The tree did not make him cursed; it announced the verdict of heaven to everyone walking past.

Saul before a cross. Now put Saul of Tarsus in front of a crucified man. For a Pharisee this text was not a difficulty about Jesus of Nazareth; it was the closing argument. God had published his verdict on a beam outside the city wall for the whole province to read. A crucified Messiah was blasphemy with a scriptural footnote, a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). Which is what makes this verse, written by that man, so astonishing. On the Damascus road the argument did not go away; it went inside out. Saul had been right that the tree published a curse. He had been wrong about only one thing: whose. For us. The two smallest words in the sentence are the whole gospel. He was cursed, and not for anything he had done.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was personally guilty or that God stopped loving his Son. To say Christ became a curse is not to say the Father was privately disgusted with him, or turned on him in temper. Jesus himself said the opposite: for this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life (John 10:17). The Son was never more precious to the Father than in the hour he was bearing our sentence, and the sentence was real, and both of those are true at once.

Why did it have to be a cross? Because God meant the manner of Christ’s death to say what it was. Any death would have shown that he died; only a death on a tree could show, in the law’s own language, that he died under the curse. The authorities who handed him over may well have wanted him crucified to show that God had rejected him, and the Romans wanted it to shame him; God used both to publish the truth they did not intend: that the curse of God was falling on this man for sinners. The shame was not an accident around the edges of the atonement. It was part of the price, and Jesus despised it for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2).

Is this fair, that an innocent man should be punished for the guilty? It would be unjust if a judge seized an unwilling bystander. But that is not what happened. The Son came willingly, as one with the Father in purpose. He is himself the Judge who was wronged, choosing to bear the penalty of those who wronged him. And he is our representative, united to us as our head, as Adam was, so that what he did counts for those who are his. God is not punishing a third party. He is, in his Son, taking the cost of our sin on himself. That is not injustice. It is the highest justice joined to the deepest love (Romans 3:25–26).

On a Tuesday. When your past sins come back to accuse you, do not answer by listing your recent improvements. Name the sin, and then say: that curse fell on him, outside the city wall, and it will not fall on me.

For worship. The law had one thing to say to every human being who came to it for a verdict, and it was right to say it. And the Son of God walked into the courtroom, took the sentence before it reached us, and carried it out of the city on his own back. The tree that was designed to publish the curse of God has become the place where the curse of God ran out.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was under God’s curse.

parallels.desc: a hanged man is cursed by God

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing of Abraham. Now the purpose clause, and Paul gives it twice: so that, so that. The cross was a rescue not only from something but for something. First, the blessing promised to Abraham, justification and life, now flows to the nations (v. 8). That promise has been travelling since Genesis 12, through Isaac and Jacob, a nation, a monarchy and an exile, and here it arrives, in a Galatian town, in the hands of people whose grandparents worshipped Zeus. The cross opened a promise made in Mesopotamia to the whole world.

In Christ Jesus. And observe how it arrives. Not around him, not because God relaxed the terms, not by God deciding after all these years that circumcision did not matter much. The blessing reaches the nations by way of one man’s cross. The Judaizers wanted Gentiles brought in through the door marked become a Jew; God brought them in through a door marked be in Christ, and it is the only door there has ever been.

Closing the circle. Second, the Spirit, and with that Paul closes the circle he opened in verse 2. He began the chapter by asking how they got the Spirit; he now says the cross is why they got him, and that he is received through faith, not law-keeping. The blessing of Abraham and the gift of the Spirit go together.

The promised Spirit. The phrase tells the reader what he is holding. The Spirit is not a bonus for advanced believers or a second stage for the especially earnest. He is the promise: God himself coming to live in Gentile bodies. When Ezekiel said God would put his Spirit within his people and cause them to walk in his statutes (Ezekiel 36:27), and Joel said he would pour him out on all flesh (Joel 2:28), this was what they were describing. The Galatians had it. They were being told they lacked something.

Am I missing a deeper blessing? The most common form of Christian discouragement is not doubt about doctrine; it is the settled suspicion that you have somehow received a lesser version of the Christian faith than other people have: that there is a fuller thing, a deeper blessing, a level of God’s favour that others reached and you did not. Verse 14 forecloses it. The blessing of Abraham and the promised Spirit are not two prizes handed out at different levels of attainment. They are one gift, purchased at one cross, received by one faith, and if you are in Christ you have them. You may grow in enjoying what you have; you will never be given more of a standing than you already possess.

How do I depend on the Spirit day by day? Begin each day by acknowledging him: you live in me, and I need you today. Before you read Scripture, ask him to open it. Before a hard conversation, ask him for the right words and a gentle heart. When temptation comes, ask him for strength in the moment, and then act, trusting that he is giving it. When you fail, do not grieve him further by hiding; confess and return. Depending on the Spirit is not a feeling you wait for. It is a posture of asking, trusting and obeying, all day long.

parallels.desc: I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul turns from the cross to an illustration from everyday law, and calls the Galatians brothers again. Once a covenant or will has been ratified, no one can add a clause to it (v. 15), and the Judaizers’ demand was exactly that, an amendment to God’s promise. The promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ (v. 16): at every fork the line of promise narrowed, Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau, then Judah and David, toward one person.

The law came 430 years after the promise and cannot cancel it (v. 17). And the inheritance cannot come both by law and by promise (v. 18): God gave it to Abraham freely, and it stands given.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise Comes First and Cannot Fail

God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s offspring came before the law of Moses and does not depend on it. The covenant of grace, God’s one plan to save sinners by grace through faith in the promised Christ, runs through the whole Bible, and the law given at Sinai served it for a season without changing its terms.

Verse 16 shows why the promise cannot fail. God made it with the one heir who would not break it, and everyone else inherits by being in him. And in v. 18 the verb is a perfect tense: God has given it, and it stands given. A promise that rests on the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything that depends on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers argued, in effect, that the law of Moses changed the conditions of the earlier promise to Abraham. Verses 15 and 17 show that this is impossible, and v. 18 shows what it would cost: not an improved promise but no promise at all.

Now: Because the inheritance rests on God’s promise and not on our performance, a believer who fails can run to his Father instead of hiding from him, and get up again as one whose house is already his.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To give a human example, brothers. The temperature drops. He has just been at Golgotha; now he takes them to a lawyer’s office for an illustration from everyday life. And he calls them brothers, the anger letting a warm word through, as it did at 1:11.

In the flow. Paul has shown from Abraham (3:6–9) and from the law’s own curse (3:10–14) that the blessing comes by faith. But a careful opponent has a reply ready: granted that Abraham was justified by faith, did God not give the law later, at Sinai, and does the later word not set the terms now? Verses 15–18 answer that objection. A promise God has sworn cannot be amended by something that came afterwards, and the promise was made to Christ. That raises the next question, which Paul faces at once: then why was the law given at all (3:19)?

A man-made covenant. The word is diathēkē, which covers both a covenant and a last will and testament, and Paul is using the overlap. His point holds either way. Once a will is signed and legally confirmed, the seals on and the witnesses signed, an interested party cannot come along later and insert a clause. If that is true of a document drawn up by men, who forget things and change their minds, how much more of an agreement God has sworn to?

An amendment is a different document. The relevance is exact. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise to Abraham. They were proposing an amendment: the promise, plus a condition. Paul says that is not a modest adjustment. It is a legal impossibility, and anyone attempting it is not adding to God’s covenant but writing a different one.

The promises. God’s promises to Abraham are repeated again and again (Genesis 12:7; 13:15; 17:8; 22:18), and verse 16 is where readers stop and frown.

Who is Christ. Paul observes that God said to your offspring, singular, not offsprings, plural, and concludes that the promise was made to one person, who is Christ. To a modern reader that looks like a trick. Offspring (literally seed) is a collective noun, singular in form, often plural in meaning, and the Hebrew zera’ and the Greek sperma behind it work the same way. Genesis 15:5 promised Abraham descendants as numerous as the stars, and it plainly does not mean one star. Is Paul playing games with grammar? He is not, and the proof is thirteen verses later. In verse 29 Paul himself uses the same word collectively: you are Abraham’s offspring, of a whole church full of people. A man does not build an argument on a word’s singularity and then use it of a crowd unless he knows exactly what the word does.

The promise always narrowed. So what is the argument? This: the promise to Abraham always narrowed. It was never simply handed to his descendants as a body. Ishmael was a son of Abraham and was not the line of promise: through Isaac shall your offspring be named (Genesis 21:12). Esau was a son of Isaac and was passed over. The line runs to Judah, then to David, then to David’s house, and at every fork it gets narrower, never wider. The singular form lets Paul say what the shape of the history was always saying: this promise had one destination, and it was a person. And Genesis itself hints at it: after the binding of Isaac God says that in Abraham’s offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, and the offspring will possess the gate of his enemies (Genesis 22:17–18). Paul is not importing Christ into the Old Testament. He is reading it the way the risen Christ taught his disciples to read it on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27).

Do all the promises of the Old Testament apply to me? All the covenant promises of God find their yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20), and if you are in Christ you share in them: forgiveness, God as your God, his presence, his Spirit, his faithfulness, an everlasting inheritance. But read each promise in its setting. Some were given to particular people for particular situations, such as a specific word to a king or to the exiles in Babylon, and they show God’s character rather than guaranteeing you the same outcome. The safe way is to ask: what does this promise show about God, and how is it fulfilled in Christ? Then you can claim it through him without twisting it.

On a Tuesday. If the promise was made to Christ, then it cannot fail, because its heir cannot fail. When you doubt whether God will keep his word to you, stop looking at your own reliability and look at his Son’s. The promise does not rest on your grip. It rests on the one to whom it was made, and you are in him.
verseByVerse.note: “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one descendant or many.

parallels.desc: in your offspring shall all the nations be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law, which came 430 years afterward. Now Paul puts a date on it. The promise is the older document by four centuries, and in any court the later paper cannot cancel the earlier one.

The 430 years. A reader with a study Bible will stop at the number, and he is right to. Exodus 12:40 says the people of Israel lived in Egypt 430 years. But the Greek Old Testament that Paul and his readers used, and the Samaritan text, read in Egypt and in Canaan, that is, 430 years from the patriarchs to the exodus in total. Paul uses this figure for the gap between the promise and the law at Sinai, counting from the promises to the patriarchs, using the text his churches had in their hands. And nothing in his argument depends on the exact figure. Four hundred and thirty years, or four hundred, or two hundred: the promise came first, and that is the whole point.

If the inheritance comes by the law. Then verse 18 states the principle underneath, the cleanest either-or in the letter. An inheritance is given; a wage is earned. Law and promise are not enemies, but they are different kinds of thing, and a single inheritance cannot be received on both terms at once. A promise is something one party swears and the other receives; a law is something one party demands and the other performs. Make my performance a condition and you have not enriched the promise; you have dissolved it.

The father and the tidy room. Illustrate it and it becomes obvious. A father tells his son that the house will be his when the father dies; it is written, signed, witnessed. Later the father says: and keep your room tidy. If tidiness is housekeeping in the ordinary sense, how a son who has been given a house behaves in it, nothing has changed. But if tidiness is now the condition of inheriting, then the son does not have a promise any more. He has a contract, and he will spend the rest of his life measuring the floor, and he will never once be sure.

Obeying God, or securing God. That is precisely the difference between a Christian who obeys God and a Christian who is trying to secure God. The behaviour can look identical from the outside. Both are up early. Both give. Both serve. The difference is invisible until something goes wrong, and then it is unmistakable: one of them fails and runs to his Father, and the other fails and hides, because the failure has just moved his inheritance.

Gave it by a promise. The verb is charizomai, to give freely, as a gift of grace, from the same root as grace itself. And it is a perfect tense: God has given, and it stands given, once and permanently. That is the tense the whole Christian life rests on. The deed was signed before Sinai, before Moses, before there was a law to keep or break, and it was signed by someone who does not revise (Romans 4:13–16; Hebrews 6:17–18).

A will that needed a death. The word Paul uses for God’s covenant with Abraham, diathēkē, also means a will, and the letter to the Hebrews draws out what that means. Where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established; a will takes effect only at death. That is why Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred (Hebrews 9:15–17). The inheritance promised to Abraham comes to us through the death of the Son, and we receive it from his hands. It was given by promise and secured in blood. It belongs first to him, the appointed heir of all things (Hebrews 1:2), and we are fellow heirs with him (Romans 8:17).

Can I lose my inheritance? Not if it rests on God’s promise, and that is exactly Paul’s point. An inheritance that depended on your performance could be forfeited any day. One given by promise depends on the faithfulness of the one who promised, and God does not break his word. That is why Scripture can speak of an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you, by God’s power guarding you through faith (1 Peter 1:4–5). True believers persevere, not because they hold on so tightly, but because they are held. If you are worried that you have lost it, the worry itself shows you care; bring it to Christ, and rest on what he has promised.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt; Paul uses the figure for the long gap between the promise and the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify or give life, why did God give it (v. 19)? Paul gives three answers. It was added because of transgressions, to name and expose sin. It was given until the offspring, Christ, should come, so it had an end written into it. And it came through angels and a human go-between, Moses, while the promise came from God directly.

Verse 20 is hard, but its direction is clear: a mediator stands between two parties, and Sinai was a two-sided covenant that Israel broke almost at once, while God alone made the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15). The law is not against the promise (v. 21); it was simply never able to give life. Scripture shut everyone up under sin so that the promise might be given to those who believe (v. 22). The law was a guardian, the household slave who walked a boy to school until he came of age (vv. 23–24), and now that faith has come, believers are no longer under a guardian (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Real, Strict, Temporary

The covenant of grace is one across both Testaments, and the law of Moses had a distinct job within it. Verses 19 and 24 show that the law was truly from God, truly binding in its time, and truly serving the promise, but it was given for a stage and not for the end. Its ending as the framework of God’s people is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

This does not mean God’s moral will has been repealed: Paul will say in 5:14 that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour. Nor were Old Testament believers second-class; they were children in the same family, under the care their age required. And v. 22 shows that the law’s severity was a mercy: every exit was closed so that the one open door would be taken.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian brought back after the child had come of age. Paul answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has ended (vv. 19, 25), and that the promise never depended on two signatures (v. 20).

Now: Many believers are adults in Christ and still live as if under supervision, expecting the stick and surprised by kindness. Verses 21–25 tell them that the guardian has done his work: they are sons, and may go to their Father as sons.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why then the law? Paul has been so severe about the law that the obvious objection now has to be faced, and he faces it head on. If it cannot justify, cannot give life, and cannot amend the promise, why did God give it at all? Was Sinai a mistake? The answer is three phrases, and each one puts the law in its place without insulting it.

It was added because of transgressions. Added is the first demotion: an addition is not the foundation. And because of transgressions means this: sin was in the world long before Sinai, but it was not yet transgression in the full sense. A transgression is a stepping over, the deliberate breaking of God’s known law, and you cannot step over a line that has not been drawn. The law drew the line. It took the vague human sense that something is wrong with us and turned it into specific counts with names on them, ten of them written on stone by the finger of God (Exodus 31:18). As Paul puts it elsewhere, he would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, you shall not covet (Romans 7:7; see also Romans 3:20; 4:15; 5:20). The law makes sin visible, restrains it, and shows our need of a Saviour.

The diagnosis, not the medicine. That sounds like a strange gift, and it is one of the kindest things God could have done. A man who feels vaguely unwell will put off the appointment for years; a man handed a diagnosis with a name on it goes that afternoon. The law is the diagnosis. It does not cause the disease and it cannot cure it, and anyone who mistakes the chart for the medicine will die holding it. But without it we would have gone on managing our symptoms and calling ourselves basically decent people, which is exactly what most of the human race is doing.

Until the offspring should come. The second demotion. The law, as the governing covenant, came with an end written into it. Not a failure but a term. It was doing a job for a period, and the period ran until the Offspring arrived, the one Paul has named: Christ (v. 16). He has arrived. Everything in the law was waiting for him: its sacrifices for the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, its priesthood for a priest who lives for ever, its tabernacle for the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14, 29; Hebrews 7:24–25). Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4): its goal, and so its term.

Through angels by an intermediary. The third demotion, and the sharpest. Scripture describes Sinai as attended by angelic hosts: the Lord came from ten thousands of holy ones (Deuteronomy 33:2), and the chariots of God were among them (Psalm 68:17). Both Stephen and the writer to the Hebrews take it for granted that the law was delivered by angels (Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2). Then Moses stood between the LORD and the people, because the people were afraid and begged not to hear the voice themselves (Deuteronomy 5:5; Exodus 20:19). Their fear was fitting: the mountain smoked and shook, and any man or beast that touched it was to die (Exodus 19:12–18). Sinners cannot stand near a holy God without someone between. Count the links in that chain: God, angels, Moses, Israel. Now count the links in the promise: God, Abraham. The law came down a staircase. The promise was handed over directly. Which is the greater? Not the one with more smoke on the mountain, but the one where God needed no one between himself and the man he was speaking to.

Where Christians differ: the uses of the law. Some say the law has no role for Christians at all; others make it the centre of the Christian life. Verdict: the Reformers identified three uses of the law. First, it shows sin and drives sinners to Christ (the use Paul focuses on here). Second, it restrains evil in society. Third, it guides believers in how to please God (often called the third use of the law), as the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments (Romans 13:8–10). The ceremonial and civil laws of Israel (its sacrifices and purity rules, and its national laws) were fulfilled and ended in Christ, but the moral law remains the rule of life, not as a covenant of works, that is, a way of earning life by obedience, but as the will of our Father (the Westminster Confession 19.5–6; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.5–6).

Why would God give a law he knew no one could keep? Because its main purpose was never to be the road by which we earn our way to him. It was given to a people he had already redeemed, as the shape of a holy life, with sacrifices built in for their failures. And it was given to show all of us, with total clarity, what we are and what we need. A law that sinners could keep perfectly would have flattered us and left us without Christ. A law we cannot keep strips away every excuse and sends us to the one who kept it for us. God was not setting a trap. He was drawing a map, and every road on it ends at the cross.

On a Tuesday. Read one of the Ten Commandments slowly this week, the way Jesus read them in the Sermon on the Mount: not only the deed but the desire, not only murder but anger, not only theft but covetousness. Let it show you where you stand. Then do what the law is meant to make you do: go to Christ with what it has shown you, and thank him that he kept it all.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law; Moses was the intermediary.

parallels.desc: I stood between the LORD and you

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an intermediary implies more than one. This is famously one of the most compressed sentences in the letter, and it is often said that commentators have proposed some three hundred readings of it. But the direction of the thought is not really in doubt, because Paul has just spent verse 19 counting links in a chain. A mediator, by definition, stands between parties, each with obligations. You do not need one where there is only one party involved. So the very presence of Moses on the mountain tells you what kind of arrangement Sinai was: a two-sided covenant with conditions, God on one side, Israel on the other, with a man in the middle holding the terms. Everything depended on both parties keeping their word, and the people had barely received the covenant before there was a golden calf at the foot of the mountain (Exodus 19:8; 32:1–6).

But God is one. When God came to Abraham there was no second party and no man in the middle. The promise was God’s alone, unconditional, depending only on him. Abraham did not negotiate; he was asleep. In the strangest scene in Genesis, God put him into a deep sleep and then passed alone between the pieces of the sacrifice: a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch walking the aisle of blood by themselves (Genesis 15:12, 17). In such a ceremony, as Jeremiah 34:18–20 shows, those who made the covenant walked between the pieces and invoked the fate of the animals on whoever broke faith. God walked it alone. He took the oath on himself, binding only himself, while Abraham lay in a deep sleep, a witness and not a party.

Two signatures or one. So the contrast is not between a harsh arrangement and a kind one. It is between an agreement that can fail because it has two signatures on it, and a promise that cannot fail because it has one, and the one who signed it is God, who does not have a bad year.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is not a mediator. Christ is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5), and he is himself God. That is exactly why his mediation is not like Moses’. Moses stood between two parties as a third man. Christ stands between God and us as one who is both, fully God and fully man, so that in him the promise rests on God alone and is brought to us by one of us.

What is a mediator, and why do I need one? A mediator is someone who stands between two parties to bring them together. We need one because there is a real distance between a holy God and sinners: not of miles but of guilt. Moses could carry God’s words to the people, but he could not take away their sin; he once offered to be blotted out for them, and God would not accept it (Exodus 32:32–33). Christ is the mediator Moses could not be. He does not only carry messages; he offers himself, and he always lives to intercede for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). You need no other go-between, no priest, saint or ritual. You come to the Father through the Son.

For worship. God put a man to sleep and swore the whole covenant by himself, knowing every century of unfaithfulness that was coming, and knowing exactly what it would cost him to keep his own oath when the other side had broken theirs. He walked between the pieces alone under the night sky, and when the time came his Son walked out to a hill alone, and kept it. If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13; Hebrews 6:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! Paul has demoted the law three times in two verses, and he knows how it sounds, so he asks the question his opponents would shout. And the answer is mē genoito, the strongest negative he owns, which he keeps for conclusions he finds unthinkable. The law and the promise both came from the same God and both serve the same purpose in his one plan. They are not rivals. They are a diagnosis and a cure, and only a fool sets those against each other.

A law that could give life. If any legal code could make a dead man live, God would have used it. The law is not being blamed for failing at a job it was given. It was never given that job, because no law can do it. It can command but not empower; it can show the way but not carry us along it (Romans 8:3). A speed limit has never once made a reckless man careful. It tells him what careful looks like and records the fact that he is not.

The true measure of our condition. That no law can give life shows how serious our condition is. If we were merely misinformed, instruction would be enough; if we were merely weak, encouragement would be enough. Scripture says we were dead in trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1), and nothing you say to a corpse improves it. We needed not better advice but resurrection.

What the law could not do. Resurrection is exactly what God has given, and he gave it in his Son. What the law could not do, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3). The law could describe life; Christ is the life (John 14:6). No code could raise the dead. A Person has, and he speaks to the dead still: the hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live (John 5:25).

Imprisoned everything under sin. Then verse 22, and the image is a prison. The verb is synkleiō: shut up together, locked in with no other door; it is the word Luke uses for a great shoal of fish enclosed in a net (Luke 5:6). And the object is not only everyone but everything, the whole realm, the entire order of things. Scripture declares all people guilty, locked in a prison with no escape (Romans 3:9–20; 11:32). To be under sin is more than to have sinned now and then. It is to live under sin’s guilt, which condemns us, and under its power, which rules us, the way a prisoner lives under the authority of the prison (Romans 3:9; 6:17). And note the jailer. It is Scripture that did the locking. God’s own word turned the key, which means our confinement is not an accident of history or a verdict we can appeal to a higher authority. It is published, and it is his.

So that the promise. That is savage, until you read the purpose clause. The imprisonment is a mercy. As long as a man believes there is another way out, he will keep trying doors. He will try being respectable, and being useful, and being sincere, and being spiritual, and each door will hold just enough to keep him busy. God locked every one of them so that we would finally turn round and see the one door that stands open, and it has a person’s name on it.

Does “everything under sin” include the good people I know? Yes, and that includes you and me. Some people are kinder, more honest and more generous than others, and God is pleased with real kindness wherever it is found. But no one has loved God with all his heart, and no one has kept the law, and a good life lived for oneself is still a life lived apart from God. The verse is not saying everyone is as bad as he could be. It is saying everyone is shut in the same prison, the respectable and the disreputable alike, and needs the same way out. That is humbling, and it is also the great leveller: the nicest person you know and the worst person you know are invited to Christ on exactly the same terms.

On a Tuesday. If nothing you can do about yourself seems to work, and the harder you try the worse the accounting gets, do not read that as God’s absence. It may well be his kindness: he is closing the exits so that you will stop trying to be your own way out and turn round to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now before faith came. Paul is using the word in a bigger sense than the act of trusting. Abraham had faith, and so did Habakkuk. He means the era of faith: the age that opened when Christ came and the gospel went out to the nations, so that faith in Christ is now the open, public, announced way in. The Old Testament believer was looking down a corridor at a door he could not yet see. We are standing in the room.

Held captive. “Held captive” is phroureō, to guard, to keep under watch, as a garrison guards a city; then the same verb as verse 22, shut in. Israel was guarded by the law, but only for a time: it was custody, not a life sentence.

Our guardian. This is the image that governs the passage. The law, Paul says, was our paidagōgos. Older English versions said schoolmaster, which is misleading. A paidagōgos was not the teacher. He was a household slave, usually an older one, often stern, sometimes harsh, and in the comic plays of the period sometimes mocked for his sternness. He usually had charge of the boy from about six until he came of age. He walked him to school and walked him home, kept him off the wrong streets, checked his manners, and had a stick and authority to use it. He was not there to educate the boy. He was there to get him to the one who would, and to keep him out of trouble on the way. The law guarded and disciplined Israel until Christ.

Three things about the guardian. So three things follow, and they answer the Judaizers. The paidagōgos was genuinely appointed: the father chose him, and the boy who resented him was resenting his father’s arrangement. He was genuinely strict, and strictness was the job. And he was genuinely temporary: nobody was under a paidagōgos at thirty. His whole office was defined by an end, and the end was that we might be justified by faith in Christ: even his strictness was aimed at the moment he would hand the boy over.
