Walked to the door of Christ. Where was the guardian taking the boy? To a Person. Jesus said that Moses wrote of him (John 5:46), and that everything written about him in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). Every lesson the law drilled into Israel, the lamb at Passover, the blood on the mercy seat, the priests who died and had to be replaced, the curse on the one who failed, was walking the boy toward Christ. And the one he is handed over to is no harsher guardian with longer lists. It is the Son himself, who says, Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:28–29).

In the flow. Paul now finishes his answer to his own question, why then the law? (3:19). It was added because of transgressions, it came through a mediator, it could not give life, and now the last point: it had a time limit. The pronoun matters as well. Paul says we were held captive, speaking as a Jew of Israel under the law; in the next verse he turns to you, all of you, Jew and Gentile together (3:26). And the guardian picture is not finished. Paul takes it up again from inside the household at 4:1–7, where the child under guardians becomes the son who cries Abba, Father.

No longer under a guardian. Christ has come. The son has come of age. The guardian’s job is done. And the Judaizers were going to the grown man in the courtyard and telling him that if he really wanted to please his father, he should send for the old slave again and ask to be walked to school.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers may live as they please. Grown sons still honour their father’s will, but from love, not as children under supervision. God’s moral will has not been repealed; Paul will spend the last two chapters of this letter telling these people how to live (5:14). What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the system of guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors, together with its ceremonies. Christians are not under the law to be saved, but they are not without law; they are under the law of Christ (1 Corinthians 9:21). Nor does it mean the Old Testament era was a mistake or that those believers were second-class. They were children in the same family, in the care their age required, waiting for the day this letter says has now arrived.

How do I stop living like a child under supervision? Many believers are technically adults in Christ and emotionally still under the guardian: still measuring the day’s performance, still expecting the stick, still surprised by kindness. Start by believing what your Father has said, that you are his son or daughter, not his employee or his ward on probation. Talk to him as a child talks to a loving father, plainly and often. When you obey, do it because you want to please him, not to keep him from punishing you. When you fail, go to him, not away. And let the Spirit’s cry of Abba, Father (4:6) become your own. It takes time to unlearn the guardian, but the guardian has been dismissed.
verseByVerse.note: The “guardian” (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a child, took him to school and kept him in line until he came of age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with what believers now are. Through faith every believer is a son of God in Christ Jesus, clothed with Christ (vv. 26–27). The divisions that ruled the ancient world, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, no longer decide anyone’s standing before God (v. 28), and all who belong to Christ are Abraham’s offspring and heirs of the promise (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a place. He is in Christ, clothed with Christ, and so shares the standing of the Son. That is why people who know their own hearts well can still have assurance: the clothing does not change with the wearer.

Verse 28 shows that the gospel does not only change individuals; it makes a community in which race, class and sex no longer decide anyone’s worth or access to God. Christians who honour Scripture differ on what the verse means for roles in church and home; this commentary holds that Paul speaks here of standing before God, and of roles elsewhere. Both sides agree on what the verse plainly says: there is no hierarchy of worth at the cross, and no smaller share in the inheritance (v. 29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A strict Jew would not enter a Gentile house; a large part of a city’s population were slaves; and a man’s testimony counted in court where a woman’s often did not. Verse 28 says those three walls do not run through the church, because everyone in it is wearing the same garment (v. 27), and v. 29 tells Gentile believers that they are full heirs, not associate members.

Now: Every congregation has people who have quietly concluded that they are second rank. Verse 28 tells them that Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building than the one he has given them.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All sons of God. The guardian has been dismissed in the verse before; now we are told what the boy has become. Not a graduate. A son. Take the words one at a time, because every one of them is aimed at something the Judaizers were saying. You: the Galatians, the uncircumcised, the ones being told they were not yet full members. All: no tiers. Sons: not children under a guardian, not wards, not apprentices, but adult sons with full rights of inheritance (4:5–7). Through faith: not through the knife. And in front of it all, governing everything, in Christ Jesus: by union with him. The sonship is not something we possess in ourselves; it is ours because we are in the Son.

Sons, not only children. A word about sons, since a modern reader may hear it as a door closing. Paul writes huioi, sons, and he does it deliberately, because in that world sons inherited and daughters generally did not. “Sons” includes daughters; the word is not about gender but about legal status, the standing of the heir. So when a woman reads verse 26 she is not listening in on something addressed to the men. She is being told that she holds the inheritance rights of a son in the household of God.

Baptized into Christ. Paul’s readers had been baptised in water when they believed, and he speaks of their baptism as the moment they were joined to Christ, because in the New Testament faith and baptism belonged together: people believed and were baptised at once (Acts 8:12; 16:31–33). Baptism is the visible sign of that union (Romans 6:3–4). What actually unites a person to Christ is the Spirit, received through faith (v. 14; 1 Corinthians 12:13); water baptism is the outward picture and public confession of it. So Paul can speak of the sign and mean the reality it signifies, as we might say “she gave her hand in marriage” and mean the whole covenant of marriage.

Have put on Christ. The clothing image. “Put on” is endyō, the ordinary word for dressing, and in the Roman world it may well have brought a particular picture to mind, since some towns in the province were Roman colonies. When a boy came of age, the family held a ceremony in which he laid aside the child’s toga with its purple border and put on the plain white toga virilis, the garment of a man, and from that day he was treated as one. Paul has just dismissed the guardian. Now he hands out the adult garment, and the garment is Christ himself. Believers have put on Christ: covered with his righteousness, identified with him (Romans 13:14; Isaiah 61:10).

What the Father sees. So what the Father sees when he looks at a believer is not first a person making progress. It is his Son’s own righteousness worn as clothing, covering everything the man is ashamed of and everything he has not yet dealt with. That is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well. The clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer. Much of life is spent dressing to be approved, by others and by God. The gospel lifts that whole wardrobe off our shoulders. The one garment that makes us acceptable to God has already been put on us, and nobody can improve on it.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some take this verse to mean that water baptism itself unites a person to Christ and regenerates them; Roman Catholic, Lutheran and some other Christians read it this way. Verdict: Paul has just said we are sons through faith (v. 26), and the whole chapter has insisted that everything comes through faith (vv. 2, 14, 26) and nothing by an outward rite performed on the body. Baptism is the sign of union with Christ, which is received by faith. It is not the cause of union. Those who are baptised with faith truly put on Christ; baptism without faith does not save (1 Peter 3:21; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 29.1; the Westminster Confession 28.5). This commentary holds believer’s baptism: the sign follows the faith it signifies, which is exactly the order in this verse: sons through faith (v. 26), then baptised into Christ (v. 27). Christians who baptise infants see baptism as the sign of the covenant given, like circumcision, to believers’ children (Colossians 2:11–12); they are our brothers, and both sides confess what this verse indisputably says: what clothes a sinner before God is Christ, received by faith.

I was baptised as an infant. Should I be baptised now? On the view this commentary holds, baptism is for those who have believed, so a believer who was baptised only as an infant has not yet received believer’s baptism and should ask for it, gladly, as an act of obedience and public confession. It is not a rejection of your parents’ love or prayers, which were real gifts. Talk it through with your pastor and read the New Testament passages on baptism for yourself. And hold your view with charity: many faithful Christians and churches, including the Westminster tradition, sincerely believe infant baptism is right. Do not make the disagreement a wall between you and them. You are clothed with the same Christ.

On a Tuesday. There is no better-dressed Christian in your congregation than you. The most disciplined believer you know is wearing exactly what you are wearing, and neither of you made it or paid for it. When a memory or a failure leaves you feeling exposed before God this week, come to him clothed in his Son.

For worship. The garment we wear was woven at a cost. The eternal Son put on our flesh so that we could put on him, and at the cross the soldiers divided his clothes among them and cast lots for his tunic (John 19:23–24). He hung there stripped, so that sinners could stand before the Father dressed. The Father did not weigh our merits before he clothed us, and no one in the great multitude before his throne will be wearing anything they made: they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 7:14).

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither Jew nor Greek. Paul now says the thing that has echoed for two thousand years. Those three pairs were not opinions about society; they were the load-bearing walls of the ancient world. Jew and Greek was the great religious and ethnic divide, so deep that a strict Jew would not enter a Gentile house. Slave and free was the great social and economic divide, and a large part of the population of a city like Corinth was property. Male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. A Jewish morning prayer recorded in later rabbinic sources, in forms that vary and probably reflect older sentiment, thanked God for not making the man praying a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Paul reverses all three. He takes those three walls and says that in Christ they do not run through the room.

No male and female. One detail in the Greek is easy to pass over. The first two pairs are neither, nor. The third changes: no male and female, which is not clumsiness but an echo. It is the wording of Genesis 1:27 in the Greek Old Testament: male and female he created them. Paul has reached past the social order all the way back to the creation account, as if to say: even the deepest distinction God made in humanity does not determine your standing in Christ.

All one in Christ Jesus. One is heis, one person: not one in the sense of identical, but one body, one new man in Christ. So what exactly is being levelled? The context answers it, because Paul has not changed the subject: he is talking about who is a son of Abraham, who is justified, who is clothed in Christ, who inherits. On that ground, the ground where a person stands before God, the three walls are gone entirely. There is not a Jewish justification and a Gentile one, a free man’s adoption and a slave’s, a fuller portion for a husband and a lesser one for his wife. One Christ, one righteousness, one inheritance, and every believer holds all of it: equally justified, equally sons, equally heirs.

Difference remains; difference as worth has gone. Is it then the abolition of the differences themselves? Plainly not in every sense, and Paul’s own letters prove it. Paul goes on being a Jew; Onesimus goes on being a slave in the eyes of Roman law while Paul works on Philemon to receive him as a brother; and men and women go on being men and women. Difference remains. What has gone is difference as a measure of worth and as a condition of access to God.

Where Christians differ: does this verse abolish gender roles? Egalitarians use this verse to argue that all distinctions of role between men and women in the church and home are abolished in Christ; they see the verse as the principle and the restrictions elsewhere as temporary concessions to Paul’s culture. Verdict: the context is about who is justified and who is an heir of Abraham: all believers equally, regardless of race, class or sex. It is about status before God, not roles in the church. The distinctions themselves are not abolished: Jews remain Jews, men remain men. Paul elsewhere teaches distinct roles for men and women in the home and church (1 Corinthians 11:3; Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Timothy 2:12), grounded in creation, not culture. Slavery is no parallel: Paul gave instructions to slaves while sowing the seeds of their freedom, urging slaves to take freedom when they could and condemning slave-traders (1 Corinthians 7:21; 1 Timothy 1:10; Philemon 16), but he never grounded slavery in creation. Equal in worth, distinct in calling: the complementarian view. And headship in Scripture is the self-giving love of Christ for his church, never domination; any abuse of a wife or of any person is a grave sin that the church must never tolerate or cover. Many faithful Christians read this verse the egalitarian way out of a real concern for the dignity of women, a concern the verse itself shares; this commentary honours them as brothers and sisters while holding the view above.

Does this verse condemn racism and snobbery in the church? Yes, plainly. If Christ has given the same standing to every believer, then any church that treats some believers as lesser because of their race, nationality, class, education or sex is denying in practice what this verse says. That was Peter’s sin at Antioch (2:11–14). It can look like separate congregations divided by colour where there is no language reason, leaders always drawn from one social group, a cool welcome for the poor or the foreigner, jokes at someone’s background. Repent of it where you see it in yourself, and gently challenge it where you see it in your church. The one table of the Lord is meant to look like the one family he has made.

On a Tuesday. Every congregation contains people who have quietly concluded that they are the second rank: the woman talked past in every church she has attended, the man whose accent or job or prison record marks him out, the late convert whose parents are not believers. In Christ you are one with them. Seek one of them out this Sunday, as Christ sought you, and listen.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you are Christ’s. The whole chapter comes to rest here, and the logic is one clean line. The promise was made to the Offspring, and the Offspring is Christ (v. 16). Therefore everything depends on one question only: are you his? If you belong to Christ, you are inside the one to whom everything was promised, and it is all yours. Now Paul uses offspring in its collective sense: in Christ, all believers are Abraham’s seed.

Not by lowering the requirements. The argument does not take the obvious route. Paul does not say you have become a good enough Jew, or you have qualified, or God has decided to be generous with the entry requirements. The requirements were never lowered. Every one of them was met by one man, and you are in him. So the Gentile Galatians do not need circumcision to become Abraham’s children. They already are, in Christ.

Heirs according to promise. Weigh the word heirs. An heir is not someone who has been given a gift; he is someone who has been given a standing, and the estate follows from the standing. He does not earn it, cannot be dismissed from it, and does not receive it because he has been useful. He receives it because of who he is in the family. You cannot work your way into a family tree (Romans 8:16–17; Ephesians 1:11).

What is actually inherited? Scripture does not leave it vague, and the vagueness of much Christian talk about the future is a loss, not a piety. Heirs of everything God promised Abraham: righteousness, the Spirit, the world to come (Romans 4:13). God himself as your portion, which is the substance of every promise (Genesis 15:1). A body that does not fail, raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). A world put right and handed over, the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5; Romans 8:17–21). A face to see, the thing Moses asked for and was not given (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4). And real service in a real kingdom (Luke 19:17). That is what stands to the account of every Galatian who believed Paul’s preaching, and it is what stands to yours.

Where Christians differ: the land and Israel’s future. Does this mean that the promises of land and nation to Israel are now void? Paul says that all who are Christ’s are Abraham’s heirs, so the promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared by everyone in him, Jew and Gentile alike. That is not a rejection of the Jewish people; Paul himself was one, and he insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). Dispensational Christians hold that the land and nation promises remain for ethnic Israel; historic premillennialists (who expect Christ to reign on earth for a thousand years after his return) also expect a future earthly fulfilment. Many Reformed Christians hold that the promise to Abraham was always larger than a strip of land: he would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the inheritance is the renewed creation, which belongs to all who are Christ’s. Reformed Christians agree that God has not cast off the Jewish people (Romans 11:1–2), and that no one inherits anything apart from Christ.

If I am an heir, why does my life feel so poor? Because you are an heir before the reading of the will. Paul will say in the next chapter that an heir, while he is a child, may look no different from a slave (4:1). The estate is real but mostly unseen, and you are living in a world that contradicts it: illness, loss, loneliness, a body that is wearing out. That is the normal Christian condition, not a sign that you have missed out. The inheritance is kept for you, not yet handed over (1 Peter 1:4). Meanwhile you have the down payment: the Spirit himself, the guarantee of what is to come (Ephesians 1:14). Live on the deposit, and look forward to the estate.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.<sup>2</sup>Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?<sup>3</sup>Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?<sup>4</sup>Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?<sup>5</sup>Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—<sup>6</sup>just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?<sup>7</sup>Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham.<sup>8</sup>And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”<sup>9</sup>So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.<sup>10</sup>For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”<sup>11</sup>Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”<sup>12</sup>But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”<sup>13</sup>Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—<sup>14</sup>so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.<sup>15</sup>To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified.<sup>16</sup>Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.<sup>17</sup>This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void.<sup>18</sup>For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.<sup>19</sup>Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.<sup>20</sup>Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.<sup>21</sup>Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law.<sup>22</sup>But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.<sup>23</sup>Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed.<sup>24</sup>So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.<sup>25</sup>But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,<sup>26</sup>for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith.<sup>27</sup>For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.<sup>28</sup>There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.<sup>29</sup>And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 carries the argument of chapter 3 to its goal. The law was a guardian for children; now Paul shows what God gives instead: full sonship, the Spirit of his Son, and the cry of Abba, Father, in the heart of every adopted child. The contrast is between two ways of living before God: the slave who must perform, and the son who belongs.

An heir who is under age owns everything and controls nothing, living under guardians until the time his father has set. So it was with God’s people under the law, until the fullness of time, when God sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law and give them adoption as sons, and sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts (vv. 1–7).

Paul then pleads with the Galatians (vv. 8–20). He reminds them how they welcomed him when he first came to them sick, and he says he is in the pains of childbirth again until Christ is formed in them. Finally he reads the story of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31): the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and believers are children of the free woman, the children of promise, heirs of the Jerusalem above.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul illustrates with an heir who is still a child: though he owns the estate, he is no better off than a slave, living under guardians until the time his father has set (vv. 1–2). So we too were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world (v. 3). But at the time God had set, he sent his Son to redeem those under the law and to adopt them as sons (vv. 4–5), and he sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts (v. 6). So they are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs through God (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Sending of the Son and the Spirit

In vv. 4–6 the Father sends the Son, and the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two sendings are distinct and belong together: the Son wins redemption and adoption for us, outside us, as a settled legal fact, and the Spirit brings them home within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls on him.

Adoption (huiothesia) is stated more clearly in this chapter than almost anywhere, and it goes beyond forgiveness. In Roman practice the adopted son took his new father’s name and inherited on the same footing as any natural son; what had changed was not his conduct but his family. Verse 7 sums it up in three words, no longer, son, heir, and adds through God, so that nobody imagines an inheritance of this size coming any other way. J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe: the Spirit, the cry of Abba, the inheritance. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and vv. 1–3 show what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians and a calendar.

Now: Verse 6 answers the believer who does not feel like a son: the Spirit is sent because you are one, so the feeling follows the status and never causes it.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 4 continues the argument that believers are God’s free sons, not slaves under the law. An heir who is a child is no better off than a slave until the day his father has set; so humanity was enslaved under the elementary principles of the world until the fullness of time, when God sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law and give them adoption, and sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying Abba, Father (vv. 1–7). Paul asks how the Galatians, now known by God, can turn back to slavery by observing days and seasons (vv. 8–11). He appeals to them tenderly: they once welcomed him as Christ himself, and he is in labour again until Christ is formed in them (vv. 12–20). Finally he reads the story of Abraham’s two sons as two covenants: Hagar, slavery under Sinai; Sarah, freedom by promise. Believers are children of the free woman, the Jerusalem above (vv. 21–31).

I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child. Chapter 3 ended with the guardian dismissed and the son given the adult garment. Now Paul takes the same picture and runs it from the other end, from inside the household. The child here is nēpios: an infant, a minor, a son not yet of legal age. And the first thing Paul says about him is shocking.

No different from a slave. Not different in law: in law he is the owner. The deeds are in his name. The land, the house, the animals, the servants, all of it is legally his. And it makes no practical difference whatever, because he is seven. He cannot sell a field or sign a contract or give an order that anyone has to obey. He eats what he is given and goes where he is taken. Watch him through the day and you could not tell him from the boy who carries the water.

Ownership and enjoyment. It also explains a puzzle in the Old Testament. Were the believers before Christ saved? Yes: genuinely, by faith, on the same ground we are, looking forward to the Christ we look back on. Then why speak of their condition as bondage? Because ownership and enjoyment are two different things. They held the title deeds to promises they could not yet handle. Abraham was promised that he would be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and he died having bought only one field, a burial plot for his wife (Genesis 23). He owned everything and held almost nothing, and he was content to wait, because he was looking for the city whose designer and builder is God (Hebrews 11:10).

But he is under guardians and managers. Verse 2 names the arrangement. The epitropoi were guardians, the men with authority over the boy’s person: his schooling, his conduct, his whereabouts. The oikonomoi were managers or stewards, who ran the property. Both were servants. Both had more practical power over the estate than its owner did. And both held it only for a time.

Until the date set by his father. That last phrase is the one to hold on to. In the ancient world the arrangements varied: Roman law fixed some ages, provincial custom left more to the father, and a man could set the term in his will. Paul fastens on the one feature every version had in common. The boy did not choose the day. The guardians did not choose the day. The father named it, and when it came, it came. God set the time for his people’s coming of age, and the date he wrote in the will was the coming of Christ (v. 4).

The Owner in the form of a slave. The picture of an owner of everything who looks no different from a slave has one perfect instance, and it is not the boy in Paul’s illustration. It is the Son. He was in the form of God, the appointed heir of all things, and he took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7; Hebrews 1:2). He grew up in a craftsman’s house in Nazareth, so ordinary to his neighbours that they could only ask, Is not this the carpenter’s son? (Matthew 13:55). The Lord of the estate entered the condition of the minors so that minors could come of age in him, as Paul goes on to say (4:4–5).

Is God unkind to keep anyone in that position? No more than a father is unkind to his seven-year-old. The guardians were not a punishment; they were a protection, the way a loving father secures an estate for a son too young to manage it. The law kept Israel, fenced her, taught her, and kept the line of promise intact until the Christ was born. And in this picture the heir is never in danger of losing the estate. His position is restricted; his inheritance is secure. Every rule that hemmed him in was a sign that something very large had been reserved for him.

On a Tuesday. Much Christian frustration is about timing: the prayer unanswered for eleven years, the change in yourself you keep asking for, the season that will not lift. Verse 2 does not promise that the date is soon. It says there is one, that it is not arbitrary, and that it was fixed by a Father, not by the guardians who seem to be running your life.

What does living as a son who has come of age actually look like? It looks like freedom of access rather than a rulebook for every step. A minor needs a rule for everything because he does not yet know his father’s mind; a grown son has his father’s Spirit and his father’s word, and he obeys from the inside. So you pray boldly, without first proving you deserve a hearing. You confess sin quickly, because a son does not hide from his father. You read God’s commands as the family’s way of life, not as an entrance exam. And you stop treating other believers’ consciences as your guardians: you are answerable to the Father himself.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way we also, when we were children. Paul takes the picture and puts the whole human race inside it. That we is broad: he is speaking to a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles, and he includes himself, the Pharisee, in the same sentence as men who grew up sacrificing to Cybele. Before Christ, Jew and Gentile alike were minors.

The elementary principles of the world. The phrase is ta stoicheia tou kosmou, and it is one of the genuinely disputed phrases in Paul. Stoicheia means things in a row: the letters of the alphabet, and by extension the ABCs, the basic building blocks of anything, and also the basic components of the world. Some take it that way here: the elementary stage of religion, the primer, the rudiments of rules and rituals the world worked through before the Son came, and to go back to them now is to be an adult sounding out letters. Others hear something darker, since Paul says enslaved, and the word could also be used of the spiritual powers thought to stand behind the elements, the heavenly bodies, the nations and their calendars (Colossians 2:8, 20). On that reading, going back to law-keeping is not merely childish; it is a return to territory that has an occupant. An older view took the word for the physical elements, earth, air, fire and water, and few now hold it.

Whichever reading. Most readers today combine the first two, and the good news is that Paul’s argument does not depend on which you choose. Whatever the stoicheia are precisely, two things about them are certain in this letter: the Gentiles were under them before they knew God (vv. 8–9), and the Judaizers’ programme would put the Galatians back under them. That is what makes verse 3 so startling. Paul has just filed the Mosaic law and the pagan festival calendar in the same drawer.

Not according to Christ. Paul uses the same phrase in Colossians, and there he sets it against one name: philosophy and empty deceit, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ (Colossians 2:8). Whatever the stoicheia are, Christ is their opposite and their conqueror. In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily; he is the head of all rule and authority; and at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:9–10, 15). The Galatians were not choosing between two religious programmes. They were choosing between masters Christ has already defeated and the Christ who defeated them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law of Moses and paganism are the same. Nothing in Paul’s writing would allow that; he will say in Romans that the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). But as ways of approaching God apart from Christ, both enslave. Paul is saying something about function, not about origin. Take any good and God-given thing, the Sabbath, the law, the sacraments, a doctrinal system, a discipline of prayer, and make it the thing that secures your standing with God, and it will do to you exactly what an idol does. It will demand, it will never say enough, and you will serve it.

Disappointment or dread. This question is uncomfortable because it catches good practices rather than bad ones. Take the most valued religious habit in your life: the daily reading, the giving, the fasting, the service. Now imagine dropping it for a fortnight, not through rebellion but through illness. Is what rises in you disappointment, or is it dread? Disappointment is a son who has missed his father’s company. Dread is a slave who has missed a quota. The habit is identical; the relationship is not. And if what rises is dread, the answer is not a better quota but the Father who has already received you in his Son.

So should I drop my routines if they have become a burden? No. The answer to a habit that has become a quota is not to abandon the habit but to change its ground. Keep reading your Bible, keep praying, keep gathering with the church: these are the ordinary means by which God feeds his children. What has to go is the idea that they hold up your acceptance. Before you open your Bible tomorrow, say to God plainly that you are already accepted in Christ and you have come to hear your Father, not to earn his attention. Then, on the day you miss it, do not punish yourself with extra. Come back the next morning as a son comes back to the table. The routine stays; the slavery goes.
verseByVerse.note: The “elementary principles” may mean the basic rules of religion, or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the fullness of time had come. Two words turn the letter. Everything before has been minority, guardians, waiting, bondage; and then God moves. The phrase is to plērōma tou chronou: the moment when the vessel was full to the brim, not a minute early and not a minute late. It is the moment God had set (v. 2). It answers a question honest readers ask: why then? Why leave the world in the dark for so long, and then act in an obscure province in the reign of Augustus (Mark 1:15; Ephesians 1:10)?

Why then? Some of the answer is visible even from here. There were Roman roads running across much of the known world, and a Roman peace that made it possible to walk them. There was one language a Galatian, a Roman and an Alexandrian could all read. There were Jewish synagogues scattered through every major city, the Scriptures in Greek, and Gentile God-fearers already attached to them, so that Paul had a hearing prepared in each town he entered. And among many in that world, confidence in the old gods had worn thin, and a spiritual hunger was growing in its place. Take one of those away and the gospel travels differently. But the deeper answer is in the sentence itself: it was the date set by his father. History was not waiting for conditions to be right. It was waiting for a Father to say now, and the conditions were the Father’s preparations.

God sent forth his Son. Every clause from here is precise. The verb is exapostellō, to send out from: from heaven, from the Father’s side. God sent forth one who was already his Son, already there to be sent. This is Christ’s pre-existence and deity in four words. The Son did not begin at Bethlehem; he came from somewhere.

Born of woman. The nearest Paul ever comes to speaking of the nativity, and the phrase is a Hebrew way of saying human, mortal, of our stock: man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble (Job 14:1). He did not appear in the world; he was carried in it, and delivered into it, and fed at a human breast. Truly human, born like any human, with every weakness of our flesh except its sin.

Did Paul know of the virgin birth? A question is often raised about this phrase, and it should be answered rather than left hanging. Paul says born of woman, not born of a virgin, and it is sometimes argued from this that he knew nothing of it. But that is more weight than the sentence will carry. Paul is not writing about how Jesus was conceived; he is writing about which side of the counter he stood on, and every clause in the verse is chosen to press him further into our situation, not out of it. His wording is at least consistent with the virgin birth: born of a woman, with no human father named. And Luke, who travelled with Paul, records the annunciation in detail (Luke 1:26–38).

Born under the law. He took his place inside the very jurisdiction that had every one of us condemned. He was a Jew, circumcised on the eighth day, presented in the temple with the poor family’s offering of two birds, taken up to Jerusalem at twelve (Luke 2:21–24, 41–42), and he kept every clause of the code that was killing us. He lived under the law and kept it perfectly, for us.

Why did Jesus need to keep the law, if he was going to die for us anyway? Because we needed two things, not one. We needed our guilt taken away, and we needed a righteousness we did not have. His death bore the curse we had earned (3:13); his life of perfect obedience supplied the record we had failed to produce. Theologians call these his passive and active obedience, but the point is simple: God does not merely wipe your slate clean and leave it blank. He writes his Son’s life on it. When the Father looks at a believer, he sees a whole lifetime, some thirty years and more, of perfect love for God and neighbour, and credits them to you (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That is why every year of the hidden life at Nazareth was for you as much as the cross.

To redeem. Now the purpose, in two halves. The first is exagorasē, the slave-market word again from 3:13: to buy out and take away. He bore the curse of the law to set its prisoners free, and the price was himself.

Adoption as sons. And then something more than release. Huiothesia means placing as a son, and it is a Roman legal term; the Roman practice is the picture. A man without a suitable heir would take a young man, often an adult, out of one family and into his own by a formal legal act before witnesses. From that day the adopted son bore the new father’s name, inherited his estate on the same footing as any natural son, and in some forms of Roman adoption his old debts and obligations were extinguished. Legally he was a new person. God’s adoption goes further than any Roman one. Roman law did allow a father later to release a son from his family; God never does. No later misbehaviour can undo his adoption, because what has been altered is not the son’s conduct but his family (John 10:28–29).

Adoption and the new birth. Two things the New Testament says about believers and their Father strengthen assurance when held together. The new birth makes a person a child of God by an inward act: a nature given, a heart made alive, so that he begins to want what he never wanted (John 1:12–13). Adoption is an outward, legal act: a standing conferred, a name given, an inheritance settled, done before witnesses and entered in the record. Adoption is also a distinct blessing from justification: we are not only declared righteous in the court, we are welcomed into the family, given the Father’s name, his care, his discipline and his inheritance (the Westminster Confession 12.1; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 12.1). One is a change in you; the other is a change in your position, done by somebody else entirely. On a day when the inward evidence is hard to find, the outward act stands exactly where it stood, because it was never yours to perform.

More than a rescue. So the gospel gives far more than most Christians expect from it. Redemption alone would have been extraordinary: the slave bought out of the market and set at liberty at the gate. God did not stop at the gate. He bought the slave, cancelled the debt, gave him his own name, and walked him into the house as a son with the same inheritance as the firstborn. That is not a rescue. That is a family.

Does sons leave out daughters? No. Paul uses sons because in the ancient world it was sons who inherited, and he wants every believer to know they have the heir’s full standing. He has just said there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (3:28). So a Christian woman is a son in exactly this sense: not lesser, not a dependant on someone else’s portion, but an heir in her own right. Elsewhere the Lord says it outright: you shall be sons and daughters to me (2 Corinthians 6:18).

On a Tuesday. Anyone who has adopted knows that the paperwork matters: the day the court signs, the child’s name is changed and no one can take it back. When you are tempted to think your standing with God rises and falls with your week, remember that your adoption was settled by the Son’s blood, not by your behaviour, and receive your Father’s correction without fearing that it means rejection (Hebrews 12:5–11).

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because you are sons. The order of the first four words settles many anxious questions. Not: cry Abba hard enough and you will become a son. Not: work up the feeling and God will respond to it. The sonship comes first, established by the Son’s redemption in verse 5; the Spirit is sent because of it. The felt experience is the consequence of the status, never the cause. Which means that when the feeling is absent, and for many believers it is absent for long stretches, in illness, in depression, in grief, in plain tiredness, nothing has happened to the sonship. A son asleep in his bed is as much his father’s son as a son laughing at his table.

Two sendings. God sent his Son (v. 4); God has sent the Spirit of his Son (v. 6). The same verb, twice. The Son was sent into the world to do something for us; the Spirit is sent into our hearts to do something in us. Salvation is the whole Godhead, Father, Son and Spirit, bringing a family home.

The Spirit of his Son. Paul does not say the Spirit of God, though he is; here he is named as the Son’s own Spirit, because what he brings into the believer’s heart is the Son’s relationship to the Father. He makes us share it. You are not given a new arrangement of your own. You are brought inside his. In practice it means you come to God the way Jesus came to him: not as a stranger hoping to be let in, but as a child who expects to be heard. Jesus taught his disciples to begin their prayers with the word he used himself, Father (Luke 11:2), and the Spirit is the one who makes that word true in your mouth.

Crying, “Abba! Father!” It is often said that Abba is baby-talk, a toddler’s Daddy. It is not, and grown men in Jesus’ day used it of their fathers all their lives. But the truth is not less moving for being accurate. Abba is the Aramaic word for father used within the family: the ordinary, warm, intimate, domestic word, not the formal word for the deity, not the reverent circumlocution of the synagogue, but the word a son would use turning round in the doorway. It is the word the Spirit puts in your mouth. And the verb, krazō, is not a whisper. It is a loud, heartfelt cry, the cry of a child who knows he will be heard.

Who is doing the crying? Paul says here that the Spirit cries, and in Romans he says we cry, the Spirit himself bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:15–16). Both are true, and together they are enormous comfort: the prayer of a Christian is the Spirit of God praying in him. So the man who says he cannot pray, who gets three words in and dries up, who feels nothing, who is ashamed of how thin it sounds, is describing the outside of something. The cry that reaches the Father is the Son’s Spirit, and he is not thin.

So should I call God Daddy? You may speak to him with the warmth and directness of a child, and you should. But Abba is not a licence for casualness. Jesus said Abba in the garden (Mark 14:36), in the hour when, Luke tells us, his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts), and in the same breath he said, not what I will, but what you will. The word holds intimacy and reverence together, as a good son’s love for a good father does. So come close, come often, come without rehearsing; and remember who it is you are calling Father. The nearness is astonishing precisely because he is so great.

No longer a slave. Then verse 7, and the pronoun changes. Until now Paul has mostly said you plural, to churches. Here he narrows to the singular, one person. He wants each believer to hear it personally.

An heir through God. Three words in that verse are worth carrying about all week. No longer: a door has shut behind you, and slavery is now your history rather than your condition. Son: the status, given. Heir: sons inherit, and believers are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). And Paul adds, through God, lest anyone suppose an inheritance of this size could be got any other way. It comes by his grace, not by the law.

In the flow. With verse 7 the long argument that began at 3:1 reaches its goal. Paul opened by asking how the Galatians received the Spirit (3:2); now he tells them who that Spirit is: the Spirit of God’s Son, given because they are sons. He showed that believers are Abraham’s heirs (3:29); now he says more: they are heirs of God. And from here the letter turns from argument to appeal. If this is what you are, Paul asks in the next verses, how can you go back to slavery (4:8–9)?

What exactly do I inherit? First and greatest, God himself: the LORD is my portion (Lamentations 3:24), and eternal life is to know him (John 17:3). Then everything that is Christ’s, because you are a fellow heir with him: the new heavens and new earth, the meek inheriting the earth (Matthew 5:5), an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4). You have a share of it now, in the Spirit, who is the guarantee or down payment of the rest (Ephesians 1:14). And it cannot be lost, because it is not kept by you. It is kept for you, and you are kept for it.

What if I do not feel any of this? Then you are in the company of many of God’s dearest children. The Spirit’s witness is not always a feeling of warmth. Often it is quieter: you cannot stop coming back to Christ; you hate your sin and want to be holy; when you are in trouble, the word that rises to your lips is still Father. Those are the Spirit’s work. Feelings come and go with sleep, health and circumstance; your adoption does not. Rest on the promise, keep praying the word Father even when it feels dry, and let the feeling follow when God gives it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is our Father in the same way he is Christ’s. Christ is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption and grace. Jesus kept the distinction carefully: I am ascending to my Father and your Father (John 20:17), not our Father as though the two were the same. But in Christ, we share his place, and the Father loves us with the love with which he has loved him (John 17:23).

On a Tuesday. Begin your praying with the word Abba, Father, and stay on it for a moment before you ask for anything. And when you are tempted to slink back to God like a hired servant, rehearsing why he should let you in, remember the prodigal: he had his speech ready, and his father never let him finish it (Luke 15:18–24).
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before they knew God, the Galatians were enslaved to beings that are not gods. Now that they are known by God, how can they turn back to slavery by observing days and seasons (vv. 8–10)? Paul fears his labour was wasted (v. 11). Then he pleads with them as a friend: he recalls how they welcomed him, sick as he was, as if he were Christ himself (vv. 12–15), and asks whether he has become their enemy by telling the truth (v. 16). The rival teachers court them for their own ends (vv. 17–18), while Paul is in labour again until Christ is formed in them (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kinds of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

When Paul sets the Judaizers’ calendar beside the pagan one the Galatians had left (vv. 8–10), he is speaking of what it does, not saying the two are morally the same: any God-given thing made the ground of our acceptance will behave like an idol. Moralism is not a minor error but a rival gospel, and it produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 contains one of Paul’s plainest statements of election, given in passing as a pastoral correction. To be known by God is for God to set his love on a person and claim him (Jeremiah 1:5). And v. 19 gives the goal of all ministry: not attendance, giving or doctrinal precision, but Christ formed in his people, taking shape from within like a child in the womb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly (vv. 14–15) and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain why: the Judaizers courted them and flattered them, then held the door a few inches short of open. Paul wanted not their loyalty to him but Christ formed in them (vv. 19–20).

Now: Verse 10 raises the question of Christmas, Easter and Sunday, and Paul answers it himself in Romans 14:5–6: what he attacks here is not the observance but the ground. Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy, and v. 13 belongs to the reader whose plans have been rerouted by illness.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
By nature are not gods. Paul now turns the argument on the Galatians’ own past. These were not philosophical atheists. Galatia was crowded with religion: the mother goddess with her ecstatic priests, the imperial cult with its temples in the larger towns, the household shrines, the local shrines at the springs. The Galatians had been intensely religious and enslaved at the same time. There was nothing behind the statues (1 Corinthians 8:4–5). The whole apparatus of fear and appeasement had been built around beings who did not exist as gods, and it had still owned them. A career, a reputation, a body, a bank balance, the approval of a parent: each can be served with the same anxious devotion, demanding more and never saying enough, and each of them too is by nature not a god.

Are idols nothing, or demons? Both, in different senses. The gods the idols represent do not exist as gods; they are by nature not gods. But Paul says elsewhere that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God (1 Corinthians 10:20). Behind the empty idol stand real spiritual powers who use the worship of nothing to enslave people (compare v. 3). So an idol is a lie with a liar behind it.

But now that you have come to know God. Paul begins a sentence and corrects himself in the middle of it.

Or rather to be known by God. Why the change? Because the first way of saying it puts the Galatians in the active seat and God in the passive one, as though the decisive event were their discovery. Paul cannot let that stand even for the length of a clause. Yes, they know God now; that is real, and it is the sweetest thing about them. But if you ask what actually happened, the verb belongs to God. They were known: sought, chosen and drawn, before they had turned a single thought toward him. Salvation begins with God’s initiative.

Known means loved. And known here does not mean God learned some facts about them. In Scripture, for God to know a person is for God to set his love on him and claim him: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5); you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2); the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19); if anyone loves God, he is known by God (1 Corinthians 8:3). Some read known by God as meaning only that God recognised or foresaw their faith. But that turns Paul’s correction upside down. He corrects himself on purpose: the Galatians came to know God because God first knew them. This is election, God’s free choice to set his love on his people before they chose him (Ephesians 1:4), and Paul introduces it not as a seminar topic but as a pastoral correction on the way past.

Known by the Shepherd. Jesus spoke of himself in the same terms. I am the good shepherd, he said; I know my own and my own know me, just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep (John 10:14–15). That is how God came to know the Galatians in this saving sense: in his Son, who knew his sheep before they knew his voice, and who paid for them with his life. To be known by God is to be one of those for whom the Shepherd died. It is the opposite of the most terrible sentence he will ever speak to anyone: I never knew you (Matthew 7:23).

Where the doctrine earns its keep. If your Christian life began with you, it can be ended by you, and every wobble is a threat to it. If it began with God knowing you, then the thing underneath your faith is not your grip. So ask the assurance question the right way round: not, do I know God well enough, but, does God know me? And the evidence that he does is that you are asking at all. Nobody who has not been sought goes looking.

Weak and worthless. Then the wound in the sentence. Weak (asthenēs): they cannot deliver what they demand. Worthless (ptōchos): literally beggarly, poor, with nothing in the account. Going back to the law as a system of righteousness is as much slavery as going back to idols. Both are religion without Christ, and both leave a man begging from a pauper.

Whose slaves you want to be once more? Why would freed slaves want to go back? Paul will not let them describe this as being pressured. Somewhere in them, they wanted it. That is the strangest fact about religious bondage: a system that tells you exactly what to do and exactly where you stand is restful in a way that grace, at first, is not. Grace gives you nothing to hold. Slavery hands you a list. Israel in the wilderness, not long out of Egypt, was already remembering the cucumbers and the melons and forgetting the whips (Numbers 11:5).

Why would anyone want to go back? Because slavery feels safe and freedom feels exposed. Under a list, you always know where you stand, and you can measure yourself against other people. Under grace, you stand where Christ has put you, and you have nothing to bring and nothing to boast about. For proud hearts that is hard. It is also the only place where rest is real. If you notice in yourself a longing for a system that would tell you precisely how good you are, treat that longing as Paul treats it: not as a sign of seriousness, but as the old slave in you reaching for his chains.

For worship. He knew us first. While the Galatians were still carrying offerings to statues that could not see them, the living God had set his love on them and was sending a sick missionary up the road to find them. We did not discover God; he came looking, found us among the idols, and called us by name, and he has written that name where no beggarly power can erase it.

parallels.desc: no gods, but the work of men’s hands

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You observe days! There is no verb of judgement in the sentence; the exclamation mark carries the whole weight. He is a Jew, raised on that calendar, and he is looking at Gentile converts keeping it and he can hardly speak. The verb, paratēreō, means to watch scrupulously, to observe with anxious care.

The whole year. Four terms, and most likely they map onto the Jewish year as a whole: the Sabbaths, the new moons, the festivals, Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles, and the sabbatical years (Colossians 2:16). Not a stray superstition, but the God-given calendar of the Old Testament, kept by people who wanted to please him, as a requirement for righteousness, on the advice of men who told them their faith was insufficient without it.

The ground, not the observance. So what is Paul attacking? Not the observance in itself. The ground. The Galatians were not marking Passover in gratitude; they were taking on the calendar as the thing that would complete their standing with God. The same act can be worship or slavery depending entirely on what it is being asked to do. Writing to Rome about holy days, Paul says that one person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike, and each one should be fully convinced in his own mind, and neither is to despise the other, because both are doing it to the Lord (Romans 14:5–6). He allows both practices in the same congregation, provided neither is made a way of earning standing with God.

Watching the clock after the hour has struck. Paul has just said that when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son (4:4). The whole calendar of Israel had been counting toward that hour. Now the Galatians are watching days and months with anxious care, as if the decisive date were still ahead and their standing hung on keeping time correctly. But the hour has come, and the one it was counting toward has been born, has died for us and has risen. To go back to watching the calendar as the ground of acceptance is to keep staring at the clock after the guest you were waiting for has arrived and is sitting at your table.

Where Christians differ: holy days. Some say this verse forbids Christians from keeping any special days, including Sunday, Christmas or Easter. Others insist on strict keeping of the Jewish seventh-day Sabbath. And many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still binds as the Christian Sabbath, now kept on the Lord’s Day, so that Paul here condemns only the Jewish ceremonial days (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8); they are serious, godly brothers, and their reading deserves respect. Verdict: Paul condemns observing days as a requirement for being right with God, as part of the old covenant law. The Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), who is himself our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Gathering on the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is not a return to the law, but a privilege of the new covenant (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10): Christians gladly set it apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom rather than as a binding law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5). Christians may also remember events like Christ’s birth and resurrection, as long as these are not made a means of righteousness or bound on others’ consciences.

So should I keep Sunday differently from other days? Yes, gladly, but as a gift, not a test. The Lord’s Day is the day Christ rose, and his people have gathered on it since the first Easter. Make it the day you meet with the church, hear the word, share the Lord’s Supper, and rest from ordinary work as far as your calling allows. Many find a quieter Sunday a great blessing to the soul. But do not make your way of keeping it the measure of other Christians, and do not imagine that a well-kept Sunday puts God in your debt. It is a feast with your Father, not a payment to him.

Everybody has a calendar. Sunday attendance, the daily reading before work, the annual conference, the fast in Lent, the family devotions after supper: all good, and all potentially either. A Christian who has missed church through flu and feels sorrow is worshipping. A Christian who has missed church through flu and feels exposed is observing days, and the cure for that feeling is not to try harder next Sunday but to hear again that Christ has done it all.

I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain. Then verse 11, and the mood drops. No thunder now. The man who has been issuing anathemas admits to being frightened. He does not say they are lost: he never quite does in this letter, and the restraint is deliberate. He says he is afraid, and he says it to their faces, which is a different and far more disarming thing than a warning. He has given these towns a great deal: if they are the churches of Acts 14, as many think, the stoning at Lystra, the nights teaching, the long roads walked twice over (Acts 14:19–23). He is telling them he can see all of it going.

Does Paul fear that the Galatians are lost? He fears for them; he does not pronounce on them. Some of those in the churches may never have been truly converted, and Paul knows that a church can contain both. But he writes to them as his little children (v. 19), and his fear is the anguish of a father. Warnings like this are one of the means God uses to keep his people from falling away (compare 5:4): the true child hears the warning and runs back, and in running back proves that God’s hold on him was real. Those whom God has truly known he will keep (John 10:28–29), and he keeps them partly by letters like this one.

For worship. All the days and months and seasons and years of the old calendar were sketches of one Person. The Sabbath pointed to the rest he gives; the Passover to the Lamb he is; the Day of Atonement to the blood he shed once for all; the feast of Tabernacles to the day he will dwell with us for ever. When the substance has come, the shadows bow to him, and his people gather on the morning of his rising not to earn his favour but to celebrate that the work is finished.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, I entreat you. The tone changes completely, and the first word is the tell: brothers, family. Then entreat, deomai, the verb for begging, the word a man uses when he has run out of arguments and is simply asking.

Become as I am. The sentence is compressed and often misread as a general appeal to imitate Paul’s character. It is more specific, and very moving. I have become as you are: Paul was a Jew of impeccable pedigree, circumcised the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). He had every marker the Judaizers were selling, by birth, and he had laid them down. He lived among Gentiles as a Gentile, ate at their tables, sat loose to the calendar, and refused to make his heritage the ground of anything (1 Corinthians 9:21). So the appeal is: become as I am, free from the law as a way of righteousness. I gave up my law-keeping to stand where you stand, on Christ alone. Do not walk into the room I walked out of.

What it cost him. The appeal is only as strong as the price behind it. Writing to Philippi, Paul listed everything he had laid down, the pedigree, the tribe, the blamelessness under the law, and said he counted it all as loss, as rubbish, because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). The word is not delicate; it is what you throw out. He had held the whole hand the Judaizers were dealing and thrown it in the fire, not because it was worthless in itself but because he had found Christ, and a man who has Christ needs no other ground to stand on: he wants only to be found in him, not having a righteousness of his own that comes from the law (Philippians 3:9).

What are you holding on to? Which puts a question to anyone reading who has never had to give anything up for Christ. Not a guilty question: some believers are simply spared it. But most of us are carrying something we have never once considered laying down: a family standing, a competence we are known for, a record of respectability, a theological rigour that has become an identity. None of those is wrong to have. Every one of them is fatal to hold on to as the thing that makes you acceptable, and the way to find out which you are doing is to ask what it would take from you if it were gone.

You did me no wrong. Then a short sentence that would be easy to skip. When he was with them, they treated him well. Nobody says that unless the other party might think he is nursing a grievance, and the Galatians could be forgiven for wondering, since people who are furious usually have a personal injury somewhere. Paul forecloses it. This is not a personal quarrel, and he wants that off the table so it cannot be used to explain away what he is saying.

The weapon he laid down. Anyone who has to say a hard thing to someone they love is tempted to let the personal hurt do the work, because a wound wins arguments. Paul refuses the advantage. He clears his own grievance out of the way so that they have nothing to react to except the truth.

How do I raise a hard truth without making it about me? Separate the issue from your feelings before you speak. Ask yourself honestly whether you are hurt, and if you are, deal with that before God first, so that it does not leak into the conversation. Then speak about the thing itself, the teaching, the behaviour, the danger, in plain words. Say, as Paul does, that you are not nursing a grievance, and mean it. Make clear that you love the person and want their good. And if they are hurt by what you say, do not reach for your own hurt to win the exchange. Let the truth carry its own weight.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A bodily ailment. Now Paul does something that changes the temperature of the whole chapter: he takes them back to the day he arrived. The gospel came to Galatia because Paul was ill. It seems he had not planned to preach there, or not then. Something happened to his body that stopped him or diverted him, and while he was in that condition he preached, and churches were born, the very churches he is now writing to.

What was the ailment? We do not know, and the honest answer is better than a confident one. Some have suggested malaria caught in the coastal lowlands, which would drive a man up onto the Anatolian plateau where these towns are. Some suggest a disease of the eyes, on the strength of the gouged-out eyes in verse 15 and the large letters of 6:11. Others have thought of the thorn in the flesh of 2 Corinthians 12. Paul does not say, and every generation of sick Christians has been the richer for his silence, because it means no one can be told that their particular affliction is not the kind God uses.

Not the obstacle but the mechanism. What he does say is that the illness was the occasion. Not the obstacle to the mission: the mechanism of it. Paul could only have seen it afterwards, which is how this usually works. The pattern is everywhere in Scripture: Joseph in the pit, Jeremiah in the cistern, John on Patmos, Paul in chains writing the prison letters. God’s habit of building his church out of interrupted plans is not an occasional exception. It is nearly the rule.

And though my condition was a trial to you. Then verse 14, and a detail that is easy to miss. Whatever it was, it was hard to look at, and it made him hard to receive. In that culture, some saw illness as a sign of demonic attack or divine displeasure. A visibly sick preacher announcing the favour of God was an awkward package.

You did not scorn or despise me. The second verb is exeptysate, from ekptyō, and it means literally you did not spit out. In that world, when you met a person visibly diseased, you might spit, to ward off the contagion and the evil eye that was assumed to be behind it. They did not. Hold that beside 3:1, where Paul asked who had bewitched them, a word that carried the idea of the evil eye. The Galatians had once refused to treat a sick preacher as a man under a curse. Now someone has looked at them and they are enchanted.

As an angel of God. That is the height of it. They took a sick, unimpressive, possibly repellent stranger and treated him as God’s messenger, even as though the Lord himself had come to town; and in the only sense that matters, he had. Whoever receives you receives me, Jesus said, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me (Matthew 10:40).

Does God really use sickness for good, or is that just something people say? He really does, though not always in ways we can see at the time, and never by making the sickness itself good. Illness is part of the curse, and Christ came to undo it. But God, who rules all things, bends even the curse to serve his children (Romans 8:28). Here the evidence is a whole province of churches. In your case it may be a doctor who hears the gospel, a nurse who watches you trust God, a friendship that would never have happened, or simply a deepening of your own faith that nothing else could have worked. You are allowed to pray for healing, and you should. You are also allowed to believe that the months you thought were wasted are not.

How should I treat a sick or weak Christian, or a weak preacher? As the Galatians first treated Paul. Do not measure a messenger by his health, polish or charm. Visit the sick, sit with the disabled, listen to the preacher who stammers, and receive Christ’s word through them. Many churches quietly honour the strong and forget the weak, and in doing so they miss the very people through whom God most often works (1 Corinthians 1:27; 12:22).

For worship. The gospel arrived in Galatia carried by a sick man, and it arrived in the world carried by a crucified one. He had no form or majesty that we should look at him, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, one from whom men hide their faces (Isaiah 53:2–3). The world spat on him, literally, and he bore it. And through his wounds the Father healed the nations. Our God has always loved to put his treasure in jars of clay, so that the surpassing power belongs to him and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then has become of your blessedness? The word is makarismos, from the same root as the Beatitudes’ blessed: the state of being congratulated, the joy and happiness of people who know they have been given everything. Paul is not asking where their doctrine went. He is asking where their joy went, and he asks it as a man who remembers what they were like.

Legalism changes the atmosphere first. That is diagnostic. Legalism does not usually announce itself by error first. It announces itself by a change of atmosphere. The doctrine is still broadly right, the meetings still happen, the language is still Christian, and the gladness has gone out of the room, replaced by an earnest, watchful, slightly anxious carefulness that everyone mistakes for seriousness. If you want to know whether a church has drifted, do not start with its confession. Start with whether anyone in it looks relieved.

The blessing David spoke of. Paul has used this word before, and his own use of it shows where the Galatians’ joy had come from. In Romans he writes that David speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered (Romans 4:6–7). That was the blessedness of the Galatians: the gladness of sinners who had heard that Christ was crucified for them and that God counted them righteous in him. It was the joy of being forgiven, and it lasts exactly as long as Christ’s work is the ground you stand on. Add law to Christ and forgiveness feels conditional again, and the gladness drains out of the room.

Gouged out your eyes. It may be a proverb for giving away what you value most, and it may be pointing at what was actually wrong with him, a hint that his ailment affected his eyes. Either way the shape is the same: there was nothing they would not have given him.

Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth? And then verse 16, a lonely sentence. The word for telling the truth is alētheuōn: truthing, dealing truthfully. It is the same word Paul uses in Ephesians when he tells the church to speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). And consider the position he is now in. He has not changed. He has said the same thing he always said. What has changed is what they are willing to hear, and the effect is that the man who loves them most is now filed as the opposition. Truth-tellers are often treated as enemies.

Two things held together. First, the possibility that you have become the enemy is not proof that you were wrong: the whole letter assumes Paul is right and unwelcome at the same time. Second, it is not proof that you were right either. Some men are treated as enemies because they told the truth, and some because they enjoyed telling it. The test is what Paul does next: he does not withdraw, and he does not harden. He goes on writing, and within three verses he is calling them my little children and speaking of labour pains. Paul wrote his hardest letters out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears (2 Corinthians 2:4). Truth-telling that has stopped hurting the one who does it has usually stopped being love.

I have lost my joy. Does that mean I have drifted into legalism? Not necessarily. Joy can be dimmed by grief, illness, depression, exhaustion or long trials, and those are not sins. But it is worth asking one honest question: has my confidence before God become tied to my performance? If you find that you feel accepted only on good weeks, that is very often where the joy has leaked away. Go back to the gospel itself. Read Galatians 2:20 and Romans 8:1 slowly and believe them about yourself. Joy grows where grace is believed, not where it is merely agreed with.

What if someone treats me as an enemy for telling them the truth? Check yourself first: were you right, and were you loving? If you were harsh, apologise for the harshness without withdrawing the truth. Then keep loving them. Do not cut them off, do not gossip about them, do not harden. Keep praying for them, and keep the door open. Paul did not stop writing to the Galatians; he wrote them this letter.

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They make much of you, but for no good purpose. Paul now names the technique, and it is worth naming plainly, because it has never gone out of use. The verb is zēloō: to be zealous for, to court, to pay ardent attention to. It could be used of a suitor. The Judaizers were not bullying the Galatians; they were paying court to them. Flattering them. Singling them out. Making them feel that they, particularly, were worth the trouble of a long journey and a personal interest.

They want to shut you out. And then the second move, which is the whole point of the first. They wanted to exclude the Galatians from Paul and from the true fellowship, so that the Galatians would depend on them and court them in return. The courting is bait; the shutting out is the hook.
