Draw a person close enough to feel the warmth of belonging, then hold the door a few inches short of open, so that the belonging is always nearly his and never quite. And it works because of something in us, not only in them. Every human heart is hungry to be noticed, chosen and approved, and whoever seems to feed that hunger can lead us almost anywhere. The only safe place for it is the one approval that cannot be withdrawn: God’s, given in Christ (3:26).

The anatomy of manipulation. That is the pattern of spiritual manipulation, the same mechanism that runs a cult, and it does not require a heretic. It happens wherever a leader’s significance depends on being needed, and it can be entirely sincere. The signs are consistent: unusual attention early; a suggestion that you have been seen more clearly here than anywhere else; a group with an inside; a standard you are always approaching; a gentle discouragement from friendships or teaching outside the group; and a quiet impression that leaving would be a betrayal rather than a departure.

For a good purpose. Paul then does something careful in verse 18. He does not conclude that all such attention is wrong. He is not sour about affection; he has just spent four verses saying how much he enjoyed theirs.

Two marks of healthy zeal. The first is purpose: for a good purpose. So the question is never whether someone is courting you. It is what they want you for. A teacher who wants Christ formed in you will be delighted when you grow past needing him, because that was the object. A teacher who wants you to make much of him will find your independence threatening, and will say so in spiritual language. The second mark is durability: not only when I am present. Attention that is switched on in the room and off outside it was never about you. Paul is doing exactly that as he writes: absent, unpopular, and still labouring over them.

Courting for another. Paul uses the suitor’s language of himself too, and it shows what healthy zeal is for. To the Corinthians he writes: I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). The false teachers courted the Galatians for themselves. Paul courts them for Christ. A faithful minister is the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom, and his joy is complete when the bride is given to her husband (John 3:29). Every true ministry keeps turning the bride’s eyes to the one Person to whom the church belongs.

What it does not mean. It does not mean warm attention from others is always manipulative, or that a church that welcomes newcomers eagerly is suspect. It means watch the motive, and watch where the attention is leading: toward Christ and the wider body of his people, or toward one leader and one group.

I think I may be in a group like this. What should I do? Start by testing it against Scripture and against wise believers outside the group. Ask: am I free to read and hear other faithful teachers? Am I encouraged to have Christian friends elsewhere? Is my standing with God tied, openly or quietly, to my loyalty here? Would leaving be treated as sin? If the answers worry you, talk to a trusted pastor or mature Christian from another church. You do not owe a group your conscience; you owe that to Christ. And if there is abuse, spiritual or otherwise, it must never be tolerated or covered: seek help, and if a crime has been committed, report it.

How do I make sure I am not the one doing this? Ask what you want from the people you help. Are you glad when they grow, find other friends and teachers, and need you less? Do you speak well of other faithful churches and leaders? Do you keep loving people who disagree with you or move on? If you are a leader, invite others to examine your influence. The aim of all ministry is that people make much of Christ, not of us (John 3:30).

On a Tuesday. You need no one’s inner circle, because the Father has already made you his child (3:26). So look at your own zeal instead: is there someone you have been warm to only while they were useful to you, or only in their presence? Send them a message this week that asks nothing back.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My little children. The anger drops out of the letter completely, and what is left is a parent. Many early manuscripts read teknia, little children, which would be the only time Paul uses that tender word; others read tekna, children, the reading most modern editions print. Either way it is a parent’s word, and it comes at the point where he has the least reason to be tender.

In the anguish of childbirth. Then the image, and it is startling from a man. Elsewhere he calls himself the churches’ father (1 Corinthians 4:15). Here he is their mother, and specifically a mother in labour: ōdinō, the word for birth pangs. He had gone through this once already, to bring them to birth when they were converted. Now he is going through it a second time, and anyone who has watched a birth knows that this is not a picturesque way of saying he is concerned. It is a way of saying he is being torn.

Until Christ is formed in you! Not until they come back to him, or see he was right, or apologise. The verb is morphoō, to take shape, from the root that gives us transformed in Romans 12:2 and conformed to the image of his Son in Romans 8:29. It is not a word for imitation or improvement. It is the word for something taking its proper shape from the inside, like a child taking form in the womb. The aim is not that they look like Paul, or keep the law, but that they look like Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18).

The metric of ministry. That is the goal of all Christian ministry, and almost everything else that gets measured is easier. A congregation can be strong in attendance, giving and doctrinal precision while Christ is no more formed in them than he was a decade ago. Paul’s metric is brutal in its simplicity: do these people look more like Jesus than they did? A ministry that produces admirers, or partisans, or well-informed critics of other churches, has produced something, but not this.

What does Christ formed in me actually look like? It looks like the fruit Paul names in the next chapter: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (5:22–23). It looks like a growing humility that does not need to be noticed, a readiness to forgive, a love for the unlovely, courage in suffering, and a deepening delight in the Father. It does not happen by willpower. The Spirit forms Christ in us through the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of the church and the daily trials God sends. It is usually slow, often invisible to the person himself, and very often seen first by others.

Change my tone. Then verse 20, and it is a very human line. He knows how the letter sounds. He has written anathemas into it, and he is not withdrawing them, but he would give a great deal to be in the room, because a letter cannot modulate and a voice can. He wants to say the same words with his face visible.

For I am perplexed about you. And then the admission. Aporoumai, from aporeō: at a loss, without a way through. The apostle who has just settled the doctrine of justification for the whole church does not know what to do about this particular set of people. That is a mercy to anyone praying for someone who has drifted. Certainty about the truth and bewilderment about a person are not incompatible. Paul had both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they needed to be born again a second time. The new birth happens once and is never undone (John 3:3–8; 1 Peter 1:23). Paul’s labour now is for their growth, that Christ be formed in them, and his labour pains are the agony of a pastor watching that growth threatened.

I am praying for someone who has drifted, and I do not know what to do. Then you are where Paul was. You do not have to have a plan to keep loving. Keep praying specifically that Christ would be formed in them, not merely that they would return to church or agree with you. Keep the relationship warm. Say the truth when there is an opportunity, and say it with your face, in person, rather than in a long message if you can. And leave the outcome with God. Paul was at a loss, and God still had the Galatians in hand.

For worship. Paul’s labour pains are an echo of a greater travail. Out of the anguish of his soul the Servant shall see and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11): Christ laboured on the cross to bring a people to birth, and he does not abandon them in the womb. What he began in us he will not leave half-formed. He is forming his Son in us now, slowly, faithfully, through every trial and every Sunday, and one day, when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — Hagar and Sarah: Two Covenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the story of Abraham’s two sons, Ishmael by the slave woman Hagar, born in the ordinary way, and Isaac by the free woman Sarah, born by promise (vv. 21–23). He reads them as two covenants: Hagar stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery with her children; Sarah for the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother (vv. 24–27). Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise, and should expect the opposition Isaac met (vv. 28–29). Scripture says to cast out the slave woman and her son, and believers are children of the free woman (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
Typology, and Why the Two Covenants Cannot Share a House

Verse 24 is not allegory of the kind that dissolves history. Paul’s premise is that it is written that Abraham had two sons, and he treats the mothers and the manner of each birth as facts. He is saying the history happened and was designed by God to carry a meaning the coming of Christ has made visible, as the risen Christ himself taught on the Emmaus road (Luke 24:27).

Verses 24–25 give the test for the whole section: what a covenant produces shows what kind of covenant it is, when it is used as a way of salvation. And v. 30 shows why grace and merit cannot be mixed: add merit to grace and the result is merit, because once our performance is part of the ground, the whole weight rests on it. Paul casts out a system, not persons; he is in labour for the people who hold it, and Genesis itself shows God caring for Ishmael (Genesis 21:17–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers presented themselves as Abraham’s true heirs. Verse 22 shows that physical descent was never the mark, v. 23 that the difference lay in how each son came to exist, and v. 29 explains why religious men were persecuting a Gentile church: if a farmer who believed last month is as accepted as a man who has kept the law for forty years, the forty years bought nothing.

Now: Verse 23 touches most of us: the situation you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long is Hagar’s tent. And v. 29 warns us to watch what rises in us when someone is blessed without having earned it.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? The sarcasm is exact, and the passage turns on it. You want the law? Then let us read it. And Paul is about to demonstrate that the Judaizers, the teachers urging the Galatians under the law, have been quoting a book they have not understood. Note the second use of the word: the law here means the Torah, the five books of Moses as a whole, not the commandments as a code. Paul is going to Genesis.

In the flow. Verse 20 ended with Paul at a loss. Verse 21 begins one more argument, the last of the letter’s long doctrinal section, and it gathers up every thread so far: Abraham and his true children (3:6–9, 29), promise against law (3:15–18), the slave and the son (4:1–7), flesh against Spirit (3:3). All of them come back in the story of two mothers and two sons. And the story leads straight into the call of 5:1: Christ has set us free for freedom, so stand firm and do not take up the yoke of slavery again.

For it is written that Abraham had two sons. Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by his free wife Sarah was Isaac (Genesis 16; 21). The whole argument rests on a fact so obvious that the Judaizers had evidently never thought about it: physical descent from Abraham cannot be the qualification, because Ishmael had it. He was Abraham’s son, circumcised at thirteen by Abraham’s own hand (Genesis 17:23–25), and outside the covenant line. Blood was never the mechanism, and the family tree proves it before you have left Genesis.

One by a slave woman and one by a free woman. The mothers’ status determined the sons’ status. A child born to a slave was a slave; a child born to the free wife was the heir. Paul will build the rest of the chapter on that legal fact.

Born according to the flesh. Then verse 23 gives the real distinction, and it is not only about the mothers’ status but about how each son came to exist. Put the two births side by side. Ishmael was produced by a plan. God had promised Abraham a son; ten years passed (Genesis 16:3); Sarah did the arithmetic on her own body and concluded that God needed help, and offered her slave (Genesis 16:1–4). It was legal, it was customary, and it worked: a healthy boy was born, exactly as intended. That is what according to the flesh means here: not immorality, but competence. Human capability doing what it can, on God’s behalf, because waiting had become unbearable.

Born through promise. Isaac was produced by nothing at all. By the time he was conceived Sarah was ninety and past every natural possibility, and she had laughed at the announcement (Genesis 18:10–14). There was no mechanism. There was a promise, and then, at the time God had said, there was a baby (Genesis 21:1–2), and nothing in between that anyone could take credit for. Is anything too hard for the LORD? That question is the question of the whole letter.

Children of promise in the Son of promise. Isaac was not the end of the promise but a link in it: through Isaac shall your offspring be named (Genesis 21:12), and Paul has already said who that offspring is: Christ (3:16). So when he calls believers children of promise like Isaac (4:28), he means what he meant before: if you are Christ’s, you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (3:29). And the question asked at the tent door was answered again at Nazareth. When the angel told a virgin that her son would be called the Son of the Most High, he met her bewilderment with words close to the ones Sarah heard: nothing will be impossible with God (Luke 1:37).

Two ways of getting a result. So the two sons are two ways of getting a result: what a capable person can arrange, and what only God can give. Everyone believes God can save; the live question is whether he needs the help. The Galatians were not planning to abandon Christ any more than Abraham was planning to abandon the promise. They were proposing to assist it.

Hagar’s tent. Turn that on yourself before Paul turns it on the Judaizers, because the instinct is universal and it usually looks like responsibility. The thing you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long, the situation you are managing, the outcome you are engineering, the good end you are pursuing by means you would rather not examine: that is Hagar’s tent. It is usually not wickedness but Sarah with a calendar, doing the sum, and being right about the arithmetic and wrong about God.

So is it wrong to plan, or to work hard? No. Abraham’s fault was not that he acted but that he acted to secure by his own means what God had promised to give in his own way, and by a means God had not approved. Christians are told to work, plan, save, seek medical help and use every lawful means. The question is whether you are using means in faith, as God’s gifts, or in place of faith, because you have stopped believing he will keep his word. A good test is whether the plan requires you to bend God’s commands. Sarah’s plan did, and it filled the tent with grief for a generation (Genesis 16:4–6; 21:9–11).

For worship. If you are a believer, you were born as Isaac was, by God’s promise and power, not by human effort. Nobody arranged your new birth; nobody could have. The God who gave a son to a woman of ninety gave life to your dead heart, and he did it so that no one could mistake whose child you are. He is the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17), and every Christian is a laugh of joy in the tent of the impossible.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by the free woman Sarah was Isaac, born by promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this may be interpreted allegorically. This sentence troubles careful readers, and it should be met head on. The verb is allēgoreō: to speak another way, figuratively. The worry is legitimate. In Paul’s century, Alexandrian interpreters, Philo above all, read the Old Testament allegorically in a way that dissolved the history: Abraham became the soul, Sarah became virtue, and whether any of it happened could seem not to matter. If that is what Paul is doing here, then the door is open for anyone to make any text mean anything, and readers who prize a plain reading of Scripture are right to be uneasy.

The history is his premise. But it is not what he is doing, and the evidence is in his own sentences. He has just insisted that it is written that Abraham had two sons: the history is his premise, not his raw material. He names the son’s mother, her status and the manner of each birth as facts. He is not saying the story stands for something instead of having happened. He is saying that it happened, and that God so arranged it that it carries a meaning the coming of Christ has now made visible. That is what the risen Christ himself did on the Emmaus road when, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). The history is real, and it was designed. If God governs history and knows the end from the beginning, then the pattern in a true story is not something a reader imposes; it is something the Author put there.

Where Christians differ: allegory in interpretation. Some use this passage to justify reading allegories into all of Scripture, finding hidden meanings unrelated to the plain sense. Verdict: Paul’s method here is closer to typology, reading real people and events as patterns God built in to point forward to Christ, than to free allegory. He does not deny the history; he sees in it what God designed it to show (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). Interpreters should first grasp the plain meaning of a text, and only find further meanings where Scripture itself warrants them. Paul, writing under inspiration, had that warrant; later interpreters must stay within what Scripture teaches.

These women are two covenants. Hagar and Sarah represent two covenants: two arrangements by which people seek to stand before God, and two families they produce. A covenant is a binding relationship that God sets up by his word, with his promises on one side and the terms of the relationship on the other: at Sinai, a law to be kept; with Abraham, a promise to be believed (Genesis 15:18; Exodus 24:7–8). The covenant of law, given at Sinai: those who rely on it as the way to righteousness are slaves. Feel what a first-century Jew would have felt: Hagar, the Egyptian slave, the outsider, the one who was sent away, is Sinai. Sinai, where the law was given in fire, is the mother of slaves.

Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia. Why is Hagar Mount Sinai? Hagar’s descendants, through Ishmael, settled in the desert lands of Arabia (Genesis 25:12–18), and Sinai lies in the region Paul calls Arabia. But the deeper link is the pattern: a slave mother, a covenant that leads to slavery, children born into it.

The present Jerusalem. And Sinai corresponds to the present Jerusalem: the actual city, the temple, the priesthood, the whole visible centre of the religion the Judaizers were selling, which had rejected Christ and clung to the law. In four clauses Paul has put the Jerusalem establishment on Hagar’s side of the family, and the Galatians on Sarah’s. It follows from everything he has argued: what a covenant produces tells you what kind of covenant it is, when it is used as a way of salvation. A system that demands performance can only ever produce people in bondage, however holy the mountain it came from and however ancient the city that keeps it. You do not judge the tree by its address.

Was the covenant at Sinai a bad thing, then? No. God gave it, and it was holy and good (Romans 7:12). It began with grace: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Its sacrifices pointed to Christ, and believing Israelites like David were justified by faith under it (Romans 4:6–8). But it was a covenant for a time of childhood (vv. 1–3): it kept Israel under strict rules, under the threat of curse, until Christ came (3:23–24). It could command but could not give the Spirit or a new heart (3:21; Jeremiah 31:31–33). So when people cling to Sinai after Christ has come, and treat its law as the way to be accepted by God, they are choosing slavery over sonship. Hagar stands for Sinai used in that way: the law cut off from the promise it was meant to serve.

Who frees the children of Sinai? Not Sinai. A covenant that bears children for slavery cannot also set them free; it has nothing to give them but its terms. The freedom Paul preaches comes from the Son, and he has said so a few sentences earlier: God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (4:4–5). Christ was born under the very law that held its children, kept it, and bore its curse, so that whoever trusts him, Jew or Gentile, is no longer a slave but a son.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish people are rejected by God. Paul speaks of the system of law apart from Christ. The present Jerusalem does not mean the Jewish people as a race; it means the system of law-keeping the false teachers offered, centred in Jerusalem. Paul grieved for his own people with great sorrow and unceasing anguish (Romans 9:1–3) and longed for their salvation; his quarrel was with a way of salvation, not with a race. Any reading of this verse that feeds contempt for Jewish people has turned Paul’s own heart upside down.

How can I tell whether my church is a Hagar church or a Sarah church? Not by the strictness of its morals, because the free children of God love his law. Ask instead what people are trusting. Is the gospel of Christ’s finished work preached clearly and often, so that sinners leave knowing they are forgiven? Do people confess sins honestly, or only hide them? Are newcomers with messy pasts welcomed as fully as long-standing members? Is obedience urged as the fruit of grace, or as the price of acceptance? Free churches can be serious about holiness; what they are not is anxious about standing.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jerusalem above is free. After the severity of the Hagar line, Paul gives the Galatians an address. They had been made to feel provincial: latecomers on the edge of the empire, whose membership depended on satisfying a committee far away in the real Jerusalem. He tells them their mother lives somewhere else. The Jerusalem above is the heavenly Jerusalem: the city of God, the true people of God, the new covenant. And she is not an idea. The writer to the Hebrews says believers have already come to it: to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebrews 12:22). John sees her coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride (Revelation 21:2). The believer’s citizenship is not pending. It is filed (Philippians 3:20).

And she is our mother. Corresponding to Sarah. Believers are children of the free woman, born from above. This is why the early church could call the church a mother: not because she gives grace of herself, but because God brings his children to birth within her through the word and Spirit, and feeds and raises them there.

Rejoice, O barren one. The quotation is Isaiah 54:1, and where it sits matters. It is the verse immediately after Isaiah 53: the very next thing said after the suffering servant, whom the New Testament names as Jesus (Acts 8:32–35), is pierced for our transgressions and makes many to be accounted righteous. The barren woman is told to sing because of what the servant has just done. Her fruitfulness is purchased. That is the logic of the whole gospel in the order of two chapters.

In its own setting. In Isaiah the barren one is Zion in exile: a city stripped, emptied of her children, desolate like a barren woman, with nothing to show. God tells her to start singing before there is anything visible to sing about, because the children are coming, and there will be more of them than the woman who never lost anything ever had.

The children of the desolate one. Paul sees this fulfilled first in Sarah, who spent decades with an empty tent while Hagar had a son, and became the mother of a multitude; and then in the church: this small, unimpressive, mostly Gentile movement, the new Jerusalem gathered from every nation, will out-populate the establishment that despises it. It has. The barren woman’s children are now counted in thousands of languages, on every continent.

The God of barren women. Look at how God has always worked. Sarah barren, Rebekah barren, Rachel barren, Hannah barren, Elizabeth barren and old, and the line of promise runs straight through every one of them, so that when the child finally comes nobody can mistake where he came from. The barren has borne seven, sang Hannah (1 Samuel 2:5). He does not build his family out of human capacity. He never has. He waits until there is nothing left to explain it, and then he fills the tent.

A word for a particular reader. This verse will find her. Some woman reading Galatians 4 is literally barren, and has been told to rejoice by people who meant well, and it landed like a stone. The text is not asking her to pretend. Isaiah’s command to sing is addressed to a woman whose grief is real and whose situation has not yet changed: that is the whole point of the verse. And it is grounded not in optimism but in what God has promised to do. Scripture never asks anyone to feel that a loss is not a loss. It does say that God’s way of filling a house has never depended on the ordinary mechanisms, that the desolate one ends the story with more, and that the emptiness he leaves in a life for a while is not a verdict on it.

Does this promise that God will give me children? No, not in the sense of a guarantee of a pregnancy. Isaiah 54 is a promise to God’s people as a whole, fulfilled in the gathering of the church, not a pledge to every childless couple. God does sometimes give children after long barrenness, and it is right to pray for them. But many faithful believers never have children, and they are not less blessed or less fruitful. In Christ, the childless are given spiritual sons and daughters, a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:4–5), and a family in the church that is as real as any household. Your fruitfulness in God’s kingdom does not depend on your womb.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church replaces Israel entirely. Jewish believers are part of the Jerusalem above too, from Peter and Paul to the present day, and the free woman’s family has always had Israelites at its heart. Christians differ on God’s purposes for the Jewish people as a nation (Romans 11:25–29), but agree that there is one family of Abraham, made up of all who believe, Jew and Gentile, and that no one enters it except through Christ.

On a Tuesday. When you feel small, provincial, behind, or excluded from the people who seem to matter in Christian circles, remember your address. You belong to the free city above, so live this week as its citizen: unafraid of the committees, generous, glad.

parallels.desc: sing, O barren one, who did not bear

verseByVerse.quote: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like Isaac. Before the hard verse comes, the assurance. Paul tells them who they are, and he does it in the plainest terms: not candidates, not applicants, not probationers, but Isaac. The miracle child. The one nobody could have produced.

How do I know which son I am? A reader will not simply accept the compliment, and he is right not to. Both sons were Abraham’s. Both lived in the same tent. Ishmael was circumcised and Isaac was circumcised, and for fourteen years Ishmael was the only son in that tent, so nobody watching could have told you which line the promise was attached to. Paul has already given the test, twice, and it is not a matter of intensity. Ishmael was not less sincere than Isaac and may well have worked harder. The difference is where each son came from. So ask what you are actually resting on when you are honest, and the answer usually surfaces fastest at the two extremes. After a good stretch, prayer flowing, temper holding, a real usefulness to somebody, does your confidence before God quietly rise? And after a bad one, does it fall? If it moves with your performance, you have been measuring the wrong thing, whatever you believe on paper; that confidence is Hagar’s, because it was produced by you. Most believers find their confidence moves a little; the answer is not despair but to rest again on Christ.

You are being told your name. The test is not, have I enough faith? That sends a man back inside himself to look for a quality he will never be able to weigh. Isaac did not qualify by being a better baby. He was born, and the birth was a gift, and the gift was announced before he existed. If you have come to the end of what you can contribute and are resting on what Christ has done, you are not being told to work up more assurance. You are being told your name.

Just as at that time. Then verse 29, and it explains something the Galatians were living through and could not account for. The reference is to Genesis 21:9. On the day Isaac was weaned Abraham threw a feast, and Sarah saw Ishmael laughing, and the Hebrew word is a play on Isaac’s own name, Yitzchaq, he laughs. Ishmael was most likely mocking the child, turning his name into a joke, at the party held in his honour. It looks small in Genesis, and Jewish tradition expanded it, but Paul calls it persecution: the older brother, produced by human arrangement, could not bear the existence of the child who was pure gift. Born according to the Spirit: Isaac’s birth by God’s power, as every believer’s new birth is.

So also it is now. That is the pattern Paul says is repeating. The people persecuting the Galatian churches were not pagans. They were religious men with a claim to Abraham, and what they could not tolerate was a family they had not qualified for.

The persecutor who was stopped. Paul knew this pattern from the inside, because he had been the persecutor: a zealous Pharisee, violently persecuting the church of God (1:13), until the risen Christ stopped him on the road and asked, Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The hostility of religious flesh toward the children of the Spirit is aimed, in the end, at Christ himself. He said so: if the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:18, 20). To be opposed for trusting grace is to share the reproach of the Son, and he counts every blow as struck at him.

Why grace provokes rage. It helps to understand why grace provokes rage rather than indifference. A man who has spent his life earning his standing has an enormous investment, and the doctrine of free grace does not merely disagree with him; it writes off the investment. If the Gentile who believed last month is as accepted as the Pharisee who has kept the calendar for forty years, then the forty years bought nothing. Nobody hears that calmly. The elder brother in the parable is furious at exactly this, and he never once says an untrue thing about himself (Luke 15:29–30).

A comfort and a warning. Two things follow. The first is a comfort for anyone bruised by opposition from inside the church. Hostility from religious people is not evidence that you have gone wrong; it begins at a child’s birthday party in Genesis. The second is a warning, and it is the more useful one. Watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it: the convert with the disgraceful history who is radiant, the newcomer given the opportunity you waited years for, the brother whose prayers appear to be answered while yours are not. That flicker is not a small sin of the temperament. It is the flesh recognising the child of promise and resenting him for it.

What does persecution from religious people look like today? It is rarely violent in most Western churches, though in some places it is. More often it is mockery, suspicion and exclusion: being called careless about holiness because you preach free grace; being treated as second-class because you do not keep a group’s extra rules; being shut out of fellowship for questioning a leader. Do not exaggerate ordinary disagreement into persecution, and do not assume every critic is an Ishmael; sometimes your critics are right. But when you are opposed for trusting Christ alone, recognise the old pattern and take heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what does the Scripture say? Paul has been arguing; now he stops and lets the text pronounce. Scripture settles it. And the sentence he chooses is the hardest in the chapter.

Cast out the slave woman. It is Genesis 21:10, and in Genesis it is Sarah who says it, apparently in anger, and the thing is very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son (Genesis 21:11). What makes it Scripture rather than a domestic quarrel is verse 12, where God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says, for a reason that is not about Sarah’s feelings at all: through Isaac shall your offspring be named. God confirmed the word. The line of promise must not be confused with the line of human arrangement, and you cannot keep both in the same house pretending they are the same thing.

What is to be cast out? Read what Paul does with it. He is not issuing instructions about persons; he applies it to the two covenants he has been contrasting for ten verses. The thing that cannot stay is the system: law-keeping as the ground of acceptance, sitting alongside the gospel as a supplementary option. Law-religion and grace cannot share the inheritance. The Galatians were trying to keep both mothers in the house. Paul says the arrangement is impossible, and not because grace is intolerant. Because the two produce different children, and one of them has no share in the estate. So the Galatians should cast out the false teachers’ message, and refuse its teachers the authority to shape the church.

Not a mixture but a failure. There is no version of Christianity in which grace and merit are balanced. Add merit to grace and you do not get a moderate position; you get merit, because the moment my performance is part of the ground, the whole weight has shifted onto it. If it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6). A little law as the basis of standing is like a little water in petrol. It is not a mixture. It is a failure.

The son remains for ever. Jesus laid down the same household law to men who boasted that Abraham was their father. Everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin, he said. The slave does not remain in the house for ever; the son remains for ever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:34–36). That is why Paul can say we are children of the free woman: not because we were born into better circumstances than the Judaizers, but because the Son has set us free, and those he frees remain in the Father’s house as long as he does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean cruelty to people. It means refusing to mix law-righteousness with grace. Paul casts out a doctrine; he spends the surrounding verses in labour pains for the people who hold it, calls them his little children, and wishes he could soften his voice. Anyone who quotes verse 30 to justify being hard with a person has read the sentence and missed the chapter. And Genesis itself handles Ishmael tenderly: God hears the boy crying in the desert, promises to make him a nation, and is with him as he grows (Genesis 21:17–20). The one cast out of the inheritance is not cast out of God’s care. Scripture is more tender than our use of it.

Does this mean my church should expel people who hold wrong views? Not on the strength of this verse alone. Paul’s target is a false gospel that adds works to Christ for justification, which he has already called accursed (1:8–9). A church must not let such teaching be taught from its pulpit, and teachers who persist in it after patient correction must not be given authority. Church discipline exists for that (Titus 3:10). But most disagreements among Christians are not about the ground of salvation, and they are to be borne with in love. And even those who are put out of fellowship are to be prayed for and pursued, with the aim of their restoration (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

Not children of the slave. The chapter lands on an identity, not a warning, and the pronoun has changed: not you now, but we. Paul puts himself in the sentence with them. Believers are free children of promise, heirs of everything. Everything that follows in chapter 5 about standing firm and not submitting again to a yoke is built on this one line: for freedom Christ has set us free (5:1). He is not telling them to become free. He is telling them what they are.

How do I cast out the slave woman in my own heart? By refusing, every day, to let your performance become the ground of your standing with God. When you have a good day, do not let it make you feel more accepted; thank God for the grace that helped you. When you have a bad day, do not let it make you feel less accepted; confess it, and rest again on Christ. Throw out the inner ledger. Then obey, gladly, because the free son loves his Father’s house and his Father’s ways.

For worship. The house of God has a Son at its centre, and he does not keep the inheritance to himself: the heir of all things has made us fellow heirs. Scripture says of the slave’s son, cast him out; the Son says of everyone the Father gives him, whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). No voice on earth or in hell can send back into slavery a child he has brought in, because the Father has put that child into hands from which no one can snatch him (John 10:28–29). We are free children of promise, and the door of the Father’s house has closed behind us, not in front of us.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman with her son

5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
In chapter 5 the letter turns from argument to life. Paul has argued for freedom: from the law as a way of being justified, from its curse, from the elementary principles of the old age. Now he shows that this freedom produces not moral chaos but something better than law-keeping ever could, and he answers two questions: what does freedom look like in practice, and if not the law, what shapes a Christian’s behaviour?

Freedom is not licence (v. 13). The Judaizers feared that a gospel without the law would produce lawlessness, and Paul’s answer is not to bring the law back but to walk by the Spirit. The whole law is fulfilled in love of neighbour (v. 14), and the Spirit grows that love in believers. The heart of the chapter sets the works of the flesh beside the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 19–23): many works, which human nature produces and which tear a community apart, against one fruit, a single character that is the character of Christ, grown by the Spirit in those who stay close to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 sums up four chapters in a line: Christ set us free so that we would be free. Freedom is the goal, not a stage on the way to a stricter religion, so believers must stand firm and not take up the yoke of slavery again, the yoke Peter said no one could bear (Acts 15:10), when Jesus offers his own easy yoke (Matthew 11:29–30).

Verses 2–6 are the warning. Whoever accepts circumcision as what completes his standing has changed systems: Christ is of no advantage to him, he is obligated to keep the whole law, and he has fallen away from grace. But believers wait by faith, through the Spirit, for the hope of righteousness, and what counts is faith working through love.

Then the appeal (vv. 7–12). Someone cut in on them as they ran. This teaching did not come from the God who called them, and a little of it changes the whole. Yet Paul is confident in the Lord about them, leaves the troubler to God’s judgement, and refuses any gospel that removes the offence of the cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

Gospel freedom is more than freedom from sin’s penalty; it is freedom from performance-based religion, the liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. This is not lawlessness. The law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk by the Spirit, rather than imposed from outside on those who must earn their standing. Luther’s paradox holds both: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.

Verse 4 describes a change of position, not of conduct. The people addressed had become more religious, not less; to fall from grace here is to step off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, not to disgrace oneself, as the phrase means today. And because Paul writes v. 10 a few sentences later, confident about the same people, v. 4 is best read as the warning that keeps them from the thing it describes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade, a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it was an exchange, and read them the rest of the contract nobody had mentioned. Verse 12 would have struck hard locally, since the mother goddess, whose chief shrine was at Pessinus in Galatia, was served by priests who castrated themselves.

Now: Standing firm (v. 1) usually means refusing to answer the question where do I stand with God today by reaching for the last few days. And v. 8 gives a test for any new teaching: does it come to you the way the God who called you came to you?

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Galatians 5 turns from argument to practice: what does freedom in Christ look like? First, stand firm in it. To accept circumcision as necessary for salvation is to be cut off from Christ and to fall from grace; believers wait by faith, through the Spirit, for the hope of righteousness, and what counts is faith working through love (vv. 1–12). Second, freedom is not licence but freedom to serve one another in love, which fulfils the law (vv. 13–15). Third, the free walk by the Spirit. Flesh and Spirit are at war in the believer; the works of the flesh shut a man out of the kingdom, the Spirit bears his fruit, and those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh (vv. 16–26). The chapter is the portrait of a freed people, drawn from the face of their Liberator.

For freedom Christ has set us free. Four chapters of argument are compressed into the line the letter is remembered by. Why say freedom twice? Because Paul is answering a question nobody had thought to ask: what is the freedom for? It is not a stage on the way to something else, nor a probationary liberty, nor a transfer to a stricter and more mature religion. Freedom (eleutheria) is the purpose of Christ’s work. Christ did not free us so that we could become slaves again; he released his people because he wanted them free.

Free from what, and free for what? Free from the law as a way of righteousness, from its curse (3:13), from the guardians and the elementary principles (4:1–9), from sin’s slavery, and from the endless anxious question of whether you have done enough. And free for God: to call him Father, to obey him from the heart, to love your neighbour without calculating. That needs saying, because a great many Christians treat grace as the doorway and law as the corridor beyond it. They will tell you cheerfully that they were saved by grace, and then describe a daily life in which everything depends on their performance. Paul says the door and the corridor are made of the same thing: the grace that brought you in is the same grace that carries you on, every day until the end: as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him (Colossians 2:6).

Stand firm therefore. The verb is stēkete, from stēkō: stand fast, as a soldier holds his position, and do not give up your ground. Freedom is not a resting state. Left alone, a free man drifts back toward slavery, because slavery is restful in a way that liberty is not. A slave is told what to do and knows exactly where he stands. Freedom asks you to live without a scoreboard, and that can feel harder than obedience.

A yoke of slavery. A yoke was the wooden frame laid across the shoulders of working animals: a picture of burden and servitude. The rabbis spoke of the yoke of the law as a glad discipline. But Peter, at the Jerusalem council, called it a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10). And it sits against another use of the word that every reader should hear beside it, because Jesus also offers a yoke: take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matthew 11:29–30). So the question is never whether a man will wear a yoke. It is whose.

Again. The verb is passive: do not let yourselves be subjected. Nobody was going to force the Galatians; they were going to agree, for reasons that felt like devotion. And again is the sharpest word in the sentence, because these were Gentiles who had never been under Moses in their lives. Paul means that a return to law-keeping would land them back where their paganism had them: performing, appeasing, never sure.

What standing firm looks like. So what does standing firm actually look like on a Wednesday? Mostly it looks like refusing to answer one question the way your instincts want to answer it. The question is, where do I stand with God today? The instinctive answer reaches for the last few days: how you prayed, how you spoke to your wife, whether you did the thing you promised yourself you would stop doing. Standing firm is declining to answer it that way. Not because the week does not matter; it matters a great deal. But it is not the ground you are standing on, and the day you let it become the ground, the yoke is back on your shoulders and nobody had to put it there.

In the flow. The verse is a hinge. Its first half sums up the picture of 4:21–31, where believers are children not of the slave woman but of the free; its second half launches everything that follows. Verses 2–12 defend this freedom against the teachers who would take it away, and 5:13–6:10 show what a freed people does with it. The letter has argued that we are free; from here it urges us to stay free and to live free.

Is it legalism to keep personal rules, like not drinking or fasting on Fridays? Not in itself. A Christian may freely adopt a rule for wisdom’s sake: to avoid a temptation, to discipline the body, to serve a weaker brother (Romans 14:21; 1 Corinthians 9:27). It becomes a yoke of slavery in two ways: when you think keeping it makes you more acceptable to God, and when you bind it on other Christians as though God had commanded it. So keep your rule if it helps you, hold it loosely, never use it to measure others, and never let it whisper that you are more pleasing to God than the brother who does not keep it.

For worship. Christ did not buy us out of the market to put us to work in a new one. He bought us to bring us home. The Son of God took the yoke of the law on his own shoulders, carried it the whole way without stumbling, and bore its curse, so that the beam would never be laid on ours again. The only yoke he lays on us now is his own, shaped by the hands of a carpenter who is gentle and lowly in heart.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals — a picture of burdensome obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look: I, Paul, say to you. He stops the argument and puts his name in the sentence. The whole weight of his apostleship, defended at length in chapters 1 and 2, is being set down on what comes next, and what comes next is alarming.

Of no advantage. Not less advantage. None. And that is startling, because on the face of it circumcision is a small thing: a rite God himself commanded, which Paul says counts for nothing either way (v. 6). So the act is not the issue. The issue is what it is being asked to do. If a man accepts circumcision as the thing that completes his standing with God, he has not added a little security to Christ. He has changed systems. And in the system he has entered, Christ is not an asset, because that system does not deal in gifts. It deals in obligations, and it has no column for what somebody else has done. You cannot have Christ as a partial Saviour.

But Paul circumcised Timothy. A reader who knows his New Testament raises a fair objection here, and Paul’s opponents were evidently raising it too (v. 11). Paul circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3), yet refused to let Titus be circumcised (2:3). How is that not inconsistency? Because the two cases are opposite in everything that matters. Titus was a test case: the demand was made in Jerusalem, as a condition, to prove that a Gentile could not be fully accepted otherwise, and Paul did not yield even for a moment. Timothy’s mother was Jewish, so to the synagogues of the region he would have counted as a Jew left uncircumcised, and that would have shut the door of every building Paul wanted to preach in. Nobody claimed it justified him. It was a matter of access, not of standing.

The principle. So the same physical act meant two irreconcilable things, and Paul’s judgement in each case was governed by one question: is anyone claiming this is necessary? When nobody is, it is a matter of freedom and he is flexible to the point of inconvenience. The moment somebody says you must, he will not move an inch. The same principle governs many secondary practices in church life.

May Christians circumcise their sons today, for health or family reasons? Yes. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything (v. 6). Paul himself had Timothy circumcised for the sake of his witness among Jews (Acts 16:3). What is forbidden is circumcision as a requirement for being accepted by God. A Jewish Christian parent may circumcise his son as a mark of his heritage; no one may make it a condition of salvation.

What would circumcision be today? Anything added to Christ as a condition of being right with God. Nobody in your church is likely to demand circumcision, but plenty of things play its part: a particular experience you must have had, a style of worship, a political position, a level of Bible knowledge, a list of things good Christians do not do, a baptism in the right church, or a feeling of being sufficiently sorry. Any of these can be a good thing or a matter of conviction. The moment it becomes Christ and something, it becomes Christ of no advantage. Ask of any teaching: does it leave Christ standing alone as my whole righteousness?

Obligated to keep the whole law. Verse 3 closes the escape route. The Judaizers were selling one item, and Paul says there is no such thing: circumcision signs you up to the whole law (James 2:10). The law is a single whole, and a man who takes hold of a corner of it has taken hold of all of it: every clause, every festival, every sacrifice, for life, without a single failure. Nobody mentioned that in the sales pitch. Paul reads them the whole contract, and no one has ever kept it.

On a Tuesday. Finish this sentence honestly: I am right with God because Christ died and rose for me, and because I... If anything comes after the and, cross it out. Then live today out of the first half alone, and do your good works as a thank you, not as a down payment.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Severed from Christ. This verse frightens people, and it should be handled with care, because the reader most likely to be holding it is not a Judaizer but a Christian who has had a bad year and has just read fallen away from grace and gone cold. So begin with what the sentence actually says, because the popular use of the phrase has almost nothing to do with it.

Not a scandal. In ordinary speech, to have fallen from grace means to have disgraced yourself: a scandal, a moral collapse, a public fall. Paul is not describing that at all. The people he is addressing have not fallen into sin. They have become more religious, not less. They are keeping a calendar and considering a rite, and they are doing it in order to please God more thoroughly. To fall from grace is not to fall into sin, as people often think, but to fall into law-righteousness: leaving the sphere of grace for the sphere of works.

Two changes of position. Both halves of the sentence describe a change of position, not of behaviour. Severed renders katargeō: to be rendered inoperative, cut off, separated, disconnected from any benefit. And Paul says who it applies to in the same breath: you who would be justified by the law. You cannot hold on to both. Justification here is acquittal: guilt removed and the believer counted right with God, though not made sinless on the spot (Romans 4:5). The only question is on what ground the verdict is given, and Paul allows only one. And fallen away is ekpiptō, falling out of grace as out of a place: you have stepped off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, and grace is where Christ does his work.

The lifeboat. Think of a man in a lifeboat who decides to swim alongside it, still holding the rope. He has not stopped believing in the boat. He has simply stopped being in it, and the boat is doing nothing for him while he is out there. Paul is not telling the Galatians that God has thrown them out. He is telling them what law-standing does: it does not add to Christ’s work, it replaces it, and there is no arrangement in which a man is partly justified by each.

Hold it beside verse 10. Six verses later, written to the same people in the same breath, Paul says: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view. The man who has just written verse 4 is confident about them. Which tells you exactly what verse 4 is for. It is not a verdict passed on the Galatians; it is the warning that will keep them from the thing described, and the warning works by being heard.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall from grace? Some take this verse to mean true believers can lose their salvation: Arminian Christians read it that way, holding that the Galatians were real believers who could forfeit their salvation by trusting in the law, and they are right that the warning is real and must not be blunted. Verdict: Paul is describing the meaning and consequence of seeking justification by law: it is a rejection of grace and Christ. Those who persist in it show they never truly rested on Christ (1 John 2:19). True believers may be confused and tempted, as the Galatians were, but God keeps his own (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29), and warnings like this one are among his means of keeping them. Those whom he justified he also glorified (Romans 8:30). Falling from grace here means abandoning the principle of grace, not a true believer being lost. That is why Paul can write verse 4 and verse 10 in the same breath.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sinning makes you fall from grace. Grace is for sinners. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

I am afraid this describes me. Does it? Ask what the verse actually describes: a person who is seeking to be justified by his own law-keeping and is at peace with that arrangement. Now ask whether that is you. If you are afraid because you know your record will not carry you, that fear is not the condition Paul is describing; it is the exact opposite of it. Nobody standing on his own performance is troubled by the news that performance will not do. A warning against a cliff is not a report that you have gone over it, and the people who read it most anxiously are almost always the ones furthest from the edge.

How would I know if I were trying to be justified by the law? Watch where your confidence goes when you think of standing before God. If you find yourself listing what you have done, how long you have been a Christian, how much you give, what you avoid, you are reaching for the rope instead of the boat. If you find yourself saying, nothing in my hands I bring, simply to the cross I cling, you are in grace. Most Christians drift between the two in a single week. The remedy is not to examine yourself harder but to look at Christ longer.

Grace has a name. What the verse requires is a change of footing, and it helps to see what the footing is. Grace is not a policy in heaven but Christ himself, given for us. Paul can say severed from Christ and fallen away from grace in one breath because they are the same loss: the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation (Titus 2:11), and it appeared in a person. The boat in the picture is the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (2:20), and his is the righteousness Paul wanted, not his own but that which comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9). So the way back is not more effort but less: stop asking whether you have done enough, look at what he has done, and stand there.

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For through the Spirit, by faith. Now Paul shows the other position. He has just said you to the ones seeking justification by law. Now he says we ourselves: the pronoun is emphatic in the Greek, drawing a line down the middle of the room. Paul is telling the Galatians which side of the line he stands on and inviting them back over it.

The hope of righteousness. Much of the sentence is about waiting. Eagerly wait is apekdechometha: to wait eagerly for a thing that is certainly coming and is not here yet. That is a striking word to use of righteousness, when Paul has spent three chapters insisting the believer is justified already. The hope of righteousness is the final verdict of acquittal at the judgement, the full and public revelation of our righteousness in Christ, and the day when we are finally and actually like him.

Righteous now, and waiting. Both are true, and holding them together is the whole balance of the Christian life. Believers are already justified (Romans 5:1): the verdict has been passed, and you are righteous in Christ now, today, with nothing outstanding. They wait confidently for that verdict to be publicly declared, and for the state that matches it, when the man you want to be and the man you are have at last become the same man. Every believer lives in the gap between those two, and the discomfort is not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

The hope has a face. The righteousness we wait for is not an abstract quality but a person. Christ Jesus became to us righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and the day the verdict is published is the day he appears: when Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4). That is why the waiting is eager rather than anxious. The believer is not waiting to find out whether his record will pass. He is waiting for the one who has already passed it for him, and when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

The legalist cannot wait. Waiting requires that the outcome be secure without your involvement, and a man whose standing depends on his own progress cannot afford to wait for anything; he has to be getting somewhere, visibly, or the whole structure wobbles. The gospel produces patient people because it has already settled the question they would otherwise spend their lives trying to answer.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. Then verse 6, a sentence that sums up a great deal of the New Testament. The first half is remarkable coming from Paul in this letter. He has fought circumcision for four chapters; you might expect him to say that being uncircumcised is what counts. He says neither does. Ethnic and religious markers are irrelevant to standing with God. The moment you make your uncircumcision a badge, you are playing the same game with the pieces reversed.

Faith working through love. Four words, and they have been fought over for centuries, so it is worth being exact. The verb is energeō: operating, energised, at work. Faith is the living thing, and love is faith at work. True faith is never idle; it shows itself in love. Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone. A faith that produces no love is not a faith that needs supplementing. It is a report of something that was never there.

In the flow. After the warning of verses 2–4, verses 5–6 give the positive picture in a single breath, and it holds the whole letter: the Spirit received by faith (3:2), righteousness as a gift (2:16), and sons who wait as heirs (4:7). Faith, hope and love all appear, with faith receiving, hope waiting and love working. And the closing phrase prepares the rest of the chapter: love will be the use of freedom (v. 13), the fulfilment of the law (v. 14) and the first fruit of the Spirit (v. 22).

Where Christians differ: faith working through love. Roman Catholic teaching has used this phrase to argue that we are justified by faith formed by love, so that love is part of the ground of justification; both sides agree that living faith always loves. Verdict: Paul says what counts is faith, and describes that faith as one that works through love. Love is the fruit of justifying faith, not part of its ground, and the grammar agrees: love is not what qualifies faith, it is what faith does. We are justified by faith alone, receiving Christ’s righteousness; the faith that receives Christ then works through love (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17; the Westminster Confession 11.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.2).

If love is the evidence, how much love is enough? That is the wrong question, and it is the question the Judaizers, with their law-keeping conditions, taught people to ask. Love is not the entrance fee; it is the sign of life. A newborn baby breathes weakly, but it breathes, and the doctor does not ask whether it breathes enough to be human. Look for direction, not quantity: is there a love for God and for his people that was not there before, and is it growing, however slowly? If it is, it is the Spirit’s work. If you are troubled by how little you love, bring that trouble to Christ, whose love for you does not depend on yours for him, and ask him to enlarge your heart.

On a Tuesday. Think of the one person in your home, work or church whom you find hardest to love. Do one concrete thing for their good this week, without telling anyone. That is not a way of earning God’s favour; it is faith, which already has God’s favour, getting to work.

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were running well. The metaphor is the stadium, and Paul uses it warmly. He is a coach watching a runner who had a good rhythm and a good line and was going to finish, and something happened.

Who hindered you from obeying the truth? The verb is enkoptō: to hinder, to block the way; in a race it is a runner cutting in across another’s lane. Someone tripped them up. So Paul is not describing a runner who got tired or lost heart. Somebody stepped in front of him. And obeying the truth means believing and living the gospel: for Paul the truth is something you do as well as something you hold.

Who got in front of you? That is a more useful diagnosis than it first appears, because Christians who have gone backwards usually blame themselves for a failure of stamina, and it is often not that at all. Somebody cut in. A teacher, a book, a friend with strong opinions, a season under a ministry that made the gospel conditional. The question Paul asks is worth asking honestly of any cooled faith: not, why did I run out of energy?, but, who got in front of me, and when? Very often there is a date.

This persuasion is not from him who calls you. Verse 8 is quiet and decisive. He does not say the teaching is unhelpful, or unbalanced, or that its advocates mean well. He says God, who called them by grace, is not the source of this new teaching. And he identifies God carefully: as him who calls you, present tense, still calling. The argument is: you know the voice that called you, because you have heard it. This is not that voice.

A test for ordinary believers. Any believer can ask this, and it is more reliable than weighing arguments: does this teaching sound like the God who called you? Not, is it strict? God is often strict. But does it come to you the way he came to you? He came with a gift, to someone with nothing to offer, and the effect was relief. When a teaching arrives and its effect is that you feel measured, watched, and slightly behind, you may not be able to refute it. You can still recognise that it is not the voice that called you. My sheep hear my voice, Jesus said (John 10:27).

A little leaven leavens the whole lump. Then verse 9, a proverb. A pinch of sour dough goes into a large batch, and nothing appears to happen for hours, and then the whole mass has changed and there is no part of it that has not (1 Corinthians 5:6). Two things follow. First, quantity is irrelevant. The Judaizers were asking for one concession, and Paul’s point is that a gospel with a small condition attached is not mostly the gospel; given time, it is a different loaf entirely. Second, the change is invisible while it is happening. Nobody in a church that is losing the gospel can feel it going. The sermons remain biblical, the meetings continue, the language is unchanged, and what alters first is only the atmosphere: the quiet arrival of measurement into a room that used to be full of relief.

Leaven and the Lamb. Paul uses the same proverb in 1 Corinthians 5:6, and there he gives at once the reason leaven has no place in the church: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). At Passover Israel cleared every crumb of leaven from their houses and ate the lamb with unleavened bread, as a people leaving slavery (Exodus 12:15–20). The church is a house where the Lamb has already died. A gospel with a condition added is old leaven carried back into the house of the redeemed, and the issue is not fussiness about doctrine but loyalty to the one who was sacrificed.

How do I tell whether a teaching is leaven or just a different emphasis? Ask what it does to the gospel of free justification in Christ. Christians differ honestly on baptism, church government, the end times and much else, and those differences, important as they are, need not touch the heart. Leaven is different: it changes what makes a person right with God, or adds a condition to Christ, or quietly moves the weight from his work to yours. Ask: does this leave me resting wholly on Christ? Does it make grace more amazing or less? Does it fit with the plain teaching of Scripture, read as a whole? If a teaching makes Christ smaller and you larger, it is leaven, however small it looks.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confidence in the Lord. After the leaven, a surprise. Nothing in the letter prepares you for that sentence. He has called them foolish, bewitched, severed from Christ, and now he says he is confident about them, and where that confidence rests is stated with precision: in the Lord. Not in their good sense, of which he has seen little, nor in the strength of his own arguments. Paul trusts that God will bring them back.

How to hold on to someone who is drifting. That is how a Christian holds on to somebody who is drifting, and the alternatives are both bad. You can be confident in the person, which is optimism, and collapses on contact with facts. Or you can write them off, which feels like realism. Paul does neither. He tells them the worst honestly and then declares his expectation that God will keep them, which is the only ground on which anyone has ever been kept, including him.

Whoever he is. The singular is interesting: a particular man, evidently, whose name Paul may not know, or a way of saying each one of them. God will judge the false teacher, however important. Paul does not organise a campaign against him; he leaves him to God.

But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Verse 11 lets slip what was being said about Paul. Somebody in Galatia had been claiming that Paul himself taught circumcision when it suited him (perhaps pointing to Timothy, or to his past as a circumcising Pharisee), and therefore that the Galatians were only being asked to do what the apostle really wanted. Paul’s answer is not a denial but a piece of evidence: look at my life. Nobody stones a man for preaching what everybody already accepts. If so, why is he still persecuted by those who demand it? The scars are the argument.

The offense of the cross. And then the phrase that explains everything. The word is skandalon: in use, a stumbling block, the stone that trips a man, or the snare that catches him. What offends is not the suffering; the world has always admired a martyr. It is what the cross says about the person looking at it: that he could not be saved by any other means, that his religion and his decency contributed nothing, that he had to be rescued like a criminal. Add circumcision, or any other requirement, and the offence drains away instantly, because now there is something for the man to do, and human pride is satisfied. A religion you can contribute to is a religion the world will tolerate. A gospel nobody is annoyed by has usually been adjusted.

The stone in Zion. The word skandalon has a history Paul knew well. Isaiah spoke of a stone God would lay in Zion, and Paul applies it to Christ: behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame (Romans 9:33; compare 1 Peter 2:6–8). So the offence of the cross is finally the offence of a person. The Messiah Israel expected would not hang on a tree under God’s curse (3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23), yet this one did, and he did it in the sinner’s place. The stone men trip over is the same stone on which a believer stands and is never put to shame.

What is the offence of the cross today? Much the same as then, though it wears modern clothes. People are offended to be told that they are sinners who cannot save themselves; that decent, religious and kind people need a Saviour as much as criminals do; that there is only one way to God, through a crucified Jew; and that their good works earn nothing. People will happily admire Jesus as a teacher or example. What they resist is being told they needed him to die for them. Do not soften those points to be liked. Explain them gently, with tears if need be, but leave the offence where God put it, because it is the same message that saves.

I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves! Verse 12 reads as a crude outburst until you know the region. Across Asia Minor, with its chief shrine at Pessinus in Galatia itself, the mother goddess Cybele was served by priests who castrated themselves in ecstatic worship. Readers in the region knew that cult. So Paul is not merely being coarse. He is saying: you want to cut flesh to be accepted by God? Then you already know what that religion looks like, because it is on your own doorstep. If the knife is the mechanism, why stop where Moses stopped? Take it to the shrine and finish the job, and become like pagan priests. It shows the Galatians that the road they are on ends somewhere they have already seen.

Is strong language ever right for me? Rarely, and with great care. Paul was an apostle writing under inspiration about wolves who were destroying a flock he had founded, and even here his target is the teachers, not the confused sheep. Elsewhere Scripture tells us to let no corrupting talk come out of our mouths (Ephesians 4:29) and to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25). If you find you enjoy biting words, that is a sign to stop. Keep your strongest language for the dangers that most threaten souls, and even then speak it with sorrow, never with relish, and never against the people who are being misled.

For worship. The offence of the cross is the glory of God in its plainest form. It says that we could do nothing and that God did everything; that the Judge stepped down from the bench and took the sentence himself; that the righteous died for the unrighteous to bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). Men have spent centuries trying to sand the rough edge off that beam, and it is the rough edge that saves. To the proud it is a stumbling block and folly, but to those who are called it is Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele in that region, who castrated themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Galatians were called to freedom, but they must not use it as an opening for the flesh; through love they are to serve one another (v. 13). The whole law is fulfilled in one command, to love your neighbour as yourself (v. 14). If they bite and devour one another, they will be consumed by each other (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

For the believer the law’s moral demands are not abolished but fulfilled, from a different source. The law commands from outside and leaves the sinner exposed; love, produced by the Spirit, moves from within. This is the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33): not a different law, but the same law, obeyed by a heart that loves the God who gave everything, not as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also answers the charge, as old as the gospel, that free grace leads to licence. Paul admits the danger and still refuses the remedy his opponents wanted. It is easy to answer licence with law, and it undoes everything. And v. 15 shows how a religion of performance destroys a congregation: once standing is earned, every other believer becomes a measurement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy. The community the Judaizers claimed to be perfecting by the law was tearing itself apart, and vv. 13–14 name the one thing that binds a church as rules never can.

Now: A church that makes the Christian life mainly about visible markers produces pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, and division. The cure v. 13 offers is not a new rule but service, given concretely to the person you still disagree with.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you were called to freedom, brothers. Paul returns to where the chapter began. God called them into freedom. And now he faces the objection that has been waiting since verse 1: if people are genuinely free, what is to stop them doing as they like?

An opportunity for the flesh. He does not dodge it. The word aphormē was used in war for a base of operations, the staging ground for an assault, and so for any opening or pretext. The flesh is sinful human nature, and Paul names the danger plainly: your liberty can be occupied. The flesh will move into the space grace has cleared and use it as a forward position, and the reasoning it offers is always theologically impeccable. I am not under law. God has forgiven this already. Grace is greater than my sin. Every one of those sentences is true, and all three have been used to excuse things that wrecked a family.

No fence, but love. Paul’s answer to that objection, which every preacher of grace meets (Romans 6:1), is not the obvious remedy, a fence: some law reintroduced at the end of the letter to keep freedom in bounds.
