Having spent four chapters demolishing law as the ground of standing, he will not smuggle it back as the ground of behaviour. His answer to the flesh is not restriction. It is love.

Serve one another. And the verb is deliberately shocking: douleuete, from douleuō, to be a slave, the root of doulos. Be slaves to one another. Paul has spent the whole letter tearing the yoke off their shoulders, and the first thing he tells them to do with their freedom is to put themselves at each other’s disposal. True freedom is freedom to love.

Free lord, dutiful servant. That is the paradox at the centre of Christian liberty, and Luther put it exactly: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. The two are not in tension, because the slavery Paul has been fighting is slavery to a system in order to be accepted, and this is bondage to a person because you already are. One is how you try to get standing. The other is what standing does.

Fulfilled in one word. Verse 14 quotes Leviticus 19:18 (compare Romans 13:8–10), and a reader may be puzzled. Paul has said the believer is not under the law, and here he quotes Leviticus. The resolution is in the verb. He does not say the law is summarised in love, as if love were a convenient abridgement. He says it is fulfilled: filled full, brought to its intended completion. The law was never an arbitrary list; every commandment in it was describing what love looks like when it meets a particular situation. Do not steal is love meeting your neighbour’s property. Do not bear false witness is love meeting his reputation. So a man who genuinely loves is not evading the law. He is doing the thing the law was written to produce, not to be justified, but as its fruit, in the way that a man who loves his wife does not need a rule against reading her letters.

A higher standard, not a lower one. So the standard is higher and not lower. A code can be satisfied; you can reach the end of a list. As yourself has no end to reach. Nobody has ever gone to bed having loved his neighbour as much as he instinctively looks after himself.

Fulfilled first in him. Before love fulfils the law in us, it fulfilled it in Christ. He came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17), and he is the one man who ever loved his neighbour as himself, and then more than himself: he loved his Father with all his heart, and his enemies all the way to the cross (Romans 5:8). So when Paul says the whole law is fulfilled in love, he is describing a life that has been lived once in full. And that fulfilment reaches us through him: God condemned sin in the flesh in his Son, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk according to the Spirit (Romans 8:3–4). Our love is not a new way of earning. It is his obedience working itself out in his people.

If love fulfils the law, can a kind person fulfil it without Christ? Not in the way the law means. Many unbelievers are kinder than many Christians, and that is a real gift of God’s common goodness. But the law’s first command is to love God with all your heart (Matthew 22:37–40), and its second asks for love as yourself, every day, from the heart, with no gaps. Nobody has managed even the second, which is why the kind person needs Christ as much as the cruel one does. And this frees the religious person too: the love the law asks for is not something either of us generates. Christ fulfilled it for us, and the Spirit grows it in us (v. 22).

So does the law still bind the believer? If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law (v. 18) means not under it as a covenant of works, a curse or the ground of our standing. It does not mean that God’s moral will has lapsed. The law still describes what love does: this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments (1 John 5:3). Love fulfils the law; it does not abolish it. The Spirit-led Christian does not need the law to make him acceptable, but he is glad of it as a description of the life the Spirit is producing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love replaces the commandments, so that we decide what love means. Love is defined by the commandments (Romans 13:9). A person who says, I am doing the loving thing, while breaking God’s commands about marriage, honesty or life, has redefined love to suit himself.

Does loving my neighbour as myself mean I must first learn to love myself? No. The command assumes that we already care for ourselves: we feed ourselves, protect ourselves, think about our own interests without being told to (Ephesians 5:29). It takes that instinct as the measure and turns it outward. The cure for a crushed sense of self is not self-love but being loved by God, which frees you to stop looking inward at all. And who is my neighbour? Jesus answered that with a Samaritan: whoever is in front of you and in need, even if he is not your kind (Luke 10:29–37).

On a Tuesday. Pick a specific person and a specific service: the washing-up nobody wants to do, the visit you keep postponing, the hour given to a lonely neighbour. Do it as one set free, not as one paying a debt. And when your love falls short, as it will, Christ’s perfect love stands in your place, and your poor service is accepted for his sake.

parallels.desc: you shall love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bite and devour. The three verbs are all taken from animals, and they escalate. Bite is what a cornered creature does: a snap, a wound, not fatal. Devour is eating, taking a part of the other. Consumed, in the next clause, is the end of the process: nothing left. Paul is describing a sequence, like wild animals fighting, and he is describing it in a church.

An argument about holiness. Paul’s if suggests that the Galatian congregations were already tearing each other apart, and what they were fighting over was how to be holy. That is not an irony but a mechanism, and it is still a common way for a good church to destroy itself.

How it works. Once standing before God is tied to performance, every other believer in the room becomes a measurement. If he keeps more than I do, he is a threat, and I must find the flaw that explains him. If he keeps less, he is a reassurance, and I need him to stay where he is. Neither of those is love, and both feel like discernment. Add a genuine doctrinal disagreement, and it all gains a righteous vocabulary, so that people who are defending their own standing believe they are contending for the truth.

Consumed by one another. He does not say the strong will eat the weak. He says everyone loses. The party that prevails is left holding a smaller, colder, more suspicious congregation than the one it was fighting for.

One for whom Christ died. Paul gives the deepest reason against devouring a brother in another letter: do not destroy the one for whom Christ died (Romans 14:15; compare 1 Corinthians 8:11–12). The believer across the room is not a rival to be measured. He is someone the Son of God loved enough to die for, and to wound him is to sin against Christ. Every bite in a church fight lands on a body that belongs to Christ.

What do you want to be true? Two practical things follow. The first is a test for a disagreement you are currently inside: ask what you want to be true about the other person. If you find you would be disappointed to discover he was right, or that his motives were good, then whatever the merits of your case, you are biting. The verse does not ask whether your position is correct. Paul obviously thought his was.

The cure is service. Second, the cure, which is in the verse before. Paul does not answer biting with a rule against biting; he has just said, through love serve one another. The specific antidote to devouring a brother is serving him: deliberately, in some concrete way, while you still disagree with him. It is very hard to keep eating a man you are carrying something for. Pressing anger produces strife (Proverbs 30:33), and quarrels come from the passions at war within you (James 4:1–2); service starves them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean truth does not matter. Paul fights hard for it in this letter. It means believers must not attack each other with cruelty. You can contend for the faith without devouring the brother who is confused about it.

My church is already in a fight. What should I do? First, refuse to add to it: no gossip, no forwarding of messages, no recruiting to a side, no conversations about people that you would not have with them present. Second, if you have a grievance, take it directly and privately to the person concerned, and then if needed to the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). Third, pray for those you disagree with, by name, asking God to bless them. Fourth, look for a way to serve someone on the other side. And if the issue is a real matter of the gospel, speak plainly but without contempt. A church can survive disagreement; it rarely survives malice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells the Galatians to walk by the Spirit, and they will not carry out the desires of the flesh, for the two are at war within them; those led by the Spirit are not under the law (vv. 16–18). The works of the flesh are plain, and those who live by them will not inherit the kingdom of God (vv. 19–21). The Spirit grows a very different harvest, against which there is no law (vv. 22–23). Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh, so they are to keep in step with the Spirit, without conceit, provoking or envy (vv. 24–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Putting the Flesh to Death, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

The Christian life has two sides: putting the flesh to death, which v. 24 states as already done to every believer, and coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The first applies to daily life what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the second is the Spirit’s fruit. The believer takes part in both by faith.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image of crucifixion, which was slow: the flesh in a believer is mortally wounded and its outcome settled, but it is still loud, and will be until the body dies. Verse 21 must be read with the same care. Scripture never confuses a man who falls into a ditch with a man who lives in it, and the ache that makes a tender conscience afraid of that verse is evidence that it is not describing him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that the law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third. The middle of Paul’s list of the works of the flesh (v. 20) described what was happening in their own congregations. And in v. 25, keep in step is built on the same root as the elementary principles that had them in bondage (4:3, 9): Paul does not tell them to stop marching, but tells them who sets the pace now.

Now: Walking by the Spirit (v. 16) is concrete rather than mystical: asking for his help before the difficult conversation rather than after it, staying in the word where he speaks, and taking the small next step of obedience you would rather not have noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say, walk by the Spirit. Here is Paul’s whole answer to the problem of Christian behaviour, and it is neither a law nor a technique. It is the answer to both legalism and licence. Walk is peripateite, from peripateō, a present imperative: go on walking, the ordinary word for how a man conducts his daily life, step by step. Not soar, not fight, not achieve: walk. By the Spirit means depending on him, following his lead, relying on his power.

In the flow. Verse 13 left a question hanging: if the law is not the fence, what keeps freedom from becoming licence? Verse 16 answers it. The Spirit is the letter’s great theme: the Galatians received him by faith, not by works of the law (3:2), and Paul asked them whether, having begun by the Spirit, they would now be perfected by the flesh (3:3). Now he shows that the Spirit who began the Christian life is also the one who carries it on.

You will not gratify. This is a promise, not a command. The Greek carries a strong double negative: you will certainly not carry out the flesh’s desires. Paul is not saying the desires will stop; he is saying they will not be carried out. And the order here is the whole strategy of Christian holiness. He does not say, stop gratifying the flesh and then you will be able to walk by the Spirit. He says walk, and the other will follow. Sin is displaced far more often than it is defeated by direct assault, because a man staring at his temptation and gritting his teeth is still looking at it.

What the flesh is. Flesh here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God: the mind that does not submit to God’s law, and cannot (Romans 8:7). It is not the body as such: several of the works of the flesh in vv. 19–21, like envy and rivalry, have nothing to do with the body.

Against the Spirit. Verse 17 is honest about the cost. This is a war within every believer, a settled state of war, and it should be said plainly, because young Christians often assume the conflict is evidence that something went wrong at their conversion. It is the reverse. Before conversion there was no war of this kind; conscience might protest (Romans 2:15), but the flesh had the field. The fight itself is a sign of life: there is now something in you that wants what God wants, and it will not be quiet.

Opposed to each other. Paul does not mean the believer is helpless. He means the two are locked in conflict, so that neither side gets its way unopposed. When the believer wants to do good, the flesh resists; when the flesh wants its way, the Spirit resists. You cannot simply drift into holiness, and you cannot sin with a quiet heart either. The conflict is real, but verse 16 has already promised which side prevails when we walk by the Spirit. That is the price of having been rescued, and it will last as long as this life does.

What walking by the Spirit looks like. It is not a mystical state or waiting for a feeling. In practice it means: depending on the Spirit consciously, asking him for help rather than relying on willpower (Luke 11:13); filling the mind with his word, since the Spirit leads through what he has written, not apart from it (Colossians 3:16, compared with Ephesians 5:18); saying no to the flesh at the first stirring, not after a long negotiation (Romans 8:13); saying yes to the next step of obedience he shows you, even small ones; and staying close to God’s people and the means of grace (the word, prayer and the Lord’s Supper), where he works. Walking is step by step: no single great experience settles it, but daily, ordinary dependence does.

Led by the Spirit. Then verse 18 puts the alternative to the law where the chapter has been heading all along. Led is agō, as in Romans 8:14, and note the passive: led. The Judaizers offered a code to be kept; Paul offers a person to be followed. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law’s condemnation, nor under it as a system of control; they fulfil it from within. And a code, however holy, can only stand outside you and tell you what to do. The Spirit is inside, and he does not merely require the life. He produces it.

The Spirit who led the Son. The Spirit who leads us is the Spirit of God’s Son, sent into our hearts (4:6), and he has led this way before. Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, tempted by the devil (Luke 4:1–2). Where Adam and Israel gave way to their desires, he refused every one. The same Spirit now leads Christ’s brothers through the same war. He is not leading us into a fight whose outcome is uncertain. He is leading us behind a captain who has already won it, and making us like him on the way.

Does being led by the Spirit mean following inner voices and impressions? Not in the sense many people mean. In Romans 8:14 and here, being led by the Spirit is about the direction of a life, the Spirit leading God’s children away from the flesh and toward holiness, not a stream of private messages about which job to take. The Spirit speaks in Scripture, which he inspired and which is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). He does work in our hearts: convicting, comforting, bringing his word to mind, giving wisdom. But an impression is never to be treated as a new word from God, and anything that contradicts Scripture is not his leading. Test every prompting by the Bible. Christians whose churches expect prophetic words today see some of this differently, and they are brothers and sisters; they too agree that every such word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some, especially in parts of the holiness tradition, teach that believers can reach a state where the flesh is eradicated and they no longer sin, and they are moved by a right hunger for holiness. Verdict: Paul describes an ongoing war between flesh and Spirit in the believer. The Spirit gives real victory, and believers grow in holiness, but the flesh is not destroyed until glory (Romans 7:14–25; 1 John 1:8; the Westminster Confession 13.2; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 13.2). The Christian life is a fight, not a state of sinless rest.

On a Tuesday. When you feel the pull of the flesh today, stop and pray: Holy Spirit, lead me. Then do not stand there arguing with the temptation. Turn your attention to something the Spirit loves: a verse you know, a person you can serve, a task you have been given. Walk away from the ditch by walking toward something.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the works of the flesh are evident. Evident is phanera: obvious, plain, on the surface. And works, erga: what the flesh produces. It is the same word Paul has used all through the letter for works of the law, and the echo is deliberate. Law-keeping and licence look like opposites, and Paul files them under the same heading, because both are things a man produces out of his own resources. Only the products differ. Fifteen are listed, in four groups. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add adultery at the start and murders after envy; the earliest do not, so most modern Bibles omit them.

Sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for all sex outside marriage. Impurity (akatharsia) is moral uncleanness. Sensuality (aselgeia) is open, shameless indulgence: not merely indulgence, but indulgence that has stopped caring who sees.

Idolatry, sorcery. Then religion goes wrong. Sorcery translates pharmakeia, from which we get pharmacy: the ancient trade of potions, spells and drugs used to bend outcomes, common across the ancient world. Both belong on a list of fleshly works because both are attempts to manage the divine: an idol is a god you can locate, and a spell is a result you can arrange.

Enmity, strife, jealousy. And then the long middle, which is where the reader should slow down. Eight sins of relationships, the largest group: enmity (hostility), strife (quarrelling), jealousy, fits of anger (outbursts of rage), rivalries (selfish ambition), dissensions (splits), divisions (factions, haireseis), envy. More than half the catalogue, and every one of them thrives in a church meeting as easily as in a tavern. These were tearing the Galatian churches apart (v. 15), and Paul has put the sins of the respectable at the centre of his list. A congregation that would be horrified by verse 19 will often carry verse 20 as its ordinary weather.

Drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. Last come sins of excess: orgies (kōmoi) were the drunken processions that ended pagan festivals. And the list is not complete. Paul is not writing a legal code but a portrait, and nobody can plead that his particular version is not itemised.

Will not inherit the kingdom. Few passages disturb tender consciences more. A believer reads the list, finds himself in it, most likely in the middle section, and concludes that the door has closed. So read the verb carefully. Do is prassō, practise, in the present tense: those who go on doing them, whose lives are characterised by them, who have made their peace with them. Not the believer who falls and repents, but the one who continues in them without repentance (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). There is a world of difference between a man who falls into a ditch and a man who lives in it, and Scripture never confuses them.

The morning after. The question is what you do the morning after. Not whether you sinned: every believer does. Whether the sin still grieves you, and whether you take it to Christ. A man in whom the Spirit lives cannot sin comfortably. The very ache that makes you afraid of this verse is the evidence the verse is not about you, and the blood of Jesus cleanses the one who brings it to him.

Heirs through the Son. The key word is inherit. In this letter nobody earns an inheritance; it comes by being a son, and sonship comes through Christ (4:4–7). The works of the flesh are the life of someone who has never been adopted, and the warning is that such a life has no share in the estate. But the same Son who won the inheritance gives his people the Spirit who cries Abba, Father in their hearts (4:6), and that Spirit makes war on every item on this list.

I keep falling into the same sin, a sexual one. Am I one of those who practise it? The question to ask is not whether you have fallen again, but which side you are on in the fight. Are you at peace with it, defending it, planning for it? Or do you hate it, confess it, and keep fighting it, even after many defeats? The second is not the life Paul condemns; it is the war of verse 17. But do not settle for endless defeat. Bring it into the light with a mature Christian friend or pastor (James 5:16). Remove what feeds it: devices, places, habits. Ask for help, practical and spiritual. And each time you fall, go straight back to Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7, 9).

Is it not harsh to shut people out of God’s kingdom for envy or drunkenness? Only if we think of the kingdom as a club with a fee. The kingdom of God is the place where God is king and love reigns completely. A heart that is set on these things, and will not let them go, does not want that kingdom; it wants itself, and heaven would be unbearable to it. And the list will not let the religious person feel safe either, because jealousy, rivalry and factions sit beside drunkenness and orgies. The holy God takes every one of these seriously enough to judge it, and seriously enough to have borne it himself in his Son. No one who comes to Christ is turned away (John 6:37), and the list in Corinthians ends with such were some of you.

Is it sorcery to take medicine? No. The word described magic, potions and drugs used to manipulate spiritual powers, often with occult practices attached. Medicine used to heal is a gift of God; Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. What the verse condemns today includes occult practices like fortune-telling, spells and seeking spirits, and the misuse of drugs to escape or to alter the mind in the way drunkenness does.
verseByVerse.note: “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the fruit of the Spirit. Note the change of word before anything else. The flesh has works; the Spirit has fruit. Works are manufactured: you decide, you exert, you produce. Fruit is grown, and it is grown by something the branch does not do. No apple was ever produced by an apple tree straining. Fruit grows naturally from life; the Spirit produces it as we abide in Christ (John 15:4–5).

One fruit, not nine. And note the singular. Not fruits, nine of them, to be collected like badges. One harvest with many flavours, one fruit with nine facets: a single character, which is finally the character of Christ himself, being formed in a person (4:19). The works of the flesh are many and fragmented; the fruit of the Spirit is one, a whole character. You do not choose patience this year and gentleness next.

Is love. Love heads the list, as it must, since verse 14 has just said the whole law is fulfilled in it. Agapē is self-giving love, the love that seeks another’s good at its own cost. It comes first and is the root of the rest (1 Corinthians 13): joy is love rejoicing, peace is love resting, patience is love waiting, and so on down the list.

Joy, peace. Joy (chara) is gladness in God, and the New Testament’s joy is not the same thing as cheerfulness of temperament; it survives circumstances that ruin cheerfulness, because its ground is outside them. Peace (eirēnē) is wholeness: first peace with God, and then, as a consequence, the inward rest of a man who has stopped negotiating his standing, and harmony with others.

Patience, kindness, goodness. Patience is makrothymia, literally long-tempered: long-suffering, a long fuse, specifically with people, bearing with them. It is the word used of God’s forbearance with us. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is gracious tenderness, not mere politeness but active usefulness to somebody. Goodness (agathōsynē) is active moral excellence and generosity: moral substance, the quality of a man who is the same when nobody is checking.

Faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Faithfulness (pistis) is reliability and loyalty: being where you said you would be, keeping your word when it costs. Gentleness is prautēs, meekness, and it is not weakness; in Greek it could be used of a powerful horse that had been broken to the bridle, so it is strength under control. And self-control (enkrateia), mastery over desires, comes last, which is a striking thing to find on a list of things the Spirit produces, since it is the one every self-help programme in the world sells. Paul says it is a fruit. You do not generate it. You receive it, and then you use it.

Against such things there is no law. A dry piece of understatement, and it lands the whole argument of the chapter. No law forbids these. The Judaizers were afraid that grace would produce lawlessness. Paul says: look at what the Spirit actually produces, and then find me the legislature that would want to prohibit any of it. There is no statute against being patient. The law was always aiming at this, and the Spirit is producing it without the law’s help.

How is the fruit of the Spirit different from the gifts of the Spirit? The fruit is character, the same in every believer and growing for a lifetime. The gifts are abilities for service, distributed differently, as the Spirit apportions to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). The fruit matters more. Paul says that without love the greatest gifts are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2), and Jesus warns of people who prophesied and cast out demons in his name and were never his (Matthew 7:22–23). A church should prize holiness above gifting.

I see almost none of this in myself. Have I got the Spirit at all? This list is often used to wound, so three things should be said. First, fruit is slow, and it is seasonal, and nobody digs up a tree in March to check. Second, you are the worst-placed person in the world to assess it: ask the people who live with you, who will almost always report growth the man himself cannot see. And third, look at what the sentence does not say. It does not say the fruit of the diligent Christian. It says the fruit of the Spirit, and he is not slow, and he is not uncertain of the outcome, and the growing was never your department.

If I cannot produce the fruit, what do I actually do? You stay connected to the vine, and you cooperate with the gardener. Abide in Christ by trusting him and staying in his word (John 15:7). Pray specifically for the fruit you lack. Put yourself where growth happens: the preaching of the word, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers. Pull up weeds when you see them, by confessing and turning from sin. And when an opportunity comes to exercise patience or kindness, take it, trusting the Spirit to give what he asks. Effort is not excluded; it is the effort of a branch staying in the vine, not of a branch trying to grow apples by itself.

For worship. Read the nine words again and you will see a face. Love that went to the cross; joy set before him that carried him through it; peace he left to his friends on the night he was betrayed; patience with slow disciples; kindness to lepers and children; goodness that no one could convict of sin; faithfulness to his Father to the end; gentleness that would not break a bruised reed; self-control at his arrest and before Pilate, when twelve legions of angels were a word away. The Spirit is making us like him. What God began in Christ he is growing in us, and one day the harvest will be complete, and the Son will be the firstborn among many brothers.
verseByVerse.note: “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who belong to Christ Jesus. That is, all true believers. Not unusually consecrated Christians: everyone who is his.

Have crucified the flesh. The tense is the key: have crucified, a past action, complete. Paul is not issuing an instruction here. He is stating what happened to every Christian, and stating it as a fact about them before it is a duty for them. United to Christ in his death, believers have put the flesh to death (2:20; Romans 6:6). At conversion they turned decisively against their sinful nature.

If it is dead, what has been fighting? This raises the obvious difficulty, and it is worth putting bluntly. Seven verses earlier Paul described a war going on inside the believer that keeps him from doing what he wants. Now he says the flesh has been crucified. If it is dead, what exactly has been fighting? The answer is in the image itself, and it is one of the most useful things in the chapter. Crucifixion was not a quick death. That was the point of it: the method was meant to be slow: a man nailed to a beam could take hours or even days to die, and for the whole of that time he was mortally wounded, fixed in place, going nowhere, and still perfectly capable of shouting at people. Crucifixion was slow, painful and final. He was finished. He was not yet silent.

The noise of a dying man. That is the condition of the flesh in a believer. The old life has received a wound it will not survive; its authority is broken, it has been condemned, and its outcome is settled. But it is still audible, and it will go on being audible until the day the body dies. So the voice you hear on a bad Thursday is real, and it is loud, and it is not evidence that nothing happened to you. It is the noise of something that has been executed and has not yet stopped.

When did this happen? Paul has already told us: I have been crucified with Christ (2:20). It happened at the cross, and it became yours when you were united to him by faith. Which is why the sentence begins where it does: those who belong to Christ Jesus.

Relief in the order. If crucifying the flesh were your project, every failure would mean starting again. Because it is Christ’s finished work applied to you, your failures are the noise of a dying man rather than the recovery of a victorious one. You are not trying to kill the flesh from scratch. You are refusing to take orders from something that is already condemned. And so believers continue to put it to death daily (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5): not to make the execution happen, but because it has.

How do I put the flesh to death in practice? Starve it and refuse it. Starve it by cutting off what feeds it: if a certain website, friendship, habit or late-night hour regularly leads you into sin, remove it, however drastic that seems (Matthew 5:29–30; Romans 13:14). Refuse it by saying no at the first stirring, and saying it in Christ’s name: this is not who I am now. Replace it with the opposite good: generosity for greed, thanksgiving for complaining, service for envy. And do it all by the Spirit (Romans 8:13), in prayer, in the company of other believers, and in the confidence that the flesh has already lost.

On a Tuesday. When the old voice shouts today, answer it out loud if you need to: you were nailed to the cross with Christ; I do not take orders from you. Then do the next good thing.

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we live by the Spirit. The if is not a doubt. The sentence takes the thing as true: since we live by the Spirit, as we do. The Spirit gives life to all believers: he is the one by whom they were born again and given a new heart that wants God (John 3:5–6; Ezekiel 36:26). The shape of the argument is the shape of all New Testament ethics: this is what you are, therefore be it. He never asks a Christian to become something in order to qualify. He tells him what he is and then asks him to live like it.

Keep in step. Then a change of verb that is easy to miss but is the whole point. In verse 16 the word was walk, the ordinary word for daily conduct. Here Paul uses a different one: stoichōmen, from stoicheō, to stand in line, a word that could be used of keeping rank, marching in line, holding formation, matching the step of the man beside you. Follow the Spirit’s lead step by step, in daily obedience, as soldiers follow the one ahead.

The word turned round. That verb is built on the same root as stoicheia, the word Paul used twice in chapter 4 for the elementary principles that had the Galatians in bondage (4:3, 9). He takes the word for the thing that enslaved them and turns it into the word for walking free with the Spirit. The Galatians had marched to a calendar and a code before. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

A different formation. So Christian freedom is not the absence of order but a different formation, with two differences. Under the law you kept step with a system that could not help you keep it; now you keep step with a person who is himself the power to do it. And under the law the marching was how you tried to get your standing; now it is what your standing produces.

Where the Spirit marches. Keeping in step with the Spirit always brings a man to the same place, because the Spirit’s whole work is to glorify Christ: he will take what is mine and declare it to you, Jesus said (John 16:14). The old march was set by the elementary principles; the new one is set by the Spirit of the Son who bought us out of them (4:4–6).

Ahead or behind. Keep in step names two ways of getting it wrong. You can march ahead of him: running on your own energy, taking initiatives you were never given, driving a ministry or a decision at a pace nothing has been given to sustain, and calling the exhaustion faithfulness. Or you can lag behind: hearing the small thing you should do, agreeing with it, and not doing it, until the agreeing has quietly become a substitute for the doing. Neither looks like rebellion; both are simply being out of step, and the correction is the same: find where he actually is, and be there. He sets the pace at something a real person can sustain over a whole life, which is exactly what the law never did.

How do I know where the Spirit is leading in a decision, like a job or a move? Begin with what he has already said. Scripture settles the moral boundaries: if an option requires sin, it is not his leading. Within those boundaries, the Spirit leads by giving wisdom, so ask for it (James 1:5), think carefully, weigh your gifts and responsibilities, consider how each option affects your love for God, your family and your church, and seek counsel from mature believers (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God’s providence with the outcome. You do not need a sign or an inner voice. Keeping in step is mostly about the next obedient step, and a wise decision made in faith is a step in step.
verseByVerse.note: “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not become conceited. A small verse doing a large job: it links the fruit of the Spirit to chapter 6’s instructions about restoring a fallen brother, and it brings the whole soaring argument down onto how you feel about the Christian three seats away. The root is named first. Conceited translates kenodoxoi, from kenodoxos: empty-glory, vainglory, glory with nothing inside it. Not glory that is deserved, and not glory that is even real; a reputation held up by air, often pride in spiritual achievements. And the moment a man’s significance depends on something that hollow, he cannot leave other people alone, because the only way to maintain a comparative standing is comparatively.

Provoking one another. So the two symptoms follow, and Paul pairs them because they are the same disease at different altitudes. Provoking is prokaleomai: challenging, as to a fight. It is what the man ahead does: needling, making sure the gap is felt.

Envying one another. Envying is what the man behind does: resenting, watching, quietly hoping for a stumble. They look like opposites and they are identical: both are a person whose eyes are fixed on another believer rather than on Christ, and whose sense of himself is being calculated from the difference. The Spirit frees us from both.

The flicker. Think of the believer whose ministry, family or reputation is flourishing most visibly in your circle, and what happens in you when good news about him is announced. A flicker of something before the congratulation catches up is not a trivial fault of temperament. It is verse 26 with your name on it, and Paul puts it directly after the fruit of the Spirit for that reason: envy cannot coexist with love, joy and peace, because it needs somebody else to have less. And the cure is not to try harder to be pleased. It is to look somewhere else. Empty glory is only attractive while it is the best glory in view. Set beside the real thing, the Son of God who had glory in full, laid it down, took the form of a slave and was executed for people who were arguing about rank (Philippians 2:3–7), the competition in the third row loses its grip. He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

Is it wrong to admire another Christian, or want to be like them? No. Paul himself says, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), and Hebrews tells us to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). Admiration thanks God for another’s gifts and wants to grow in the same direction; envy resents them for having what you lack and is secretly glad when they stumble. The difference shows when they succeed: admiration rejoices, envy aches. If you notice the ache, confess it, and then thank God aloud for the very thing you envied. That is how the Spirit turns envy into love.

On a Tuesday. You were received with empty hands, so you have no standing to defend: neither look down nor look up enviously, but look to Christ. Then pick the person you most often compare yourself with, and pray for their blessing by name, specifically, for the thing you most envy or most look down on.

For worship. There is only one glory that is not empty, and it belongs to the one who emptied himself. He had no need to provoke anyone, because he had nothing to prove, and no reason to envy anyone, because all things were his. Beside him our little rivalries look like children quarrelling over pebbles at the foot of a mountain, and in him we have all the glory we will ever need.
